## [Four Gemini 4 Argon agents autonomously beat Minecraft's Ender Dragon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22319) ⭐️ 9.0/10

A team of four Gemini 4 Argon agents, each controlling a Minecraft player through the open-source Mineflayer library, autonomously defeated the Ender Dragon in a randomly generated survival world on Easy difficulty. Over 27 hours and 14 minutes they wrote 2,783 programs, coordinated via in-game chat and shared memory, and died 605 times, with no human assigning roles or writing game logic. This is claimed to be the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents using only the standard Mineflayer library, without pre-scouted seeds or human-written game-specific tools. It demonstrates long-horizon planning, self-programming, and multi-agent coordination sustained over thousands of dependent steps, capabilities that map directly onto complex real-world software engineering and enterprise tasks. The agents started from a randomly generated world on Easy difficulty and were allowed to plan, write, and debug every program themselves, with researchers only able to watch via a live dashboard and pause or stop the run. The paper also describes the team's strategies — dividing work, sharing learned knowledge, and recovering each other's dropped items — and explicitly discusses the limits of the result.

## [Claude Solves Origins of NIST ECDSA Curve Seeds](https://www.anthropic.com/research/ecdsa-curve-origins) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Anthropic's Frontier Red Team reported that Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 elliptic curve seeds, finding they were generated by the C library's lrand48 random-number generator seeded with a Unix timestamp rather than by SHA-1 hashing of memorable strings. One seed, B-163, remains unexplained. This resolves a decades-old cryptographic mystery that fueled speculation about a possible NSA backdoor in widely used elliptic curves, potentially restoring trust in standards like P-256 that underpin TLS and digital signatures. It also demonstrates frontier AI's ability to perform novel cryptographic research, raising questions about the widening capability gap between closed model providers and the public. The seeds were generated over a period of months using lrand48 seeded with Unix timestamps, meaning discarded candidate curves cannot be inspected, so a deliberate search for special properties remains theoretically possible but would require significant effort. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits no known pattern and may simply be a typo in the published value.

**Background**: NIST published the P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 elliptic curves in FIPS 186-2 in 2000, specifying they were generated randomly per ANSI X9.62 by hashing an arbitrary seed with SHA-1. The seeds themselves were never explained, leading cryptographers like Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes to call the controversy 'a riddle wrapped in an enigma' and prompting Filippo Valsorda to offer a bounty for solving them. ECDSA is widely used for digital signatures in TLS and other security protocols.

The article highlights that libjxl's maximum effort produces files 2–7% smaller for photos and ~25% smaller for screenshots and illustrations, but takes 9–46 seconds—50–180x longer than its default—while jixel achieves similar results in a couple of seconds. The discussion also underscores that codec maturity, encoding speed, and real-world visual fidelity matter as much as raw benchmark numbers. The article notes that libjxl's slow speed at efforts above 7 is mainly due to an iterative evaluation-optimization loop of the perceptual error metric Butteraugli, which tunes quantization weights. Community members also shared practical AVIF encoding settings using ffmpeg with yuva444p and alphaextract for transparency, and one commenter argued that AVIF can erase fine highlights on detailed images like an F1 car.

## [37-Year-Old OpenBSD Kernel Bug Exploited for Root Access](https://calif.io/research/big-fish) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Security firm Calif published a proof-of-concept exploit on October 16, 2026 that chains a roughly 37-year-old integer overflow in OpenBSD's original BSD-derived kernel code with a separate kernel flaw to gain root on OpenBSD 7.9. Both vulnerabilities have since been patched. The exploit bypasses OpenBSD's KARL kernel-address randomization along with SMAP and SMEP hardware protections, underscoring that even one of the most heavily audited codebases can harbor decades-old flaws. It highlights the limits of code review, fuzzing, and static analysis for finding certain classes of kernel bugs. The main bug is an integer overflow dating back about 37 years to the original BSD source code, which was chained with a kernel use-after-free to achieve local privilege escalation on OpenBSD 7.9. Interestingly, the flaw appears to have been accidentally fixed in NetBSD during a rewrite of that code in August 1999.

A local privilege escalation exploit lets an attacker with limited access gain root, the highest privilege level on the system.

<a id="item-9"></a>
## [RealtimeBench and TORSI: Evaluating LLM Agents Under a Live Clock](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20665) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces RealtimeBench, a benchmark of 180 tasks across six game types that evaluates LLM agents while games keep running during inference, plus TORSI, a two-timescale self-improvement method. Two rounds of TORSI raise the model Jev's average test score from 13.51 to 24.19 on a 0-100 progress scale, improving all six game types. Most agent benchmarks pause the environment while the model thinks, which hides a core weakness of LLM agents: reasoning and tool calls take time, so a correct action can arrive too late in a continuously changing world. RealtimeBench exposes this gap, and TORSI's results suggest that separating slow deliberation from fast execution could make agents viable in real-time settings such as live games, trading, or robotics. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when games keep running, illustrating a speed-versus-quality tradeoff. In TORSI, a slow teacher studies failures and tests corrections in paused games between attempts, then writes reusable instructions for a fast student that acts without teacher calls during gameplay, with validation scores deciding which updates are adopted; the instructions also improved three other models without retuning.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents are systems that use a large language model to perceive an environment, reason, and take actions such as calling tools or issuing game commands. Existing benchmarks like lmgame-Bench and TheAgentCompany typically let the agent think while the environment waits, which does not reflect real deployments where the world keeps changing. RealtimeBench instead keeps games running during inference, and TORSI borrows the idea of recursive self-improvement, where an AI system improves its own behavior, organizing learning and action across two timescales.

## [IneqAgent Combines LLM Reasoning and Symbolic Computation for Lean4 Inequality Proofs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20681) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers introduced IneqAgent, an agentic framework that integrates LLM reasoning with symbolic computation backends to prove inequalities in Lean4. Using DeepSeek-V4-Flash, it solves 175 of 186 problems (94.09%) across four benchmarks, achieving the highest overall success rate among evaluated methods. This work shows that combining LLM agents with exact symbolic computation can substantially advance automated theorem proving for inequalities, a domain where purely neural approaches often struggle with exactness. It could accelerate research in formal mathematics and AI-for-math, and the Lean-verified strengthenings of Dittert's conjecture and certification of the Holens-Djokovic inequality demonstrate real mathematical value beyond benchmark performance. The framework uses lemma-level Monte Carlo Tree Search to coordinate lemma construction, goal reformulation, and symbolic backend selection, with complementary sum-of-squares, Bernstein, and successive difference-substitution backends producing exact certificates for local Lean proof generation. Across four backbones, IneqAgent achieves higher success rates at low LLM inference cost thresholds than a Direct Agent baseline, with lower mean inference costs over each method's successful runs.

**Background**: Lean4 is a proof assistant and functional programming language based on the calculus of inductive constructions, used to formally verify mathematical proofs. IneqAgent combines these techniques so that an LLM proposes proof steps while symbolic backends generate exact, machine-checkable certificates.

## [Self-Improving Agent Grows Its Own DSL Without Ground Truth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20809) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.20809) presents a self-improving agent that uses two nested loops over a small exact domain-specific language (DSL) to achieve exact question answering without any reward, judge model, or answer key. The inner loop only answers questions when two independently written expressions agree on every record, while the outer loop discovers missing capabilities and authors new operators, admitting them only when an independent second implementation agrees and the result obeys a conservation law. This work challenges the dominant paradigm of keeping skills based on reward, judge approval, or compression, showing that exact correctness can be achieved through independent verification alone. It could influence future research in program synthesis, AI reasoning, and autonomous agent design, particularly for domains where answers must be exactly right, such as financial ledgers or clinical records. The admission rule rejects 138 of 138 buggy operator variants under an independent reference, even one written by a different model family, whereas admit-if-it-runs, self-consistency, and compression signals admit most of them. The inner loop roughly triples the answerable-question set, and the outer loop self-extends on disjoint starting sets, with the mechanism transferring across model families and two further domains (business-ledger and clinical-encounter QA), growing answerable sets more than tenfold and nearly twentyfold.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Program synthesis is the task of automatically constructing a program that satisfies a high-level specification, and a domain-specific language (DSL) is a small, specialized language with a restricted grammar and primitives tailored to a particular problem domain. Traditional DSL synthesis relies on manually designed grammars or expert-crafted operators, and self-improving agents typically keep new skills based on reward signals or judge models, which can be unreliable when exact correctness is required. This paper introduces operator induction, where the agent invents new DSL operators without ground truth, using independent verification and conservation laws as admission criteria.

On a benchmark of 220 prompts covering 11 categories of temporal constraints, TSG improves specification satisfaction accuracy over classifier-free guidance (CFG) by 9.5–20 percentage points across five models with minimal memory overhead. Its attention-steered forward pass produces a denoising direction that augments classifier-free guidance (CFG), though the approach is demonstrated on a specific benchmark and may depend on the quality of attention traces.

Researchers introduced Modality Self-Play (MSP), a training framework that uses proxy textual descriptions of unseen modalities as semantic bridges instead of real paired cross-modal data. The method achieves zero-shot modality composition, letting models trained on one real anchor modality reason over multiple modalities at inference time. Paired cross-modal datasets are expensive to curate and hard to scale, so removing this requirement could significantly lower the cost and broaden the accessibility of multimodal LLM development. MSP still relies on modality-text pairs, pretrained contrastively trained encoders, and modality-distribution bridge calibration; ablation studies show learned bridges improve alignment while anchor-supporting proxy descriptions enable effective cross-modal composition. It achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results on multiple multimodal benchmarks.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.21182) systematically studies latent chain-of-thought across 21 model-task configurations covering three training recipes, three reasoning tasks, and two backbones. ## [Adversarial Agents Cause Hidden Belief Collapse in Multi-Agent LLM Discussions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22138) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.22138) shows that in ten-agent factual discussions, just one or three adversarial agents asserting a plausible false answer can drive benign agents to privately adopt that false belief at rates of 44.8% and 60.5%, respectively, compared to only 0.6% without an attacker. Crucially, the study finds the reverse of typical human conformity: benign agents privately hold the false answer in 51.6% of exposed turns but publicly endorse it in only 19.7%, meaning much of the influence remains invisible in the discussion. This finding challenges the core assumption behind multi-agent LLM systems—that peer discussion and critique will catch individual errors—by showing that a minimal adversary can silently corrupt private beliefs even when public consensus appears stable. It has significant implications for AI safety, robustness, and the design of multi-agent debate or verification frameworks, since hidden belief collapse may go undetected by public-facing monitoring. The experiments span six models and three factual-QA datasets, probing each benign agent's private answer through a separate hidden call after each round. Agents that retain the true answer often fail to defend it, the false answer spreads among benign agents once adopted, and baseline knowledge does not predict robustness.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-agent LLM systems use groups of language-model agents that discuss, critique, and check one another, under the assumption that collective deliberation reduces individual errors. Prior conformity research in humans typically finds public agreement without private change, but this paper tests whether LLM agents exhibit the opposite pattern under adversarial pressure. Adversarial attacks on LLMs, such as prompt injection or false assertions, are a known risk, but their effect on private versus public beliefs in group settings has been underexplored.

## [VPD Decomposes Language Model Parameters into Interpretable Subcomponents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20748) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new paper introduces adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD), a method that breaks a language model's parameters into simple subcomponents which preserve the network's input-output behavior even when many subcomponents are ablated, including under adversarially chosen ablations. The authors demonstrate VPD on a 67M-parameter language model, decomposing its weight matrices into rank-1 subcomponents. This work addresses a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability: understanding how parameters and nonlinearities perform computations, not just how intermediate representations are structured. By enabling a new kind of 'circuit' analysis over parameter subcomponents, it could help researchers reverse-engineer the algorithms learned by neural networks and improve AI transparency. VPD optimizes for decompositions where only a small fraction of subcomponents are needed to account for the network's behavior on any given input, encouraging short and mechanistically faithful descriptions. The method was applied to a 67M-parameter model, and the authors note that more work is needed to deepen understanding of how networks use parameters to compute behavior.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Mechanistic interpretability is a subfield of explainable AI that aims to understand the internal workings of neural networks by analyzing their concrete structures, algorithms, and circuits. Prior work has uncovered substantial structure in intermediate representations, but little progress has been made in understanding how parameters and nonlinearities compute on those representations. VPD builds on this by decomposing parameters themselves, rather than only activations.

## [Initiative Vector Controls Turn-Taking in Full-Duplex Speech Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20763) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.20763) identifies a single late-layer residual-stream direction, called the 'initiative vector', in full-duplex spoken language models that governs whether the model takes the conversational floor at each frame. Extracted from the model's own conversations without training or annotation, this direction can be scaled during generation to shift the speech ratio from 6-12% to 42-61%, and a short reference recording is enough to transfer a specific speaker's turn-taking style to the model. This is a significant mechanistic interpretability result with practical implications: it shows conversational personality in full-duplex dialogue models is not frozen into the weights but is a readable, steerable direction that can be calibrated per person. It could enable personalized conversational AI that adapts its turn-taking behavior to individual users without retraining. The same direction both reads the turn-taking decision, anticipating speech onsets up to 800 ms ahead, and shifts it when scaled during generation, with effects consistent across conversations, model weights, and corpora. The transfer is reference-specific: swapping in another speaker's reference worsens the match in 93-98% of cases, whereas the best uniform dose is indistinguishable from no steering.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Full-duplex spoken language models listen and speak simultaneously, deciding at every frame whether to take the floor, which gives each model a fixed conversational personality. The residual stream is the pathway in Transformer-style networks along which representations are carried and updated across layers, and mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer such internal representations. Previous controls on turn-taking mostly acted from outside the model, and none had identified the internal quantity that sets how much the model speaks.

## [SHRED: Demonstration-Free Self-Play for Heterogeneous Traffic Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20866) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without any human driving demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that rely on demonstration-trained reference policies. This work suggests realistic, interactive traffic behavior can emerge purely from closed-loop self-play rather than costly large-scale human driving datasets, which could lower the data barrier for building traffic simulators used to train and evaluate autonomous vehicles. It also shows heterogeneous self-play improves planning, with especially large gains in interaction-heavy scenarios, pointing to a scalable paradigm for multi-agent autonomous driving research. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo, and SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Self-play is a reinforcement learning technique in which agents improve by interacting with copies or versions of themselves, famously used in games like AlphaGo. Heterogeneous-agent reinforcement learning deals with settings where agents have different dynamics, constraints, and objectives, unlike homogeneous settings that rely on parameter sharing. SHRED applies these ideas to traffic, where vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists behave fundamentally differently.

## [Screwtape Pipeline Evades Frontier AI Action Monitors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20941) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers present Screwtape, an adversarial transcript editing pipeline that converts real agent transcripts into attacks evading action-only monitors. Applied to 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts across 252 runs, it produced 35 verified attacks, six of which were confirmed by human review to also evade a held-out monitor from a frontier developer. This demonstrates that a red-teamer without access to a developer's infrastructure can find confirmed failures in that developer's production monitor, undermining safety claims that rely on action-only monitoring. Developers can use these attacks to patch blind spots, while evaluators can treat them as counterexamples to monitor-based safety assurances. The edited actions are never actually executed; instead, an LLM verifier rejects attacks inconsistent with the original transcript or below a severity bar, and the attacker iterates until the monitor no longer flags the edit. The authors expect more attacks when the pipeline runs inside the developer's infrastructure with frontier attacker models lacking refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor.

Monitor red-teaming is a systematic methodology for stress-testing these monitors against evasion tactics, often using benchmarks like SHADE-Arena to measure detection performance. Screwtape fits into this line of work by automatically generating adversarial transcripts that expose monitor weaknesses.

## [Paper Exposes Approval Vulnerabilities in AI Agent Step-Up Authorization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21063) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.21063) defines twelve attacks on the approval path of AI agents — including decoy recipients, amount cancellation, card padding, label spoofing, enrollment squatting and threshold splitting — and tests them against Google's Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), Microsoft's action-bound approval design, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) elicitation. The authors audit ten agent runtimes and propose ASU (Agent Step-Up), a trusted rendering gateway that renders approval cards from a canonical effect descriptor, signs the digest with a phone passkey, and executes only the stored call, with Tamarin proofs and 27,108 scripted trials plus 609 AgentDojo attack pairs validating the defense. As AI agents increasingly execute high-stakes actions like sending money, deleting files, or emailing outsiders, the approval prompt is often treated as a security second factor — but this paper shows that assumption fails across major protocols and runtimes. The findings affect anyone deploying agentic commerce or autonomous workflows, and the proposed ASU gateway offers an actionable reference defense for the emerging agent authorization ecosystem. The audit found no third-party verifiable approval record and no flood limits where measurable, with post-approval argument changes in four of eight runtimes that had measurable binding. ASU's trusted card cuts forged-narration attack success from 0.54 to 0.03 and raises the attack catch rate of 15 language models from 0.30 to 0.98, though at the cost of refusing 16 percent of harmless near misses; a second device adds nothing measurable over a trusted on-host confirmation, and flooding still succeeds 0.45–0.60 of the time against a modeled approver.

A new arXiv paper (2610.21128) tests the assumption that consistency can proxy for correctness in label-free evaluation, using four financial QA datasets, ten consistency dimensions, and two frontier model families. It finds that 60% of all incorrect answers fall in the high-consistency region (consistency ≥ 0.8), and 77.7% of these show complete answer collapse, meaning identical wrong answers across all perturbation variants. The phenomenon is robust to the choice of consistency threshold t, persisting from t=0.50 to t=1.00, and is shared across model families, though it is concentrated in specific intersections of perturbation dimension and domain. The authors map where this high-consistency/incorrect quadrant occurs, analyze its stability properties, and discuss implications for evaluation pipelines that substitute agreement-based signals for human labels.

It finds that stronger evaluators accept more tampered outputs, with mean acceptance rising from 88.6% for rule-based scorers to 94.1% for GPT-5-nano, and proposes a manifest-hash identity channel that detects zero-output-shift tampers with zero samples. The paper proves a PAC-style bound showing that tampers with zero output shift are undetectable from outputs at any sample size, while a manifest-hash identity channel detects them with zero samples; behavioral fingerprinting identifies the model component above chance (76.7%) but covers only one of six stack components. A trigger-conditional tamper invisible on the evaluation suite produces 48–100% harmful outputs, with the rate rising as model capability increases.

MaLoW keeps memory at a fixed size by writing history into LoRA weights instead of a growing cache, and the authors report only modest latency overhead compared with prior memory approaches. T2-Z introduces a test-time optimization method that augments a robotic world model with a learnable environment latent, capturing unobservable environmental factors such as friction, mass, and human-defined rules without supervision. Across 7 simulated settings and 4 real-world robotic tasks, it reduces object prediction error from 15.20 to 7.00 and raises action success from 33.73% to 72.96%. This work addresses a fundamental challenge in robotics: world models must account for environmental factors that are neither directly observable nor explicitly specified, and T2-Z shows these can be inferred from as little as a single test-time interaction. The approach could influence future research in robotic world models and embodied AI by enabling rapid adaptation to previously unseen environmental configurations. During training, T2-Z alternates between a world-model optimization stage that fixes the latents and learns general action-conditioned dynamics, and an environment-latent optimization stage that freezes the world model and optimizes the conditioning latents, allowing latent structure to emerge purely through world prediction. At test time the world model remains frozen while a newly initialized environment latent is optimized from one or more interactions, and ablations show efficient inference from as little as a single trajectory.

Researchers introduce ReTerm, a self-improving terminal agent trained to recover from its own failed terminal tasks, supported by a curated ReTerm-10K dataset for SFT cold start and a new online RL algorithm called ReTerm-GRPO. Built on Qwen3.5-9B, the resulting ReTerm-9B model achieves 34.8% Pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2.0, a 14.6-point improvement over the base model. ## [CTXGAP Study Finds Coding Agent Reports Omit 40.7% of Task-State Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20003) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces CTXGAP, a measurement study that quantifies the gap in task-state recoverability between coding agents' user-facing reports and their full recorded execution contexts. Across 37 coding tasks and 4,799 valid probes, full-context readers recovered 92.7% of task-state information while report-only readers recovered only 52.0%, a 40.7-point gap that persists at 34.8 points even at the final checkpoints of 30 verified fixes. The findings have direct implications for AI safety and human oversight of autonomous coding systems, since supervisors cannot investigate failures they were never told occurred. As coding agents take on more autonomous software engineering work, report-based task-state recoverability emerges as a complementary evaluation dimension that could shape how agent transparency is measured and improved. Human annotation identified 'states mentioned without enough supporting detail' as the largest category of unrecovered information, and model-assessed supervision-relevant states retained substantial gaps. Full terminal scrollback improved recovery to 73.6% but still trailed full context, while context-informed rewrites under matched report lengths improved recovery by about eight points without a detectable targeted-over-natural advantage; positive gaps persisted across harnesses and independent DeepSeek execution and measurement.

## [Product Interactions: A Unified Algebraic Formalism for Deep Learning Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02573) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2602.02573v2) introduces Product Interactions, an algebraic formalism that unifies convolutional, attention, state-space, and equivariant neural architectures under a single construction principle by treating multiplication, rather than linear transformation alone, as a primitive architectural operation. Within this framework, the authors derive convolutional and equivariant networks as symmetry-constrained first-order interactions, recover Mamba as a third-order self-interaction, and establish attention as a third-order interaction, then use the principles to build a simplified-algebra dynamical layer that improves both accuracy and throughput over Mamba on CIFAR-10. This work reframes neural architecture design as an algebraic construction problem, where the choice of algebra defines admissible interactions and symmetry constrains their structure, potentially offering a systematic methodology for analyzing existing models and designing new ones rather than relying on ad-hoc empirical construction. If validated, it could influence how researchers approach architecture search and unify disparate lines of work in deep learning theory. The framework is generative: composing multiplication operators generates higher-order architectures, and experiments show that interaction order affects accuracy non-monotonically while symmetry constraints boost learnability. Equivariance is incorporated by constraining the algebraic product via symmetry, with translation equivariance yielding convolution and SO(3)-compatibility producing the Clebsch-Gordan product and tensor-field interactions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Modern deep learning has produced a diverse zoo of architectures — convolutional networks for images, attention-based transformers for sequences, state-space models like Mamba for long-range dependencies, and equivariant networks that respect geometric symmetries — but these are typically developed as separate empirical constructions despite sharing recurring principles. State-space models such as Mamba build on structured state space sequence models (S4) to model long dependencies efficiently without attention, while equivariant networks are designed to preserve symmetries inherent in data such as translation or rotation. This paper attempts to show that these seemingly distinct families are special cases of one algebraic construction based on multiplication and self-interaction order.

Researchers introduced LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced "Lemon"), an LLM-native markup language that explicitly encodes structure and semantic metadata in text inputs so that instructions and data are distinguished when passed to a model. The paper describes its design requirements, shows how LLMON meets them, and provides preliminary empirical evidence that the added information benefits both model training and inference. A new arXiv paper (arXiv:2605.12863v2) introduces language-based agent control (LBAC), a programming model that requires AI agents to generate programs that are well-typed within surrounding scaffolding code, so that unsafe programs are rejected by the type-checker before execution. The authors demonstrate LBAC through three case studies: I/O sandboxing via filesystem capabilities, data provenance, and information-flow control. LBAC preserves substantial expressiveness: agents may perform arbitrary side-effect-free computation and recursively invoke subagents, which retain full tool access subject to the same or potentially more restrictive policies. The approach combines static typing with runtime enforcement to ensure policies apply across the entire application.

## [ANEForge Enables Direct Python Programming of Apple Neural Engine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17090) ⭐️ 8.0/10

ANEForge is a new Python package that programs the Apple Neural Engine (ANE) directly, bypassing CoreML entirely. It compiles a lazy tensor graph built from 58 fused operators and 19 native bridge operators into a single ANE program dispatched through the same daemon and kernel-driver stack Apple uses internally. Previously, developers could only reach the ANE through CoreML, which treats it as an optional scheduling target and can silently fall back to CPU or GPU. ANEForge gives ML systems researchers and edge AI developers deterministic, direct access to the ANE, enabling efficient inference and even on-engine training that was not possible before. The package supports native fused attention, streams int8, int4, and sparse weights, keeps decoder and optimizer state resident across steps, and runs forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer update on the engine. A small fused program completes in about 90 microseconds, near the 70-microsecond dispatch floor, and a pretrained ResNet-18 forward pass runs end-to-end in 0.33 milliseconds.

## [RT-J: 86M Relational Transformer Needs 10x Fewer In-Context Examples](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17867) ⭐️ 8.0/10

Researchers introduced RT-J, an 86M-parameter relational foundation model pretrained on the Join dataset, a collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks. Using long contexts of up to 8,192 database cells, a lightweight random-walk retriever, context tuning, and ensembling, RT-J matches strong feature-engineering pipelines on RelBench in-context regression tasks while requiring 10x fewer examples on average. This work pushes the frontier of context-efficient prediction on relational data, showing that large-scale pretraining with real-world semantics and context engineering can dramatically reduce the data burden for adapting models to new databases. It could significantly benefit scientific and industrial applications where labeled examples are scarce, and it strengthens the trend toward general-purpose relational foundation models. RT-J is pretrained on up to 8,192 database cells and uses a novel lightweight random-walk retriever to select in-context examples, then scales test-time compute via context tuning and ensembling. On RelBench in-context regression tasks, it matches feature-engineering pipelines using LLM-agent or RDBLearn featurizers with TabICLv2 or LightGBM predictors, but the abstract does not report absolute performance numbers or comparisons against other relational foundation models.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Relational databases store data across multiple linked tables, and predictive tasks on them traditionally require extensive feature engineering or large labeled datasets. Relational foundation models (RFMs) are pretrained neural networks that operate directly on such multi-table data, aiming to generalize to new databases and tasks with little adaptation. In-context learning allows a model to make predictions from a few labeled examples provided in its input, without updating weights. RelBench is a standardized benchmark for evaluating predictive machine learning on relational databases.

## [A^2-Failures: A Taxonomy of 20 Failure Modes in Agent-to-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19342) ⭐️ 8.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.19342v2) introduces A^2-Failures, a taxonomy of 20 agent-to-agent (A2A) failure modes organized into four categories: discovery and delegation, grounding and record consistency, verification, and conduct and fidelity. The taxonomy is derived from analyzing more than 2,500 recorded runs across 488 scenarios spanning eight families such as legal, CRM, security, and commerce, and the run logs are released on Hugging Face. Existing multi-agent failure studies assume a single orchestrator, a shared workspace, or a single principal, so this work fills a critical gap as autonomous agents increasingly negotiate across organizational boundaries on behalf of different principals. Its findings are likely to influence both academic research and the practical design and evaluation of A2A protocols and systems. Three findings hold across every harness, model, and scenario studied: discovery and interaction are driven by task phrasing rather than the availability of peer agents; no agent verifies a peer's factual claim on its own initiative, so a system inherits the reliability of its least reliable participant unless the protocol performs the check; and aggregate outcome scores credit the task-completing agent while remaining blind to coordination, verification, and conduct failures beneath it.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Agent-to-Agent (A2A) is an open protocol that defines how AI agents built by different vendors or frameworks discover one another, exchange messages, and coordinate tasks across system boundaries, typically over HTTP. In such settings each agent has its own environment and holds information and authority the other cannot see, and their interests may be cooperative, mixed-motive, or competitive. Prior failure taxonomies such as MAST (14 modes from 1,642 traces) assumed shared workspaces or a single orchestrator, which this paper explicitly removes.

## [Transcripts Can Predict Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20667) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.20667) investigates whether full model transcripts from saturated benchmarks can still predict capabilities on held-out, unsaturated items. It finds that pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to using only saturated benchmark scores. Benchmark saturation is a growing problem as leading models approach perfect scores, eroding the ability of benchmarks to differentiate models and inform AI safety cases and frontier policies. This work suggests that existing benchmarks can retain value if evaluation protocols are redesigned to extract capability signals from transcripts rather than just scores. The study simulates saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and evaluates pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and deterministic transcript features or embeddings. It finds that capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections but concentrated in reasoning and tool-call channels, and that predictive power does not always generalize across distribution shifts, such as underestimating early 2025 reasoning models.

**Background**: Benchmark saturation occurs when leading AI models achieve near-perfect scores on a benchmark, making score differences uninformative about meaningful capability. Benchmarks like MMLU and GPQA are widely used to track progress, but once saturated they lose discriminative power. This paper explores whether the rich information in how models solve tasks—their transcripts—can extend the useful life of such benchmarks.

## [AlphaDiana Measures Whether Agent Harnesses Actually Improve Reasoning Accuracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20675) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.20675) introduces AlphaDiana, a modular measurement system with interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers that preserves harness-native control loops while separately controlling file reuse and memory retention. Testing three open-source models and three open-source harnesses across five answer-based benchmarks (plus two interactive benchmarks for two models), the authors find that harnesses do not consistently improve reasoning accuracy. The finding challenges the common assumption that adding tools, skills, and memory scaffolding to a model reliably boosts agent performance, showing that gains on previously unsolved questions can be outweighed by losses on questions the model already answered correctly. This has direct implications for how the AI agent community designs, evaluates, and reports harness-based systems. The inconsistency extends to component-level interventions: neither skill guidance nor retained history reliably improves accuracy, and the paper notes that low output-token entropy can accompany wrong answers, while less output per execution can mean more output tokens per correct answer when accuracy falls. AlphaDiana links answer correctness and execution status to traces and resource records, enabling comparison and failure diagnosis under shared task and resource policies.

**Background**: An agent harness (also called scaffolding) is the software infrastructure surrounding a large language model that turns it into an agent — driving model and tool calls, managing conversation state and context, applying approval policies, and keeping multi-step tasks progressing. Verifiable reasoning tasks are problems whose answers can be checked automatically, such as formal theorem proving or code generation, making them useful for objective evaluation. AlphaDiana is designed to measure how these harnesses and their components affect agent outcomes.

A new arXiv paper (2610.20676) shows that corrective correctness feedback in formal verification suppresses the very evidence that specification-completeness auditing aims to uncover. Across 12 Verus/Rust tasks and four model families under matched call budgets, independent no-feedback discovery more than doubled certified-witness yield compared with IntentShield's corrective-feedback loop (59.0% versus 27.1%). The finding is counterintuitive and actionable for AI-for-code and formal-verification workflows: it suggests that completeness auditing and correctness repair have opposing immediate objectives, so preserving admitted failures before repairing them can yield stronger specification repair. Phase-Revised contracts reached 81.3% implementation success versus 62.5% for IS-Revised, indicating practical gains for teams using Verus/Rust. A format-matched iterative control attributes the larger share of the gap to feedback content rather than independent restarts, and the advantage holds in every model family and survives parser repair. However, most certified witnesses still fail held-out cases, and the effect does not reproduce in the available Dafny and Lean evaluations, establishing an empirical boundary around the studied Verus/Rust workflow.

## [CNRF: Counterfactual Risk Fields for Selective VLM Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20679) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.20679) introduces Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields (CNRF), a framework that constructs context-matched benign-harmful counterfactual pairs and uses their representation differences as risk directions, estimating neighborhood support separately from risk. Across three VLMs and five multimodal jailbreak families, CNRF reports 86.06–89.30% macro defense success rate while retaining substantial benign-task utility. Representation-based VLM defenses typically learn to separate harmful from benign inputs, but separation alone does not establish what a risk score means or when it should be trusted. CNRF reframes the problem as constructing applicable evidence for selective risk decisions, which could reduce unnecessary blanket rejections and improve the reliability of safety interventions in multimodal systems. The framework separates risk estimation from neighborhood support so that unfamiliarity is not conflated with harmfulness, and a victim-adaptive interface accommodates different safety observations across VLM architectures, routing selected requests for same-victim response review. Controlled experiments show that query-matched references and preserved context-direction correspondence materially improve risk ranking in the low-false-positive regime.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Vision-language models (VLMs) are multimodal generative models that take image and text inputs and produce text outputs, and they are vulnerable to multimodal jailbreak attacks that elicit harmful responses. Selective prediction is a framework in which a system may abstain from a decision when uncertainty exceeds a threshold, routing it to human review, and counterfactual pairs are matched inputs differing in one attribute, commonly used to probe model behavior. CNRF combines these ideas by using counterfactual benign-harmful pairs to define risk directions in representation space rather than learning a simple harmfulness boundary.

A new arXiv paper (2610.20845) identifies a 'skill-policy co-evolution trap': self-improving agents that jointly train a policy model and a skill bank become fragile once deployed skills drift, because the shared 'cooperative acceptance' rule ties policy competence to the exact bank it trained with. The authors introduce CODA (CO-evolution Drift Audit), a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol with new metrics for consistency under meaning-preserving edits and resistance to corrupted skills, showing worst-case success drops 5-13 points and erases 52-93% of the delivered bank's gain across four methods and five benchmarks. This matters because skill-policy co-evolution is a leading paradigm for building autonomous, self-improving agents, and the paper shows that current evaluation protocols systematically hide a deployment-time failure mode. If skill banks are updated more frequently than policy models are retrained — as is typical in production — agents may silently lose most of their learned competence, affecting anyone deploying such systems. The paper proves theoretically and empirically that fragility is not incidental but stems from the cooperative acceptance rule shared by these methods, and that sensitivity to skill drift grows as co-evolution training proceeds. CODA simulates drift and measures worst-case success, consistency under meaning-preserving edits, and resistance to corrupted skills, providing a shared standard for auditing future methods.

**Background**: Self-improving agents often use a skill bank — a library of reusable subroutines or workflows — alongside a policy model that decides how to act. ## [RSHD Recovers GRPO Supervision from All-Failed Rollout Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21018) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.21018) introduces Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), which lets a policy write a corrective note about each failed reasoning attempt without seeing a reference answer, then re-solve the problem with that note in context. A note is admitted only if its replays succeed more often than the original group did, after screening out notes that simply state the answer, and the admitted replay is distilled back into the plain-prompt policy. GRPO currently learns nothing from problems where every rollout fails, because there is no successful exemplar and no nonzero group-relative advantage — precisely the hardest problems the model most needs to learn from. RSHD recovers supervision from those groups and reportedly improves over GRPO across model families, sizes, and two training domains, with gains carrying over to out-of-domain evaluation sets. Admission is decided by fresh replay successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, and the only judge is the outcome verifier, so only the policy is trained and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. The paper reports consistent in-domain improvements across model families and sizes and two training domains, though it remains an unvalidated preprint.

**Background**: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning algorithm that scores each answer against a group of other answers to the same prompt and normalizes rewards within that group, avoiding the need for a separate value critic. Hindsight distillation is a related family of techniques that improves LLM training by learning retrospectively from trajectories after task execution, for example by generating textual hints or corrective feedback from failed attempts. RSHD combines these ideas by turning failed rollouts into tested, hindsight-derived supervision for GRPO.

## [RRI Uses Adversarial Meta-Prompt Evolution to Fix Model-Written Rubrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21040) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Recursive Reward Improvement (RRI), a method that inserts a reward-hacking adversary into the proposer-solver loop of recursive self-improvement. Before a solver trains on a generated task, the same model writes a deliberately useless answer that games the rubric and an honest answer without seeing the rubric, then up to two repair steps revise the rubric until the honest answer wins. On HealthBench Professional, RRI improves the adjusted score over a Generation Only baseline by 10.9 points at 9B and 12.4 at 27B, and by 10.3 points without any external model. Open-ended expert tasks such as clinical report generation lack automatic answer keys, so recursive self-improvement loops must rely on model-written rubrics that solvers can easily exploit. RRI directly targets this reward-hacking failure mode, and its gains transfer to unseen benchmarks (6.6 points on PRBench Hard and 8.0 on ProfBench for the 27B model), suggesting a practical path toward safer self-improvement in domains without verifiable rewards. The adversary and the honest answer are produced by the same model, and the exploits it finds are fed back to rewrite how future tasks and rubrics are generated, creating a meta-prompt evolution loop. Gains are largest on difficult and writing-heavy tasks, and the paper also analyzes exploitable points in model-generated question-rubric pairs to support future open-ended self-play research.

## [Probe-and-Resume: When and How to Evaluate Agent Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21088) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21088) shows that Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) does not significantly improve task success in terminal-based computer-use environments, because critics rank intermediate continuations only modestly better than chance. The authors propose Probe-and-Resume, a policy that invokes the critic only when the agent claims to be finished, giving it read, write, and execute access to a fork of the current and initial state; on Terminal-Bench 2.1 this raises success by 8.4 percentage points over MCTS with conventional critics and approaches the Codex CLI agent's success rate at less than half the cost. This work challenges the assumption that test-time search with MCTS is broadly beneficial for LLM agents, showing that the timing and access granted to the critic matter far more than the search algorithm itself. The findings could reshape how agentic systems are evaluated and built, especially for terminal and computer-use agents where cost and reliability are critical. The paper identifies two sources of poor critic performance: the agent's observations omit environment state needed for evaluation, and intermediate states offer limited evidence of eventual success, so environment access alone improves ranking only slightly. Probe-and-Resume addresses this by letting the critic probe a fork of the state with read, write, and execute permissions, potentially performing destructive actions to surface hidden state, after which a rejected agent resumes from where it stopped.

## [CleanRM: Calibrating Sample-Wise Noise in RLHF Reward Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21138) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CleanRM is a new method that uses a small set of clean preference samples to calibrate sample-wise noise ratios in noisy feedback via optimal transport, then trains a reward model with a noise-corrected surrogate loss. The authors prove the resulting objective is unbiased with respect to the clean risk, and experiments show it outperforms state-of-the-art denoising baselines while improving downstream RLHF alignment. Preference data used in RLHF is inherently noisy due to subjective human judgments, annotation mistakes, and imperfect LLM judges, and standard reward modeling on such data yields a biased estimate of the clean risk. CleanRM's ability to correct this bias with only a few clean samples could make reward models more reliable and improve the alignment of large language models in practice. Unlike classical denoising methods that assume a uniform noise ratio across all samples, CleanRM explicitly models sample-wise noise by aligning the joint distribution of preferences reverted from noisy feedback with that of clean feedback using optimal transport. The theoretical guarantee of unbiasedness is a key contribution, though the method still depends on the quality and representativeness of the few clean samples provided.

Optimal transport is a mathematical framework, related to the Wasserstein distance, for comparing and aligning probability distributions, and it has become a popular tool in machine learning for distribution matching.

By making teacher supervision sensitive to question conditions, CCE-OPD reduces erroneous reasoning steps and could improve the reliability of distilled reasoning models, benefiting researchers and practitioners who compress large language models into smaller students. The method uses a fixed-prefix comparison with a frozen teacher and a bounded log-probability contrast to reweight the teacher distribution, and it achieves the strongest results on four transfer benchmarks. The evaluation focuses on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and diagnostic reasoning states, so generalization to other domains such as code or open-ended dialogue remains to be tested.

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own generated trajectories while a stronger teacher provides supervision along those rollouts, which helps address exposure bias where students encounter partial sequences at inference that they rarely saw during training. ## [Paper Defines 'Standing' for Releasing AI Assistant Promises in Multi-Party Chat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21203) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21203) introduces the concept of 'standing' for commitments made by an AI assistant in multi-party chat, specifying that only the creditor or someone authorized by the creditor or operator policy may release a promise. Controlled experiments across six models reveal two distinct systematic errors: unauthorized release (obeying someone without standing) and override (executing a promise that has already been released). As AI assistants increasingly operate in team settings and multi-agent systems, correctly handling who can cancel a promise is critical for trust, accountability, and safety. The finding that models systematically mishandle commitment release suggests current assistants could be manipulated into dropping or wrongly executing obligations, with implications for enterprise workflows and agentic deployments. Error patterns differ by model scale: smaller open models tend to override the creditor (Qwen3.5-9B: 69%), while larger models drop promises on a peer's direct word (Qwen3.8-27B: 89%; gpt-6.1-sol: 83%), and nearly all act on a bystander's 'go ahead after all'. Oracles dissociate the two errors, and a self-kept commitment ledger stops override in four of five models; with a one-paragraph release policy it raises gpt-6-luna's strict accuracy from 49% to 83%.

## [Longer Thinking Makes Reasoning Models Read 'Some' and 'Or' Literally](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21204) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21204) shows that increasing a reasoning model's thinking time systematically cancels scalar implicatures — the everyday inference that 'some' means 'not all' and 'or' means 'not both' — in most tested open reasoning models and in GPT-5. Using a fixed-weights setup that varies only thinking length and a second tool that truncates reasoning at successive points, the authors trace this to a two-stage process in which models first entertain the enriched pragmatic reading and then suppress it later. This reveals a trade-off between logical and pragmatic interpretation in reasoning models, meaning that giving models more time to think can make them less human-like in everyday language understanding even as they improve on context-driven inferences like indirect answers. The authors argue that evaluations of reasoning models should measure how they interpret language, not only how accurate they are, which has implications for AI alignment and natural language understanding. The study keeps model weights fixed and varies only the amount of thinking, and an exploratory inference-time remedy — answering from the model's early enriched reading — recovers the implicatures without losing literal accuracy. The effect is observed across most tested open reasoning models and GPT-5, while context-driven inferences such as indirect answers actually improve with more thinking.

**Background**: Scalar implicature is a pragmatic phenomenon in which a weaker term like 'some' suggests the denial of a stronger term like 'all' on the same scale, even though 'some' does not logically exclude 'all'. The paper introduces Uncertainty-aware Rubric Weighting (URW), a training-free framework that quantifies criterion-level uncertainty in rubric-based LLM evaluation using conformal calibration. URW elicits soft uncertainty signals from paraphrased judgment templates and converts them into per-criterion weights via split-conformal p-values with provable coverage guarantees, consistently improving pairwise preference accuracy and downstream RL alignment. Rubric-based evaluation is widely used to score LLM outputs and to generate reward signals for reinforcement learning, so treating all criteria as equally certain can inject misleading training signals. By explicitly modeling and down-weighting uncertain judgments, URW could make LLM evaluation and alignment more reliable, affecting researchers and practitioners who build reward models or use LLM-as-judge pipelines. URW is training-free and operates on a fixed pool of paraphrased judgment templates, using split-conformal p-values to assign per-criterion weights with formal coverage guarantees. The approach targets binary judgments from an LLM verifier and is evaluated on pairwise preference accuracy and downstream RL alignment rather than on a single benchmark score.

## [Information Density Predicts and Steers LLM Chain-of-Thought Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21286) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21286) investigates whether variation in information density across chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning steps predicts answer correctness and can serve as a controllable inference-time target. Across six model scales, two training paradigms, and 60 GSM8K problems, the authors find that lower LP variance predicts correctness in supervised fine-tuned (SFT) models but this relationship weakens with scale and reverses in reinforcement-learning (RL) distilled models, and they introduce Entropy-Gated Density Routing (EGDR), which improves accuracy by 10.0 percentage points without external guidance. This work suggests that the statistical texture of reasoning steps — not just their content — carries predictive signal about correctness, and that training paradigm may matter more than model size in shaping that signal. If validated, density-based metrics and steering methods like EGDR could offer lightweight, self-supervised tools for evaluating and improving LLM reasoning at inference time. The paper measures density with two independent metrics: LP variance (variance in mean per-token negative log-likelihood across steps) and the Caveman compression ratio. Direct inference-time density steering sharply reduces accuracy from 60.0% to 8.3%, while pre-generation nudging combining hint injection with contrastive KV-cache steering improves accuracy by 13.3 percentage points, and synthetic experiments show models trained on uniform data learn complexity-favouring distributions 2.0 to 2.6 times more accurately than simplicity-favouring ones.

Negative log-likelihood is a standard loss measuring how surprised a model is by each token, so its per-step variance reflects how unevenly information is spread through a reasoning chain. Caveman compression is a semantic compression method that strips predictable grammar while preserving factual content, and its compression ratio serves here as a second, independent density measure.

A new arXiv paper proposes scoring bank accounts directly as nodes in a heterogeneous graph derived from a bank's relational schema, using per-column encoders, relative-time encoding, and HeteroGraphSAGE message passing with temporal constraints. ## [FedSkillGit Uses Version Control Commits for Federated LLM Skill Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21348) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FedSkillGit proposes a federated skill evolution framework that replaces full-document updates with bounded sets of patches over named rules, where each client submits patches plus a local experience summary that passes a two-stage privacy filter before leaving the client. The server deduplicates submissions, merges surviving patches into a candidate skill, and publishes it only when clients' validation scores improve on the current version; experiments on three datasets and three language model families show up to 22% improvement over state-of-the-art baselines and performance approaching centralized evolution without sharing raw client data. This matters because federated skill evolution for LLM agents has been hampered by privacy leakage, wasted communication on nearly unchanged documents, and poor attribution of individual client contributions, all of which FedSkillGit directly addresses. If it holds up, it could make collaborative agent skill improvement practical for deployments where data owners cannot pool raw traces, spanning AI/ML and distributed systems. The design uses commits rather than whole documents, so each client submits a bounded set of patches over named rules plus a local experience summary, and a two-stage privacy filter screens the pair before transmission. The server deduplicates patches and experience, updates a global experience document read only by optimizers, and merges surviving patches into a candidate that clients score on their own validation sets before publication.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Federated learning lets multiple data owners collaboratively train or improve a model without sharing raw local data, typically by aggregating model updates on a server. LLM agents can improve by evolving reusable natural-language skills from execution experience, but in real deployments that experience is distributed across owners who cannot pool raw data, which motivates federated skill evolution. A natural first design has each client evolve the whole skill document and upload it for server-side aggregation, but that approach leaks client-specific content, wastes communication on nearly unchanged documents, and obscures individual contributions.

## [SIF: Selective Internal Feedback Boosts LLM Reasoning Without Verifiers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21392) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces SIF, a reinforcement learning method that combines comparative reward construction with selective policy updates to train language models using only internal feedback. Across three backbones and 12 mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks, SIF's final checkpoints outperform the best-validation checkpoints of Intuitor and Vigor, gaining 4.71 percentage points over Intuitor on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B. This matters because reinforcement learning for LLM reasoning typically depends on costly external verifiers or ground-truth labels, and SIF shows that carefully filtered intrinsic signals can match or beat such methods. It could make reasoning post-training cheaper and more broadly applicable, especially in domains where verified answers are scarce. SIF compares ranked token-level self-certainty profiles across multiple windows and peers, assigning positive rewards only when both levels of voting provide sufficient support, and uses sample- and group-level filtering to decide which responses enter policy optimization. Analyses show better accuracy retention during continued optimization, and test-time training experiments show sustained gains with as few as four rollouts per prompt.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement Learning from Internal Feedback (RLIF) is an alternative to RLHF and RLVR that uses the model's own intrinsic signals, such as token-level entropy or self-certainty, instead of external rewards or labeled data. Intuitor, an ICLR 2026 paper, is a representative RLIF method that uses self-certainty as the sole reward, while Vigor is another prior method compared against in this work. A known problem is that confidence and correctness can diverge, so optimizing average self-certainty may raise confidence while degrading reasoning accuracy.

## [DCBench-440 Reveals LLMs Fail at Counterfactual Data Center Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21397) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces DCBench-440, a benchmark with two arms: 200 generative questions over STRIPS planning worlds covering five US AI data center deal archetypes, and 240 multiple-choice questions grounded in quoted site records and emission equations. Across open-weight models, accuracy ranges from 12.5% to 71.5% on generative questions and 58.3% to 92.5% on multiple choice, but no model exceeds 4.0% exact match when asked to list every action available at a decision gate. AI data centers are committed years before they draw power, and LLMs are increasingly used to help screen these high-stakes decisions without any test of whether they understand what each commitment rules out. This benchmark exposes a fundamental limitation in current LLMs' counterfactual reasoning, with implications for AI evaluation, energy planning, and sustainability research. The strongest models list 72-85% of the actions that would change the project's state but omit most permitted actions that change nothing; even when those omissions are excused, the best exact match is still only 24%. The benchmark uses search-verified gold answers, and no tested shortcut exceeds 12% on any question type, adding rigor to the negative result.

DCBench-440 applies this to AI data center buildout, where early discrete choices such as grid versus on-site gas, evaporative versus dry cooling, and which county to file in lock in capital, water, and carbon trajectories.

## [MemCut Benchmark Tests Whether LLM Agents Truly Forget User Secrets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21405) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced MemCut, a benchmark of 456 hand-designed secrets embedded in long-horizon conversations with fully annotated evidence trails, to evaluate user-requested forgetting in LLM agents' long-term memory. They propose two recovery metrics—native recovery and residual recovery—and establish three reference deletion baselines tested across five memory designs and four LLMs. As LLM agents increasingly rely on long-term memory to store personal user data, the inability to reliably delete sensitive information on request poses a serious privacy risk. MemCut provides a systematic way to measure deletion effectiveness, which could spur further research into AI safety, privacy, and machine unlearning for agentic systems. The benchmark reveals that disclosure removal reduces native recovery far more than residual recovery, and LLM-guided deletion of ten additional turns from twenty retrieval candidates still leaves 39-76% residual recovery. Subset sweeps across 144 facts, three systems, and two models show that widening the retrieval pool at a fixed budget reduces residual recovery more than deleting all original candidates, identifying candidate coverage as a bottleneck.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Long-term memory has become a crucial component of LLM agents, allowing them to store and retrieve information across conversations, but most research focuses on accurate retrieval rather than forgetting. Machine unlearning for LLM agents, sometimes called agentic unlearning, aims to remove specified information from both internal model parameters and evolving external memory. MemCut addresses the understudied problem of user-requested forgetting in this external memory.

## [JevAgentHarness Lets Small Decision Models Share Agent Control with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21412) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21412) introduces JevAgentHarness, a framework for benchmarking, deploying, and training decision models that share control with LLMs, alongside the AgentDecisionBench benchmark and the open AgentDecision-4B model. The authors report that on tasks unlike its training data, an agent solved 91.5% of tasks with AgentDecision-4B versus 82.0% with Jev, and on in-distribution tasks, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1-89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster without losing 3 or more points of task success. LLM agents currently call a large model at every step, making long tasks slow and costly, and this work shows that delegating multiple-choice decisions to small specialized models can cut cost and latency substantially while preserving task success. It matters for anyone building or operating agentic AI systems, and it contributes a new benchmark and open model to the agent-efficiency ecosystem. The paper reports that the decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and that without a fitted confidence threshold, delegating tool choices lowered success by 19.0 points; JevAgentHarness fits this threshold per choice on the agent's own trajectories and lets the LLM decide below it. AgentDecisionBench tests decision models from isolated questions up to control of a running agent on public benchmarks and the DecisionGym environment, which generates customer-service tasks with 60 near-miss distractor tools and noisy tool output.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents are programs that use a large language model to take actions such as calling tools, fixing software, or serving customers, and the harness is the program that runs them and calls the LLM at each step. Many of these calls are effectively multiple-choice decisions, like which tool to call next, so a smaller decision model such as Jev can answer them directly at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. A confidence threshold determines when to trust the small model and when to fall back to the LLM, and training on states the agent reaches after its own mistakes helps the small model handle situations it would not otherwise see.

## [LoCD: Localized Context Distillation for LLM Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21427) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.21427) introduces Localized Context Distillation (LoCD), a method that first localizes the critical spans of a student model's trajectory that need revision, then has a teacher regenerate only those spans from the student's own prefix, training the student on the regenerated segments. Experiments across math reasoning, code generation, and agent tasks show LoCD consistently outperforms strong baselines with more stable training and smaller, sparser parameter updates. Context distillation is a key route for letting deployed LLMs keep improving from interaction experience without retraining from scratch, and LoCD directly targets the trade-off that has limited both existing variants. If the results hold up, it could offer a more compute-efficient and stable way to do continual learning for reasoning, coding, and agentic systems. The method concentrates learning on the most informative states while keeping exposure bias low, and the paper reports smaller and sparser parameter updates than baselines, suggesting less disruptive updates to the model. As an arXiv preprint without community discussion or independent validation yet, the claims remain to be reproduced.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Context distillation trains a student model to mimic a teacher that has access to privileged information (such as retrieved context or interaction experience) which the student will not have at deployment. Off-policy context distillation trains on teacher-generated trajectories and suffers from exposure bias, while on-policy context distillation trains on the student's own rollouts, whose states are often uninformative. LoCD is designed to resolve this dilemma by combining the strengths of both approaches.

LoopAhead introduces a speculative decoding framework for looped transformers that uses a lightweight lookahead drafter (LAD) built on early-loop states to predict multiple future tokens, while deeper-loop feedback prunes incorrect speculative branches and the full-depth model makes final token decisions. It achieves up to 7.82x decoding speedup over standard autoregressive decoding while preserving the target model's output distribution. Looped transformers improve parameter efficiency by reusing the same layers, but their sequential decoding latency remains a major bottleneck for deployment. Unlike prior pipelined self-speculative decoding, LoopAhead assigns complementary roles to different recurrent depths: early loops draft longer lookahead token sequences, deeper loops decide which branches to continue or pause, and the full-depth model verifies final outputs. The reported 7.82x speedup is lossless, meaning the output distribution matches standard autoregressive decoding.

**Background**: Speculative decoding is an inference-time optimization in which a small draft model proposes several candidate tokens that a larger target model verifies in a single forward pass, preserving the target's output distribution while cutting latency. Looped transformers, by contrast, repeatedly apply the same shared Transformer layers across recurrent loops, improving parameter efficiency but making each token's generation still sequential. Self-speculative decoding removes the need for a separate draft model by using the same model's earlier or shallower computations to draft tokens.

## [AgentPerturb: A Controlled Framework for Evaluating LLM Agent Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21624) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AgentPerturb introduces a two-dimensional evaluation framework that jointly characterizes perturbation targets and perturbation types, and applies it to quantify the robustness of frontier LLM agents on the APEX-Agents and Toolathlon benchmarks. The study finds that perturbations consistently degrade agent performance, that agents rarely recognize altered inputs, and that successful perturbed trajectories often require substantially more computation. As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in complex, noisy real-world environments, this work provides a systematic way to measure and diagnose their fragility, showing that current frontier models silently propagate corrupted information rather than detecting and recovering from it. The findings point toward concrete training objectives—covering diverse noise forms and rewarding verification, uncertainty awareness, and recovery—that could shape how future agent systems are built and evaluated. The framework uses a two-dimensional view that separates perturbation targets from perturbation types, and the dominant vulnerabilities were found to vary across task environments, meaning robustness results are environment-dependent rather than universal. Trajectory-level analysis reveals the failure mechanism—agents fail to recognize altered inputs and propagate corrupted information without verification—and a focused cost analysis shows perturbed-but-successful runs can consume substantially more computation.

## [Paper Proves Self-Improvement Gates Cannot Be Both Reliable and Complete](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21646) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.21646) formalizes the structural difficulty of evaluating self-improvement updates in autonomous agents, modeling agents as programs and improvement as a potentially non-computable semantic score. It proves that no terminating procedure — including randomized gates with bounded error — can simultaneously guarantee reliability (never accepting a non-improvement) and non-conservatism (never missing an available improvement), while showing that a bounded regime with finite proposal budgets allows exhaustive simulation to recover both guarantees. As LLM-based agents increasingly write code, call tools, and modify their own prompts and components, automated gates such as reward models or automated reviewers are being proposed as safety mechanisms. This paper shows that such gates face a fundamental computability barrier in unbounded settings, meaning safety guarantees for fully autonomous self-improvement cannot be achieved by gate design alone and must instead rely on bounded evaluation regimes. The paper studies two evaluation abstractions — a certifier that approves or rejects updates, and a search procedure that tries to output an improving candidate if one exists — and uses self-referential constructions to force failure in the fully general case. It also identifies a practical decidable regime (bounded evaluation plus a finite proposal budget) where exhaustive simulation yields a terminating search with the desired guarantees, but shows the limit of this recovery: a chain of accepted updates can raise the bounded score every round while the true score falls.

**Background**: Computability theory studies what problems can be solved by algorithms, and its foundational result — Turing's proof of the undecidability of the halting problem — shows that no general algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary program will eventually halt. Self-improving AI systems, in which an agent proposes and adopts modifications to its own code or prompts, require some automated gate to decide whether each proposed update is genuinely better. This paper connects those two ideas, arguing that the gate must be a terminating computable procedure while genuine semantic improvement depends on unbounded program behavior, creating a mismatch that mirrors classical undecidability results.
