## [DeciCAD: A Domain-Native Harness and Learning Pipeline for CAD Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21755) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DeciCAD introduces a domain-native agent harness for computer-aided design that exposes semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions, paired with a learning pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and geometry-grounded online reinforcement learning (RL). Across four CAD benchmarks it achieves the best F1 and IoU while cutting model-output tokens by 45–88% compared with a general-purpose coding harness; under matched supervision, SFT raises F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437, and subsequent online RL lifts geometry availability from 66.5% to 73.5% and F1 to 0.7880. The paper shows that the decision space induced by an agent harness materially shapes both agent execution and policy learning, suggesting that domain-native harness design may matter as much as model scale for specialized professional tasks. This has implications for anyone building LLM agents in domains with persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures, such as CAD, engineering, and robotics. The harness provides semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions, and the learning pipeline extracts causal decision supervision from interaction trajectories. The reported gains are measured against a general-purpose coding harness, and the RL stage is described as geometry-grounded, improving geometry availability from 66.5% to 73.5%.

**Background**: An agent harness (also called agent scaffolding) is the software infrastructure surrounding a large language model that turns it into an agent: it defines which tools exist, what the model observes, what actions are allowed, and how state persists across steps. In CAD, agents must handle persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures, making the harness's decision space especially consequential. Intersection over Union (IoU), also known as the Jaccard index, measures the overlap between predicted and ground-truth shapes and is a standard metric for geometric tasks, while F1 balances precision and recall.

## [PhysClosureBench Tests Whether AI Agents Can Close Physics Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21767) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced PhysClosureBench, a benchmark of 50 expert-verified, goal-specified physics research tasks spanning strong-field, attosecond, and neighboring areas, evaluated with a 20-criterion Atomic Score and a new Research Closure (RC0–RC4) metric. Across seven frontier LLMs, Claude-Opus-5 achieved the highest mean Atomic Score (6.29/10) but reached full RC4 closure in only 32.7% of attempts. The results expose a persistent gap between AI agents' local scientific accomplishments and their ability to reach complete, evidence-supported research conclusions, which matters for AI-for-science efforts and for how agent evaluation is designed. It suggests that strong benchmark scores on sub-tasks do not yet translate into reliable end-to-end scientific closure. The benchmark leaves agents to organize the investigation and decide how to generate and validate evidence, and 36.2% of attempts scoring at least 8/10 still fell short of RC4. Case-level analysis attributes incomplete closure to misinterpretation of generated results and unresolved physical applicability limits, and all seven models reached RC4 on substantially fewer tasks across all three runs than in at least one.

## [RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Ternary Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21808) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RoleQ introduces a structural quantization framework that assigns scaling factors based on the functional roles of Transformer units—vectors reading from the residual stream get one scale per output unit, while those writing to it get one per input unit—rather than following the weight matrix layout. This rule requires no search, calibration, or stored state, and in a rotated basis it matches a per-layer axis search at half the solver work, cutting perplexity by up to half compared to layout-based placement across model sizes from 0.6B to 14B. This approach enables converting existing checkpoints to 1.59 bits per weight in just a few GPU-hours, a fraction of the cost of learned ternarization, and leads every post-training ternary method at matched or lower memory-resident bits on perplexity, zero-shot accuracy, and MMLU. It could significantly lower the barrier to deploying large language models in memory-constrained environments while preserving factual knowledge and task accuracy that conventional sub-4-bit quantization often sacrifices. The framework works on both integer and ternary grids, and a sparse second ternary plane placed by per-unit Fisher saliency keeps the matmul multiplication-free while recovering what ternary loses first: at 8B parameters, a fraction of a bit returns about half the MMLU that conversion costs, well ahead of random or Hessian-based placement at equal bits. Notably, per-row scales leave MMLU at chance level, highlighting the importance of role-based placement.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Ternary weight quantization restricts model weights to three values (−1, 0, +1), drastically reducing memory footprint and eliminating most floating-point multiplications, but it typically requires training from scratch or long fine-tuning. The residual stream is the central information highway in Transformer architectures, where each layer reads from and writes to a shared vector space via residual connections. Perplexity measures how well a language model predicts the next token, with lower values indicating better predictive performance, while MMLU is a widely used benchmark for evaluating factual knowledge and reasoning across many subjects.

## [OntoAct: Neuro-Symbolic Agents via Ontological Abstraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21983) ⭐️ 7.0/10

OntoAct is a new hypothesis-based neuro-symbolic framework that converts individual experiences into reusable axioms over entity types, relations, and conditions, letting an LLM propose hypotheses and actions while a symbolic verifier checks their supporting conditions against current observations. The authors also introduce Tacit-FLE, a benchmark built on the Factorio Learning Environment for diagnosing and repairing hidden faults in existing factories using inherited operational records, and report leading task performance across Tacit-FLE, Mars, and ALFWorld with efficient interaction and inference. The work targets a core weakness of current LLM agents: the inability to turn experience into reusable, transferable knowledge and to know when that knowledge applies. By pairing neural hypothesis generation with symbolic verification, it contributes to the broader neuro-symbolic trend that industry has begun adopting to curb LLM hallucination and improve reliability, and the Tacit-FLE benchmark gives the community a harder testbed where a repair action may fail and agents must re-diagnose through interaction. Tacit-FLE distributes evidence across a synthetic maintenance corpus of inherited operational records, and crucially an executed repair may leave the fault unresolved, forcing agents to reassess diagnoses rather than assume success. The framework's symbolic verifier explicitly identifies missing evidence, and new observations plus intervention outcomes update hypothesis assessments to guide subsequent actions; the paper is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community validation yet.

**Background**: Neuro-symbolic AI combines neural networks, which excel at learning statistical patterns from data, with symbolic AI, which handles explicit rules, knowledge representation, and automated reasoning; it is often called the third wave of AI and has been adopted industrially to reduce LLM hallucination. Ontological abstraction here means organizing experience into general categories of entity types, relations, and conditions, so that patterns learned in one situation can be stated as axioms and reused elsewhere. ## [GraphACM: Graph-Based Action Consistency for LLM Agent Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22031) ⭐️ 7.0/10

GraphACM introduces a graph-based framework that merges equivalent states across multiple rollouts of the same task into a directed, action-labeled graph, enabling fine-grained action comparisons at shared decision states. It defines node-level and global action consistency measures, using the global score as an uncertainty proxy, and achieves an average AUROC of 0.811 for task-success prediction across three LLMs on ALFWorld, AppWorld, and WebShop. Existing behavioral-consistency methods collapse consistency into a single task-level score, which cannot reveal where agents diverge or whether actions are compared under equivalent decision contexts. By providing state-conditioned, fine-grained consistency signals, GraphACM offers a more reliable uncertainty signal for predicting agent success or failure, which matters for deploying safer and more trustworthy LLM agents in complex interactive tasks. The framework outperforms the strongest behavioral-consistency baseline (0.729 AUROC) and verbalized confidence (0.769 AUROC), reaching 0.811 on average. The approach is evaluated across three LLMs and three benchmarks, though the abstract does not specify the exact model versions or the computational overhead of graph construction and merging.

## [FAOP Brings Database Normal Forms to AI Agent Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22061) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.22061v1) proposes Functional Agent Operating Procedures (FAOP), a formal theory that treats each AI agent workflow as a typed function over scoped state and subjects an entire library of procedures to four progressive normal forms: Decomposed (FNF-1), Typed (FNF-2), Factored (FNF-3), and Scoped (FNF-4). The authors also define a sound algebra of equalities that turns refactoring and parallelization into compiler rewrites, add orthogonal extensions for verified termination (+V), optimization (+O), and time/cost bounds (+B), and implement the theory in SkillBase, an AOP management system with a separate runtime executor. Regulated sectors increasingly require agent workflows to be traceable, auditable, reproducible, access-controlled, and bounded in time and cost, yet today's AOPs are typically coarse-grained files where steps bundle actions, copies drift apart, and any step can reach any tool. By making integrity, isolation, typing, termination, cost, and optimization compile-time concerns across an entire library, FAOP could give organizations database-grade discipline over their AI agent procedures rather than relying on runtime hopes. Once normalized, every atomic step becomes a separate entity with a declared contract that can be type-checked, scope-confined, bounded, tested, traced, and audited on its own; an architectural-level classifier (0-3) even determines whether a workflow needs AI at all. The work is still a preprint with no community discussion yet, and its immediate practical impact remains uncertain.

**Background**: Database normalization, first proposed by Edgar F. Codd as part of the relational model, structures relational schemas according to a hierarchy of normal forms (1NF through 5NF and beyond) to reduce redundancy and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies. Relational algebra provides a formal semantics for query languages, allowing equivalences to be proven and queries to be rewritten. FAOP borrows both ideas, applying normal forms and algebraic rewriting not to tables but to multi-step AI agent procedures, which the paper calls Agent Operating Procedures (AOPs).

## [Prism-1 Fixes Order and Rival Dependence in LLM Decision Reads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22066) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.22066) shows that standard ways of extracting decisions from language models — single-choice question prompting, shuffled-order training, order averaging, sorted options, and invariant set architectures — each violate at least one axiom of rational choice: order-independence or Luce's choice axiom. The authors propose Prism-1, which reads every option in its own block at shared positions in a single forward pass, and report that no shuffle changes any of its answers while no added irrelevant option moves its choice among the others. Web systems increasingly derive tool, intent, and interface decisions from language models, where the option set and its listing are controlled by other components and can change or be manipulated. The finding that one shuffle changes 12-20% of SCQ answers and a well-chosen added option steers 4-34% of decisions means deployed LLM decision systems can be silently unstable or steerable, so a read that satisfies both axioms by construction has direct reliability implications. By Luce's theorem, a read satisfies both axioms only if it is a softmax over scores that each depend on one option alone, which in a transformer holds by construction only if no token scoring an option sees another. On five benchmark sets with Qwen3-8B and Gemma 4 12B, SCQ prompting trained on the same data still changes 7% of its answers under one shuffle and an added irrelevant option steers 12% of its decisions, while Prism-1 stays within one point of that baseline's accuracy and is 2-4 points more accurate once only reordering-surviving answers are counted.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: System One decision models take a state and a set of options — such as intents, tools, or interface elements — and return a distribution over those options in one forward pass without generated reasoning. Luce's choice axiom (formulated by R. Duncan Luce in 1959) states that the relative odds of choosing one item over another are unaffected by the presence or absence of other items, a property known as independence from irrelevant alternatives. Standard practice builds such models by reading decisions out of language models via single-choice question prompting, sometimes with shuffled-order training, order averaging, sorted options, or set-invariant architectures designed to ignore input order.

This matters because it reframes multimodal safety from post-hoc output filtering to proactive clarification at the intent level, a gap that existing reasoning-based defenses do not address. Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, SAFE-PRO consistently improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves over-refusal, and surpasses GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety, suggesting practical value for deploying safer multimodal assistants. SAFE-PRO optimizes under a reward that prioritizes safety while penalizing over-refusal, and the authors provide a theoretical analysis of gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk under RCU. The approach is validated on the new SSUI-Dialog dataset and seven benchmarks, though it remains a specialized contribution rather than a paradigm shift.

## [SRD Lets Language Models Learn from Unverified Peer Solutions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22080) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.22080) proposes Shared Residual Distillation (SRD), an on-policy self-distillation method that lets a language model improve by learning from its own unverified peer solutions without first determining which are correct. SRD raises mean AIME24-26 avg@12 from 11.02 to 16.20 on Qwen3-1.7B, from 19.07 to 45.46 on Qwen3-4B, and from 21.39 to 54.44 on Qwen3-8B. Most post-training methods for reasoning models rely on reference answers, verifiable feedback, or external teachers, which are expensive or unavailable in many domains. SRD shows that a model can extract useful supervision from its own unverified generations, potentially lowering the cost of improving reasoning capabilities and broadening post-training to settings without ground-truth labels. SRD compares how peers change the prediction distribution relative to a control, retaining only adjustments that agree in direction and are conservative in magnitude, so no complete solution is ever treated as correct. The trained model needs no peers at inference time, and controlled ablations support the shared-residual construction, with no degradation observed on two general-capability benchmarks.

**Background**: Self-distillation is a technique in which a model is retrained using its own predictions rather than, or in addition to, original labels. On-policy learning means training on trajectories generated by the current policy, which in reinforcement learning helps align training with the model's own behavior. SRD combines these ideas: instead of distilling from a stronger teacher or verified answers, it distills from the model's own peer solutions, using their shared residual effect on the output distribution as a learning signal.

## [DropKV Decouples Residual-Output Perturbation for Near-Optimal KV-Cache Eviction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22130) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DropKV introduces a principled KV-cache eviction framework that decouples the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring, circumventing the NP-hard combinatorial optimization that limits existing methods. It provides a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under an empirically verified cone condition, and a fused Triton kernel implementation delivers a 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup and up to 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup. KV-cache memory grows linearly with context length and has become a critical bottleneck for scaling LLMs to long-context inference, so a method that is both theoretically grounded and practically fast could directly improve serving throughput and cost. DropKV outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on RULER and LongBench at equivalent cache budgets while achieving the lowest inference latency among eviction methods, making it relevant to anyone deploying long-context LLMs. The approximation guarantee holds only under a cone condition that the authors verify empirically on three long-context LLMs rather than prove universally, and the reported speedups are measured on the scoring kernel and matched-batch prefill rather than full end-to-end generation. The fused Triton kernels avoid materializing the full attention matrix, which is what enables the 19.8x scoring-kernel speedup.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Transformer-based LLMs cache key and value vectors for every past token so they do not recompute them during autoregressive generation, but this KV cache grows linearly with sequence length and consumes large amounts of GPU memory and bandwidth. KV-cache eviction methods discard less important KV pairs to fit a fixed cache budget, and recent approaches try to minimize the resulting output perturbation instead of relying only on attention-score heuristics. Minimizing that perturbation is an NP-hard combinatorial problem, so prior work either uses mathematically suboptimal heuristics or designs that are hard to implement efficiently on GPUs.

Researchers propose Compatible Routing (CART), a method that explicitly coordinates the adaptation of the projector and the language model in Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). CART maintains task-specific experts for both modules, combines them via weighted mixtures inferred from expert relevance and cross-module compatibility, and introduces relevance-guided expert consolidation to control model growth, achieving state-of-the-art results. To limit parameter growth, relevance-guided expert consolidation merges experts with similar relevance profiles across samples within each module.

## [RADAR Framework Repairs and Audits LLM Confidence Scores](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22139) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces RADAR (Repair, Adopt, and Diagnose After Recalibration), a reliability framework that separates confidence repair from the decision to deploy it and from auditing residual errors. It proposes Probe-Anchored Isotonic Calibration (PAIC), which learns a monotone map from correctness-probe predictions on unlabeled target prompts, and reports that across 47,400 replayed raw-score allocations, paired betting adopts candidates with lower held-out test risk in 42.95% of allocations versus 15.09% for one-sided empirical Bernstein. Under squared loss, the authors decompose prediction risk into outcome noise, information hidden by the score, and mapping error, with an additional pooling gap when repair is restricted to order-preserving maps. PAIC's excess risk depends on the probe's score-conditional bias and fitting error rather than its overall accuracy, and the auditing component uses a prompt-clustered kernel test to detect feature-aligned residual errors while accounting for dependent answers from the same prompt.

Researchers released LEASH, a training-free framework that escalates control from a weak computer-use agent to a strong one only when the weak agent's latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and then keeps the strong agent under a shadow observer. On OSWorld across four model backbones, LEASH beat random escalation by 6.55–11.94 points at matched escalation rates, and with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B reached 73.66% task success at $0.4117 per task, matching always-on Claude Opus 5 (72.90%) while cutting inference cost by 19.2%. Running a frontier model at every step of long-horizon computer-use tasks is expensive, so a reliable way to decide when to escalate could make agent deployment far more cost-effective without sacrificing success rates. The shadow-observer layer also addresses a practical safety gap: black-box APIs expose no internals, so continued oversight of the strong agent has been hard to implement. LEASH works in three layers: initial task uncertainty for early routing, step-level uncertainty for runtime escalation, and a shadow observer for post-handoff oversight. Its uncertainty estimator compares the weak model's hidden states against those from past successful and failed trajectories, reusing activations already produced during action generation, so it needs no extra forward pass or dedicated monitor training.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Computer-use agents are AI systems that operate software interfaces to complete multi-step tasks, and long-horizon versions of these tasks can require dozens or hundreds of actions. Weak-to-strong escalation is a strategy in which a small, cheap model acts by default and a frontier model takes over only when necessary, but the hard part is knowing when to hand off. Uncertainty quantification for LLM agents aims to estimate when a model is likely to fail, and this paper applies that idea to the escalation decision.

## [EliteReplay Preserves Solution Diversity in RL Post-Training via Quality-Diversity Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22290) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.22290) proposes EliteReplay, a post-training recipe that combines GRPO with an 'elite' archive built by quality-diversity search. On multiple text-to-SQL tasks, EliteReplay achieves higher pass@128 than all baselines, producing up to 77% more distinct correct strategies and covering both interpretations of ambiguous questions nearly twice as often as the strongest baseline on AmbiQT. RL post-training is widely used to improve LLM accuracy on verifiable tasks, but it often causes behavior sharpening—narrowing the set of solutions the model can produce. EliteReplay shows that accuracy and solution diversity can be improved together, which matters for tasks with ambiguous or multiple valid answers and for the broader LLM post-training community. Before training, EliteReplay uses the frozen base model to collect solutions spanning distinct approaches, then during training combines GRPO with a replay loss on this elite archive. It preserves most of the base model's correct strategies and outperforms existing methods in strategy retention, with practical benefits demonstrated on the AmbiQT ambiguous-question benchmark.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning algorithm popularized by DeepSeek-R1 that reduces compute requirements by comparing groups of sampled responses instead of using a separate value network. Quality-diversity (QD) search is an evolutionary paradigm that seeks a population of high-performing yet behaviorally diverse solutions, often maintained in an 'elite archive' such as MAP-Elites. EliteReplay brings these two ideas together to counter behavior sharpening in LLM post-training.

## [Random Projection Offers a Lightweight Alternative to Differential Privacy for RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22297) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.22297) proposes using random projection to protect datastore privacy in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. By applying the same random projection to both datastore and query embeddings, the method provably preserves semantic similarity while mitigating data extraction attacks, outperforming differential privacy (DP) baselines in retrieval and generation quality with comparable empirical privacy. RAG systems are widely deployed to ground LLMs in external knowledge, but they risk leaking sensitive datastore content through retrieval. This work shows that a simple, lightweight random projection can serve as a practical privacy-preserving baseline, potentially making private RAG more accessible than heavier DP-based approaches. The method applies the same random projection to both datastore and query embeddings, which theoretically preserves semantic similarity between queries and retrieved items. Experiments across multiple RAG architectures and datasets show superior retrieval and generation performance compared to prior DP-based methods, with comparable empirical privacy under strong attack models.

However, this introduces privacy risks: attackers may extract sensitive information from the datastore through crafted queries. Differential privacy (DP) is a formal framework that provides strong privacy guarantees but often degrades utility; random projection is a dimensionality-reduction technique that can obscure embeddings while approximately preserving distances.

## [LangDiT: A Transformer Backbone Designed for Continuous Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22330) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.22330) introduces LangDiT (Language Diffusion Transformer), a transformer architecture systematically optimized for continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) rather than borrowed from causal LLMs or image Diffusion Transformers. LangDiT combines feature and query-key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning, achieving a new state of the art with 21.72 GenPPL at 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL at 128 NFEs on unconditional 1024-token OpenWebText generation, and 11.33 / 27.51 GenPPL in Plaid-style formulations. This work shows that transformer architecture itself, not just training objectives or samplers, is a fundamental source of improvement for continuous diffusion language models, which have lagged behind autoregressive LLMs in text generation quality. It could give researchers a plug-and-play backbone that improves multiple CDLM formulations at once, potentially accelerating the competitiveness of parallel (non-left-to-right) text generation. The gains are achieved while keeping each model's underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler unchanged, isolating architecture as the source of improvement. The paper reports results at both 1024 and 128 denoising NFEs (number of function evaluations), showing the architecture helps in both high- and low-compute sampling regimes, though the abstract is truncated and full limitations are not yet visible.

**Background**: Diffusion models generate data by iteratively denoising random noise, and they dominate image and video generation; applying them to language is harder because text is discrete while Gaussian noise is continuous. Most CDLM work so far reused either causal LLM transformers or image-oriented DiTs, which were not designed for the noise-conditioned, non-causal nature of language diffusion.

## [KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22331) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.22331v1) introduces KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes each query into atomic knowledge conditions and groups trajectories by the subset of conditions they have satisfied, rather than by surface observations. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO outperforms outcome-only GRPO and process-supervision baselines GiGPO and IGPO by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with an 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems. Credit assignment is a core bottleneck in training long-horizon search agents, where a single terminal reward cannot tell which of many search decisions actually mattered. By grounding process rewards in acquired knowledge rather than noisy observations or model-internal signals, KnowGPO offers a more reliable training signal that could improve sample efficiency and final accuracy for deep research agents, an increasingly important class of LLM applications. The method represents each trajectory step by the subset of satisfied knowledge conditions, groups trajectories sharing the same knowledge state for within-group comparison, and uses the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps as an environment-grounded process reward. It is a preprint without peer review, and the approach depends on being able to decompose queries into atomic knowledge conditions, which may be nontrivial for open-ended tasks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning trains agents to maximize cumulative reward, but in long-horizon tasks the credit assignment problem arises: when a reward arrives after many actions, it is hard to determine which earlier decisions caused it. Deep search agents tackle knowledge-intensive questions through multi-turn interactions with search tools, producing long, heterogeneous trajectories with noisy retrieved context. Outcome-based RL such as GRPO gives only one terminal reward per trajectory, while process-supervision methods like GiGPO and IGPO try to assign finer-grained credit but often rely on surface-level states or model-internal signals that become unreliable in deep search.

## [LLMs Show Evaluation Awareness in Indic Languages, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22333) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.22333) tests four instruction-tuned models from three families across five Indic languages plus English, finding that models refuse harmful requests more often when told they are being tested. In Indic languages, refusal rates for harmful requests rose by 14.4 percentage points on average, and the test cue also raised refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. This is the first systematic study of evaluation awareness in Indic languages, which are spoken by over a billion people, showing that safety evaluations in these languages may not reflect how models treat everyday users. It has direct implications for multilingual AI safety testing and deployment, as models may behave more cautiously during evaluations than in real-world use. The study tested four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English, using cues that varied whether the model was told it was monitored and whether the monitoring was a safety test. The authors released all 47,880 judged responses to support further work, and the test cue brought Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English but also increased over-refusal of benign requests.

## [MLExpert: A 35B Agentic Model for Autonomous ML Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22344) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proposes a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) optimization and applies it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert raises the base model's average medal rate from 37.9% to 72.7%, matching larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. This work targets AI4AI, the idea of using AI to build and improve AI systems, which is widely seen as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement. If learned MLE optimization generalizes beyond Kaggle-style tasks, it could substantially accelerate automated ML research and reduce the human effort needed in model development pipelines. The method combines hierarchical agentic supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL), which treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward, supported by asynchronous collection and policy correction. The authors also built the Kaggle-MLE Factory to generate executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation, and report gains on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization.

## [FDE-Gym Benchmark Tests AI Agents on Real Customer Delivery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22350) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced FDE-Gym, a benchmark of 95 end-to-end delivery tasks drawn from 20 real customer scenarios across 18 sectors, where agents must clarify ambiguous requirements, work in live systems, and interact with scripted stakeholders. Evaluating 13 model configurations from seven providers, the best configuration achieved a mean score of 0.56 and fully resolved only 14 of 95 tasks. This benchmark exposes a substantial gap between solving well-specified coding tasks and delivering effective AI systems for real customers, highlighting that discovering unstated constraints is the primary bottleneck. It could reshape how the AI agent community measures progress, shifting focus from ticket-based benchmarks toward realistic, stakeholder-driven delivery evaluation. FDE-Gym scores deliveries by improvement in the customer's own success metric, normalized between 0 (unchanged system) and 1 (reference solution), with penalties for stakeholder messages, trial runs, and waiting time. Even on 23 tasks where the best configuration obtained every key fact from stakeholders, it reached a normalized business uplift of 0.8 or above on only 10, showing that information discovery alone does not explain the gap.

## [CoTS: Training-Free Competitive Token Selection for Latent LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20642) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.20642) introduces Competitive Token Selection (CoTS), a training-free framework that reframes latent intervention in LLM reasoning from binary mode selection into continuous, token-level allocation. CoTS uses the probability competition between the top-2 candidate tokens to dynamically balance discrete commitment and soft exploration at each decoding step, and the authors report consistent gains over standard CoT and state-of-the-art training-free latent reasoning methods across six reasoning benchmarks. Latent reasoning is an active research direction that aims to overcome the expressive bottleneck of discrete Chain-of-Thought, but existing methods rely on global soft activation or hard uncertainty thresholds that treat intervention as all-or-nothing. By making the intervention strength continuous and threshold-free without extra forward passes, CoTS could offer a simpler, more adaptive recipe that other latent reasoning systems can adopt. The method is training-free and requires no manually tuned switching thresholds or mixing coefficients, and it introduces no additional forward passes, since it only uses the probability gap between the top-2 candidates to modulate how much the soft representation contributes. The abstract reports experiments on six reasoning benchmarks, and code is released at github.com/OkinoYu/CoTSReasoning, though the paper is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves LLM reasoning by having the model generate explicit intermediate steps in natural language, but this forces every thought to be decoded into discrete tokens, limiting expressive bandwidth. Latent reasoning instead performs multi-step inference in continuous hidden states or soft embeddings—probability-weighted mixtures of token embeddings—preserving richer intermediate representations and alternative reasoning paths. A key open question is when to commit to a discrete token versus when to keep exploring softly, since confident steps favor commitment while ambiguous steps benefit from retaining multiple plausible alternatives.

They evaluated 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, generating 41,824 adversarial trajectories and 720 benign reference runs, with mean attack success reaching 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification. As LLM agents gain autonomy to run shell commands, modify code, install dependencies, and call remote services, indirect prompt injection becomes a critical security risk that existing evaluations—focused on isolated malicious strings or single-step tool calls—fail to capture. INFUSE provides a standardized, realistic testbed that could shape how the industry measures and hardens agent robustness before widespread deployment. Per-model attack success rates (ASR-L) ranged widely from 3.2% to 41.9%, and existing guard models offered only limited protection, while prompt-level instructional hardening reduced mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model-dependent security-utility trade-offs. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/judydnguyen/infuse.

**Background**: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an attack in which adversarial instructions hidden in external content—such as files, web pages, or tool outputs—are interpreted by an LLM agent as legitimate task directives, a risk catalogued as LLM01 in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Long-horizon agent workflows involve multi-step dependencies, tool failures, and many interaction surfaces, which greatly expands the attack surface compared with single-turn chat. Prior benchmarks typically tested isolated malicious strings or narrowly scoped agent configurations, leaving a gap for end-to-end evaluation.

## [Verdict-MQ Encoder Answers Many Typed Questions in One Pass](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20778) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all typed questions about it in a single pass, using a structured attention mask that makes the state encoding independent of the questions and keeps questions from influencing each other. On a typed-decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict-MQ matches soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist across all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061). This work matters because automating organizational workflows requires answering many small typed questions about a single piece of state with probabilities reliable enough to act on without human review, and doing so in one pass rather than one pass per question could substantially cut inference cost. It also shows a smaller open encoder can beat a larger specialist model on this benchmark, which is relevant for teams building efficient decision-automation pipelines. The advantage survives per-system temperature scaling, and its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so the authors read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher rather than a pure capability gain. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC but loses on RACE and BoolQ, where training is unstable; a controlled comparison shows giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9-3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4-2.5x per-case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: A standard cross-encoder jointly encodes an input pair so tokens can attend to each other, which makes it strong for ranking and fine-grained semantic tasks but means each question requires a separate pass over the input. Structured attention masks constrain which tokens can attend to which others, and here they are used to make the shared state encoding independent of the questions. The benchmark evaluates probabilistic predictions with KL divergence, which measures how much an approximating distribution differs from a true one, and the Brier score, which measures squared error of predicted probabilities.

## [ReasonUni Adds Reasoning to Reconstructive Post-Training for Unified Multimodal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20781) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ReasonUni proposes a reasoning-augmented reconstructive post-training framework for unified multimodal models (UMMs), in which the model first reasons about what and how to edit an image and describes the target state before generating the target image. It also introduces TreeGRPO, a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images per path and aggregates visual rewards to jointly update both the understanding and generation modules under a unified objective. Existing reconstruction-based post-training for UMMs is perception-centric and provides limited supervision for reasoning about structure, intent, and transformation, so ReasonUni's approach could push unified models toward genuine mutual gains between image understanding and image generation. If the reported consistent benchmark improvements hold, it suggests a practical post-training recipe for the increasingly popular class of models that handle both multimodal inputs and outputs. The framework couples image-to-text understanding and text-to-image generation as dual tasks: given an original image and an editing instruction, the UMM reasons about the edit and describes the target state, then generates the target image conditioned on that understanding output. TreeGRPO samples multiple reasoning paths and candidate images per path, then aggregates visual rewards to update both modules under a unified objective, with experiments across multiple benchmarks showing consistent gains in both understanding and generation.

**Background**: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) integrate modalities such as images and text in a single architecture to jointly perform reasoning and generative tasks, but it remains debated whether their understanding and generation branches truly share unified semantic representations. ## [CoTranslator Converts Reverse CoT into Forward CoT for Efficient Reasoning Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20828) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose CoTranslator, a model that learns to translate reverse chain-of-thought (RCG) responses into the distribution of verified forward chain-of-thought (FCG) responses, trained on a small set of paired reverse and rejection-sampled forward data. Across six student models and six math benchmarks, it improves average accuracy over semantic suppression by up to 5.82 percentage points, and for two 4B students retains 95.0% of rejection sampling's accuracy using only 35.9% of its estimated compute. Reasoning distillation is a key technique for transferring multi-step reasoning from large teacher models to smaller student models, but obtaining verified CoT data efficiently is a bottleneck. CoTranslator addresses the known trade-off between expensive-but-verified forward generation and cheap-but-mismatched reverse generation, potentially making large-scale reasoning distillation substantially cheaper and more practical. The method is trained on a small set of paired reverse and rejection-sampled forward responses, and without retraining it transfers to a new mathematics dataset, a different teacher model, and STEM problems, improving average STEM accuracy by 4.88 and 4.31 percentage points for 4B and 8B students respectively. The abstract is truncated, so full architectural details and limitations are not fully visible.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation transfers multi-step reasoning from a large teacher model to a smaller student model by training the student on teacher-generated reasoning traces. Forward CoT generation (FCG) produces question-only responses that match the student's answer-free inference setting but can require many expensive teacher calls for hard problems, while reverse CoT generation (RCG) conditions on the known answer, making it cheaper but prone to post-hoc rationalization and a mismatch with inference conditions. Rejection sampling (RS) is a common technique that generates multiple candidate responses and keeps only those verified as correct, yielding high-quality but costly training data.

## [Amortizing Sequential Bayesian Experimental Design into Reasoning LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20832) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.20832) trains LLMs to perform sequential Bayesian experimental design by explicitly optimizing information-gain rewards for the reasoning that guides action selection, rather than relying on the model's own beliefs. On the Twenty Questions task, the resulting policies improve information acquisition and task performance, beat both inference-time and training-time BED baselines at substantially lower computational cost, and generalize to unseen categories. This suggests that adaptive information gathering can be learned as a generalizable reasoning skill in LLMs, which matters for any application where a model must ask clarifying questions or choose informative actions, such as clinical dialogue. The paper also reports positive transfer from Twenty Questions training to Medi-Q, a real-world clinical dialogue benchmark, hinting at broader applicability beyond toy tasks. The approach specifies the experimental generative model independently of the LLM's own beliefs, allowing optimization of expected information gain under a chosen model, and the authors investigate design choices including alternative generative-model constructions, reward estimation, hypothesis-space specification, multi-step objectives, and computational costs. The reported gains come at substantially lower computational cost than BED baselines, though the evaluation centers on Twenty Questions and Medi-Q rather than a wide range of experimental-design domains.

**Background**: Bayesian experimental design (BED) is a decision-theoretic framework that selects experiments or actions by maximizing expected utility, most commonly the expected information gain (EIG), which measures the expected reduction in uncertainty about latent parameters. Amortization means training a model once so that inference or decision-making becomes fast at test time, instead of solving an expensive optimization problem for every new query. This paper applies that idea to LLMs, teaching them to internalize the sequential BED policy as a reasoning skill.

## [Study Probes How Vision-Language Models Handle Negation via Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20852) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.20852) analyzes attention patterns in vision-language models (VLMs) to understand how they process negation, comparing model attention to human gaze on affirmative versus negated statements. The study finds that models generally do not follow human-like attention patterns when resolving negation, suggesting they rely on mechanisms outside of attention. Negation is fundamental to language understanding, and VLMs' failure to process it effectively can lead to errors in high-stakes applications like image retrieval and visual question answering. This work provides empirical evidence that current models may not use attention to handle negation, raising important questions for interpretability and model design. Layerwise analysis shows PaliGemma2-3B shifts object attention to the alternative under negation, but headwise ablations suggest this is a byproduct rather than a negation processing mechanism; LLaVA-1.5-7B also displays a spatial bias towards left-side objects. All evaluated models show a performance discrepancy between affirmative and negated questions.

## [Why Majority-Vote Rewards Track Verifiable RL: A Batch-Gradient Explanation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20898) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.20898) argues that majority-vote rewards in reinforcement learning work not because individual labels are correct, but because the relevant unit of analysis is the batch-level gradient update. The authors decompose the majority-vote update into a shrinkage term and a misdirection term relative to the gold update, and show that misdirection vanishes as batch size grows whenever label errors are incoherent across prompts. This provides a theoretical justification for a widely used but poorly understood technique in LLM alignment and self-training, where models are trained on pseudo-labels generated by majority voting over their own samples. It suggests that practitioners can rely on self-generated labels as a substitute for verifiable rewards as long as errors are incoherent, which could reduce dependence on expensive human annotation or verifiable reward functions. Measuring per-response gradients on five models, the authors find that majority-vote errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null, and that the majority-vote update agrees with the gold update as closely as two independent gold updates agree with each other. Randomly flipping up to 30% of gold labels leaves the update direction intact, while the same fraction flipped by a shared rule destroys it; the equivalence is local, as gold-reward training still ends ahead on held-out majority accuracy.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) trains LLMs using rewards based on objectively checkable outcomes, such as whether a final answer is correct, and has been used in models like DeepSeek R1 and Tülu 3. Because verifiable rewards are not always available, a common alternative is to use majority voting over a model's own samples as pseudo-labels, a form of test-time reinforcement learning. It was previously puzzling why this works, since majority vote only returns a model's modal answer and cannot add information about correctness at the prompt level.

## [Semantic Layers, Orchestration, Compaction Help Only Matching Agent Behaviors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20959) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.20959) presents a large-scale behavioral study of three context-engineering techniques (CETs) — semantic layers, orchestration, and compaction — evaluated alone and combined across seven LLMs on 1,514 long-horizon tasks from five benchmarks. The study finds that data agents without CETs fall into three behavior groups (investigators, premature answerers, and early stoppers), and each CET only converts its benefit into accuracy when it matches the agent's behavior group. The results challenge the assumption that context-engineering techniques are universally beneficial, showing that the same CET can actually hurt investigators — orchestration makes them overconfident and costs 5 percentage points, while compaction makes them repeat steps. This offers actionable guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based data agents by selecting CETs based on agent behavior, task demands, and accuracy-cost trade-offs. The evaluation covers behavior, accuracy, and cost across 1,514 long-horizon tasks, and finds that combining CETs yields smaller gains and losses than the sum of their individual effects. The paper derives guidance for choosing CETs by agent behavior, task demands, and accuracy-cost trade-offs, though it is characterized as an incremental empirical contribution rather than a paradigm shift.

## [EigDiff uses CLIP eigensamples to shrink diffusion training data up to 14x](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20999) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces EigDiff, a method that performs principal component analysis in the latent space of a pre-trained CLIP model to derive eigenvectors, then uses those eigenvectors as reference points to select a compact, representative training subset for diffusion models. Experiments across multiple diffusion models and datasets show training data can be reduced by up to 14x and subset selection accelerated by up to 1607x with only marginal performance differences. Training diffusion models is notoriously expensive because it requires large-scale datasets and many denoising steps, so cutting data needs by an order of magnitude could substantially lower compute costs and make diffusion training more accessible to smaller teams. It also shifts attention from the dominant step-distillation research direction toward data redundancy as an underexplored lever for efficiency. The method deliberately works in CLIP latent space rather than pixel space to avoid sensitivity to affine transformations of eigenimages, and the selected subset combines exemplars (images whose embeddings are closest to the eigenvectors) with diverse images. The reported 14x data reduction and 1607x selection speedup come with only marginal performance variation, though the abstract does not specify which diffusion models or datasets were tested.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Diffusion models learn to reverse a gradual noising process over many small denoising steps, which makes them powerful but extremely costly to train. CLIP is a contrastive vision-language model that maps images and text into a shared high-dimensional embedding space, which is useful for measuring semantic similarity between images. Principal component analysis (PCA) is a classic dimensionality-reduction technique that finds the directions of greatest variance in data, and EigDiff repurposes those principal directions as anchors for choosing which training images to keep.

## [Tracking the Unembedding Matrix During Language Model Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21025) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces parameter-trajectory crosscoding, a method that fits a single sparse dictionary to every token's readout row across all checkpoints, requiring only checkpoint weights rather than activations. Using it on Pythia, the authors identify a narrow early window (0.4–1.1% of pretraining) where the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. This work shows that behavioral timelines—when a model first outputs a correct token—can conflate what the model encodes with what its readout can express, meaning many developmental transitions dated early in training may reflect readout learning rather than capability acquisition. It offers a new tool for interpretability and training-dynamics research, with implications for how we evaluate when models truly acquire skills. The method differs from activation-based crosscoders by operating directly on checkpoint weights, and experiments with small models pretrained from scratch show that increasing the readout's learning rate makes it develop earlier and closes the encoding-expression gap sooner, with little effect on final loss.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: In transformer language models, the unembedding matrix (or readout) maps the final hidden state to vocabulary logits, and it is learned alongside all other parameters during pretraining. Sparse crosscoders are dictionary-learning tools that align activations across layers or checkpoints to track feature emergence, but they typically require activation data. This paper adapts that idea to parameter trajectories, enabling readout tracking from weights alone.

## [PremiseCheck Cuts Peer-Review Fact-Checking Cost in Half](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21046) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced PremiseCheck, a framework that fact-checks human and AI peer-review comments by having an LLM rewrite each comment into explicit premises without reading the paper, then using a cheap decision model to verify each premise against the paper. Alongside it, they released ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels factual errors in review comments across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences while also measuring cost and latency. Peer review is under growing strain from rising submission volumes, and both human and AI reviewers frequently misstate what a paper actually says, so a cheaper, faster way to catch such errors could improve review quality and academic integrity at scale. The work also matters because it shows how to combine frontier LLMs with lightweight decision models to get high accuracy at a fraction of the cost, a pattern relevant well beyond peer review. When each comment is checked individually, PremiseCheck achieves accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at roughly half the cost, and on NLP reviews specifically at about a quarter of the cost and less than half the latency. The key insight is that cheap decision models fail on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions, so decomposing comments into explicit premises lets a small model handle the verification step.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Peer review is the process by which experts evaluate research papers before publication, and reviewers sometimes make factual claims about a paper that are simply wrong, whether written by humans or generated by AI. Fact-checking those claims is hard because a frontier LLM must read the entire paper for every single check, which is expensive and slow. Decision models are lightweight systems that score whether a given statement holds in a text; they are cheap and fast but struggle with complex, multi-part statements. PremiseCheck addresses this by splitting the task: an LLM rewrites comments into simple premises, and the decision model verifies each premise against the paper.

## [TBRM-RLOO: Bellman-Consistent Trajectory RL for LLM Arithmetic Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21060) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes TBRM-RLOO, a Bellman-consistent trajectory reinforcement learning framework that combines Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization (TBRM) with a Reinforce Leave-One-Out (RLOO) group strategy and hindsight goal relabeling to convert sparse terminal rewards into dense token-level signals. On the Countdown arithmetic reasoning task, it boosts Pass@1 to 0.55–0.64 and achieves a state-of-the-art Pass@16 accuracy of 76.0–84.0%, outperforming SFT, IPO/DPO, and RLOO baselines while stabilizing gradient variance better than GRPO. Sparse terminal rewards are a core bottleneck in applying reinforcement learning to LLM reasoning, and this work shows that a value-based Bellman-consistency approach can outperform the dominant policy-based methods like GRPO on a verifiable arithmetic task. If the gains generalize, it could shift more LLM RL pipelines toward value-based objectives and offer better single-sample efficiency plus test-time scaling. The method uses the model logits to parameterize Q-values, value function, and policy under a KL-regularized RL framework, and the RLOO group strategy reduces gradient variance of the Bellman residuals. Evaluation is limited to the single Countdown task, so generalization to broader reasoning domains remains unverified, and the reported Pass@16 range (76.0–84.0%) suggests sensitivity to configuration or seeds.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning for LLM reasoning typically relies on policy-gradient methods such as PPO and GRPO, which can suffer from high gradient variance when rewards are only given at the end of a trajectory. Bellman Residual Minimization (BRM) is a classical value-based alternative that directly enforces Bellman consistency, and Trajectory Bellman Residual Minimization (TBRM) adapts this idea to LLMs by parameterizing Q-values and value functions from model logits. RLOO is a REINFORCE variant that uses multiple responses per prompt and a leave-one-out baseline to reduce variance, while hindsight goal relabeling reinterprets past trajectories as demonstrations for alternative goals to accelerate learning under sparse rewards.

## [Label-Free Reliability Estimation for Language Model Ensembles via EM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21085) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21085) proposes treating an ensemble of language models as a jury rather than an electorate, estimating each expert's reliability from agreement and disagreement patterns alone using Expectation Maximisation (EM) on unlabelled answer configurations. On a 1560-question benchmark with nine experts of up to 3B parameters, the method performs comparably to the same fusion rule with label-fitted weights, showing no statistically significant advantage from supervision. This work suggests that reliable model fusion may not require expensive ground-truth labels, which could make LLM ensembles far more practical in domains where labelled data is scarce or costly. It also reframes ensemble reliability estimation as a latent-variable inference problem, potentially influencing how future model-fusion and uncertainty-estimation systems are designed. The decision rule reduces to a log-odds weighted linear score over the experts' answer distributions, so what changes is not how the jury votes but how it learns whom to trust. The method outperforms the best single model with matched self-consistency and the strongest label-free alternative on the full benchmark, though the experiments are limited to relatively small experts (up to 3B parameters).

**Background**: Ensemble methods combine predictions from multiple models to improve accuracy, typically by assigning each expert a fixed reputation or weight learned from labelled data. Expectation Maximisation (EM) is an iterative statistical algorithm for finding maximum likelihood estimates when a model depends on unobserved latent variables, alternating between an expectation step and a maximisation step. This paper applies EM to a jury model where each question has a latent true answer and each expert reports it with unknown reliability, inferring those reliabilities purely from unlabelled answer patterns.

## [SIEVE Resolves Topological Collapse in Equivariant Point Cloud Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21087) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.21087) proves a topological obstruction in SE(3)-equivariant masked autoencoding for 3D point clouds, showing that standard masking forces the model to hallucinate orientation without a reference frame. The authors propose SIEVE (Scalar Invariant Extraction Via Equivariance), which uses a spherical projection mask to preserve global pose while obfuscating local semantics, and experiments confirm it avoids the predicted collapse where constant and noise masks fail. This work exposes a fundamental theoretical incompatibility between two popular ideas in 3D vision — masked autoencoding and SE(3)-equivariant networks — and offers a principled fix, which could guide future self-supervised learning designs for point clouds. The resulting embeddings improve over coordinate-based baselines and hand-crafted geometric descriptors, with the largest gains on generalization to unseen shape categories, suggesting practical benefits for 3D perception tasks. SIEVE compresses point cloud geometry into invariant scalar embeddings, and its spherical projection mask sidesteps the obstruction by construction rather than by heuristic masking. The paper is a preprint without community discussion yet, so the claims have not undergone peer review.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: SE(3)-equivariant networks are designed so that rotating or translating the input rotates or translates the output in a corresponding way, which is useful for 3D data such as point clouds. Masked autoencoding is a self-supervised technique that hides parts of the input and trains the model to reconstruct them, and it has been adapted to point clouds (e.g., Point-MAE) by partitioning them into local patches. Topological obstructions refer to situations where the geometric or topological constraints imposed on a model's latent space make certain training objectives impossible to satisfy, leading to optimization or representation failures.

A new arXiv paper (2610.21139) introduces stochastic optimization with mixed-fidelity first-order oracles, where oracles can have systematic bias and state-dependent variance, to decide when to use more expensive, higher-fidelity LLMs for downstream tasks. It develops two cost-aware meta-algorithms: a restarted cost-aware policy for known bias whose cumulative cost is no larger than the best fixed oracle in hindsight, and a budgeted certification scheme for unknown bias that uses occasional trusted-gradient evaluations to eliminate biased oracle sources. The meta-algorithms are realized using biased stochastic gradient extrapolation (SGE) and recursive regularization under state-dependent noise as subroutines. Synthetic and LLM-completion experiments show the adaptive policy skips several expensive LLM oracles and substantially reduces cumulative cost relative to fixed high-fidelity alternatives while achieving comparable accuracy; the unknown-bias case exposes an explicit tradeoff between certification cost and delayed detection of biased sources.

## [LLM Working-Memory Limits Stem from Interference, Not Attention Precision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21176) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.21176) dissociates two competing accounts of LLM working memory by testing 15 pretrained models from three families (70M to 14B parameters) plus minimal transformers on the N-back task. It finds that attention heads already attend to the correct target on most missed matches, and that suppressing non-target letter identity improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all conditions, while sharpening attention yields negligible gains. The result suggests LLM working-memory limits are a readout problem under interference rather than a failure to locate information, which could redirect architectural and interpretability efforts toward interference suppression instead of attention sharpening. It also strengthens the parallel between LLM attention and human working-memory interference accounts, relevant to both AI/ML researchers and cognitive scientists. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, though the model's own decisions barely distinguish the two. In larger models the task is spread over more heads and removing interference helps more, while in minimal transformers precision limits a single attention layer but a second layer removes this constraint.

**Background**: The N-back task is a classic working-memory paradigm in which a subject must decide whether the current stimulus matches the one shown N trials earlier; performance declines as N grows, and errors cluster on lures that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect position. LLMs reproduce this human signature, but it was unclear whether they do so for the same reason. Two accounts compete: a precision account, where softmax attention cannot concentrate weight on the item N positions back, and an interference account, where attention selects the right item but competing item content corrupts the decision. Linear probes are a mechanistic-interpretability tool that trains a simple classifier on a model's internal activations to test whether a specific feature is linearly decodable.

## [FedSumUp: Auditable Privacy-Aware Representation Sharing for Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21194) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FedSumUp introduces a learnable lossy compressor that runs on clients to produce compact, visually interpretable representations, letting users directly audit the privacy-utility tradeoff. It also proposes a data-free closed-loop optimization strategy that trains the compressor on the server by minimizing the discrepancy between original and twice-compressed representations after structure-preserving upsampling. Federated data condensation methods typically upload synthetic data that can leak sensitive information and are vulnerable to reconstruction attacks, while also imposing heavy client-side computation. FedSumUp addresses both problems simultaneously, making privacy-preserving federated learning more practical for resource-constrained edge devices and giving users a tangible way to assess privacy risks. Experiments on BloodMNIST, CIFAR-10, and ChestMNIST show reconstruction PSNR as low as 8.56 dB (synthetic PSNR as low as 5.45 dB), client runtime reductions up to 96.5% (from 778s to 27s on ChestMNIST), and competitive accuracy (89.72% ChestMNIST, 82.24% BloodMNIST, 65.63% CIFAR-10), while remaining robust to non-IID data distributions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Federated learning trains a shared model across many clients without centralizing raw data, but recent work shows that shared model updates or synthetic data can still be exploited by reconstruction attacks to recover private training samples. Federated data condensation compresses each client's local dataset into a small synthetic summary to reduce communication and computation, yet generating that summary is itself costly and can preserve sensitive details. Learnable lossy compression uses neural networks to compress data while preserving task-relevant information, and FedSumUp applies this idea to produce auditable representations instead of raw synthetic samples.

## [New RSS Metric Quantifies Feature Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21240) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS), a metric that identifies large feature responses in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that recur in a consistent direction when prompts are transformed while preserving the underlying request. The authors evaluate RSS across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, showing a reproducible redistribution profile on held-out prompt variants, and provide code at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score. This work matters because it separates recurring representation change from actual downstream failure, offering interpretability researchers a principled way to tell whether a feature shift in an SAE actually affects a model's readout or decision. It could improve how safety readouts and other downstream classifiers are audited for robustness under prompt paraphrasing. For a fixed linear readout, the paper derives an exact decomposition showing how response magnitude, readout coefficients, directional alignment, and the clean margin jointly determine downstream consequences. In two frozen safety readouts, combining RSS support erosion with the full clean margin yields recurrent failure AUROCs of 0.935 and 0.958 using median supports of only 20 and 19 features, compared with 0.965 and 0.964 using full erosion.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Sparse autoencoders are a popular interpretability tool that decompose a language model's internal activations into sparse, human-interpretable features, as shown in work such as Cunningham et al. (2023). A key open question is whether changes in these features under prompt transformations reflect meaningful model behavior or are merely artifacts, since a feature change observed on one transformed prompt need not recur or affect downstream computation. RSS addresses this by focusing on large, consistently directed feature responses and testing them on variants excluded from selection.

## [System1-Arena Benchmark Tests Which Decisions Need System-1 vs System-2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21244) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced System1-Arena, a benchmark with 92k questions across 105 tasks from 268 public sources and 138 closed-loop environments, designed to compare System-1 models (single forward pass, like Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API) against System-2 generative reasoning models. They evaluated 30 models, finding that the largest System-1 models match or exceed fast closed LLMs in non-agentic accuracy with better-calibrated probabilities at one-quarter the latency, while a reasoning LLM was most accurate at roughly 70x the cost. This benchmark addresses a timely question of which discrete decisions can be delegated to fast, cheap System-1 models versus slower generative reasoning, which directly affects the cost and latency of deploying LLMs in production decision pipelines such as phishing detection, routing, and agent control. Its scale and diversity make it a valuable resource for the AI/ML community evaluating the emerging System-1 model paradigm. The benchmark spans four groups—text classification and knowledge, applied decisions, evaluation and control, and agent and action—and includes real-time closed-loop environments from web shopping and SWE-bench coding control to robotics, games, and driving. In closed loops, large open LLMs succeeded most often (up to 32.9%), while small System-1 models rarely succeeded, suggesting System-1 models are best suited to non-agentic bounded decisions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: System-1 and System-2 refer to dual-process theory in psychology: System-1 is fast, intuitive judgment, while System-2 is slow, deliberate reasoning. In LLMs, System-2 approaches generate step-by-step reasoning tokens, whereas System-1 models like TypeSafe AI's Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API return probabilities over predefined options in a single forward pass without autoregressive text generation. This benchmark systematically measures where each paradigm excels.

## [FPoT Quantization Enables 4-Bit Multiplier-Free LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21257) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new paper introduces Fractional Power-of-Two (FPoT) quantization, which uses a base-√2 (half-octave) grid instead of the standard base-2 grid to achieve practical 4-bit weight quantization while keeping a fully integer shift-add datapath. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weights and activations, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline and comes within 0.4 percentage points of the uniform integer baseline. Multiplier-free inference is a key efficiency bottleneck for deploying large language models, and FPoT shows that 4-bit quantization can be both hardware-friendly and accurate. This could benefit researchers and practitioners working on model compression and hardware acceleration, since the method is framework-agnostic and can be combined with existing state-of-the-art PTQ techniques. The method combines a base-√2 weight grid with uniform integer activations, a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and a lightweight 1-adder √2 approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization. This yields a processing element with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier, and the results hold across seven models and three bit-widths.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the cost of large language model inference by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers, avoiding expensive retraining. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization is attractive because multiplying by a power of two can be implemented as a simple bit shift, eliminating the need for hardware multipliers, but its coarse base-2 grid causes significant accuracy loss at low bitwidths. FPoT addresses this by using a finer base-√2 grid while still preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath.

## [New Metric Measures How Well Sparse Autoencoder Features Compose Additively](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21261) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint introduces SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR), a metric that quantifies the behavioral variation left unexplained above a chosen interaction order in sparse autoencoder (SAE) representations. Across 18 model and behavior settings, learned SAE coordinates showed lower first-order residuals than sum-preserving random rotations of the same subspace, but pairwise terms still improved held-out coalition ordering in every setting. This work provides a rigorous way to test whether SAE features behave compositionally, a core assumption in mechanistic interpretability and AI safety. The finding that learned coordinates are more compositional than random rotations but not fully additive suggests that faithful joint explanations and interventions must account for feature interactions beyond individual effects. Under independent feature subset sampling, population SAR equals the normalized energy of interactions above the chosen order and bounds coalition ordering error for the optimal low-order approximation. In a combined steering experiment, pairwise modeling raised rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduced ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606, with code available at the OpenSAE GitHub repository.

**Background**: Sparse autoencoders are a popular tool in mechanistic interpretability that decompose a model's dense activations into sparse, linearly decoded features, aiming to make internal representations more interpretable. Compositionality refers to whether these features combine additively to produce downstream behavior, an assumption often made when interpreting or steering models. This paper introduces a metric to measure deviations from that additive assumption and compares learned SAE coordinates against random rotations to isolate the effect of the representation itself.

Researchers introduced TRACER, a training-free multimodal harness that builds minute-level action records from continuous hospital video and merges them with clinical records into hourly patient behavior reports, queried by an LLM agent. ## [TRACER: Trajectory-Aware Tool Retrieval for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21267) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TRACER introduces a retrieval front-end that indexes observed tool-call sequences in a trie and ranks continuations using a learned blend of empirical and contextual priors. On a mixed retail-and-telecom τ² environment, it improves GPT-5.4's tool-selection accuracy by 4.7 points while cutting input tokens per step by 80%, exposing only 5 of 128 tools. Exposing entire tool registries to LLM agents is costly and degrades selection accuracy as registries grow, so TRACER's token reduction and accuracy gains could make large-scale agent deployments more practical. Across six environments and four models, it beats full-registry selection in 21 of 24 model-environment pairs, with average gains of 6 to 10 points. The three exceptions where TRACER trails full-registry selection do so by at most 2.2 points, and in autonomous full-turn execution it matches GPT-5.4's full-registry task success with 61% fewer input tokens per step. The paper also analyzes failures in both regimes to identify directions for future work.
