**Background**: LLM agents typically choose tools from a registry, but passing the whole registry into the context window is expensive and can confuse the model as the number of tools grows. A trie is a tree-like data structure that stores sequences by shared prefixes, making it well suited to indexing and extending observed tool-call trajectories. TRACER combines this structure with a learned ranking of likely next tools, so the agent sees only a small relevant subset.

## [Loud and Clear: Fixing the Visual Evidence Bottleneck in Multimodal Document RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21318) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.21318) shows that in multimodal document RAG, retrieved pages remain underused even when the correct pages are retrieved: on SciEGQA oracle pages, five prior methods supply only 0.7K–2.7K visual tokens per query, yet raising the page-only budget from 1K to 32K improves accuracy by 15.22 points. The authors propose two requirements—Loud (fully using visual token capacity) and Clear (refining pages so evidence stands out)—and implement them as Loud and Clear (LoC), which combines higher-resolution pages with OCR of query-relevant regions without ground-truth annotations or extra training, beating eight prior methods and surpassing ColQwen3 by 8.88, 3.09, and 4.22 points on SciEGQA, ViDoRe-v3, and MMLongBench-Doc. This work shifts attention from retrieval quality to the generator's input representation, showing that a major accuracy bottleneck in multimodal document RAG lies in how retrieved pages are fed to the vision-language model rather than in finding the right pages. The findings give practitioners a concrete, training-free recipe (higher-resolution pages plus OCR of relevant regions) that could improve document QA systems in scientific, financial, and enterprise settings. The paper reports that at a fixed 16K token budget, adding ground-truth crops improves accuracy by 3.75 points over page-only input, and that full-page scaling outperforms repetition and tiling at matched budgets; for Clear, suppressing surrounding content helps without enlarging selected regions, and adding OCR of those regions to page images beats either input alone. LoC also outperforms its page-only variant under the same visual token budget, though results are limited to three benchmarks and the work is a preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

## [STOPD Accelerates On-Policy Distillation via Truncated Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21337) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which randomly truncates student rollouts at a sampled stopping position and corrects the resulting sampling bias using blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). The authors prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon, while experiments show 25-48% fewer generated tokens and 1.3-2.2x training speedups with accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD. On-policy distillation is a widely used technique for transferring capabilities from large teacher models to smaller students, but generating full rollouts and computing teacher feedback for every token is a major computational bottleneck. STOPD offers a theoretically grounded way to cut that cost substantially, which could make OPD more practical for resource-constrained teams and large-scale training pipelines. The method samples a stopping position per rollout before generation and lets the student generate until that position or natural termination, then applies blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling weight variance. The theoretical guarantees include expectation-preserving gradient sums and one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon, and evaluations span multiple teacher-student pairs, task domains, and optimizers.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on trajectories it generates itself, while a teacher model provides dense token-level feedback on those trajectories; this differs from static imitation of teacher-generated text and helps reduce distribution mismatch between training and inference. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) is a classical statistical technique that reweights observations by the inverse of their sampling probability to correct for bias when the sampled population differs from the target population. STOPD combines these ideas by treating truncated rollouts as a biased sample and reweighting them to match full-rollout training.

## [PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21390) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PriorityFEC introduces a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that orders high-importance KV blocks earlier in the transmission stream and protects them with a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism that schedules repair packets before the TTFT deadline. Implemented on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluated with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets, it achieves superior task quality over compared transport schemes, with advantages most pronounced under stringent deadline constraints. Cross-agent KV-cache reuse is a promising way to eliminate redundant prefill in edge multi-agent LLM systems, but unreliable links and strict TTFT deadlines make full cache delivery infeasible. PriorityFEC shows that jointly optimizing model-side KV utility and transport-side reliability can preserve task quality under these constraints, which matters for latency-sensitive edge deployments of collaborative LLM agents. PriorityFEC constructs a utility-aware source stream by ranking KV blocks by importance and placing high-utility blocks at earlier transmission positions, then uses receiver feedback to adaptively schedule FEC repair packets before the TTFT deadline. Evaluation uses Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on a distributed edge serving prototype, with gains over baseline transport schemes growing as deadlines tighten.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: In multi-agent LLM systems, when one agent passes context to another, the receiving agent often must re-run prefill over the shared context, wasting computation. Reusing the upstream agent's KV cache avoids this, but the cache must be transferred over the network before generation can start, and TTFT (time to first token) measures the latency from request to first output token. Forward Error Correction (FEC) adds redundant packets so receivers can recover lost data without retransmission, which is well suited to unreliable, latency-sensitive edge links.

A new arXiv paper (2610.21404) identifies a failure mode called 'aggregation-induced drift' in multi-reward LLM post-training, where symmetric aggregation of primary and auxiliary rewards improves aggregate reward while degrading primary-task performance. The authors prove that deterministic conditional-mean GRPO converges to auxiliary-favoring behavior under symmetric aggregation, and propose Trust-Anchored Gating (TAG) to provably reverse this selection. This work matters for researchers and practitioners using RLHF and multi-reward optimization, as it reveals that common aggregation strategies (symmetric, constrained, normalized) can silently undermine the primary objective. TAG offers a calibration-insensitive defense, achieving 0.581 pass@4 versus 0.220 for additive aggregation on Qwen3-4B with a brevity reward, while shortening responses by 44%. The paper formalizes the failure through a one-step multi-reward decision formulation and proves that under symmetric aggregation, deterministic conditional-mean GRPO converges to auxiliary-favoring behavior when auxiliary rewards are more reliably obtained, regardless of initialization. TAG first elects an anchor channel based on policy drift from optimizing each channel alone, then gates auxiliary credit on anchor satisfaction, structurally eliminating credit for auxiliary-only outcomes while preserving additional credit for joint success.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: LLM post-training often combines a primary reward (e.g., correctness) with auxiliary rewards (e.g., brevity or efficiency) to improve task performance and response properties. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning algorithm that scores a group of answers per prompt and rewards answers for beating the group average. Reward hacking occurs when models exploit reward signals in ways that boost measured reward but not the intended objective.

## [V-SHARE: First Provable Convergence Guarantees for Advantage-Based RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21448) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce V-SHARE, an advantage-based value-learning algorithm that combines cross-action value sharing with an importance-weighted Bellman-residual correction, and provide the first complete theoretical characterization of such methods, including asymptotic convergence and non-asymptotic finite-sample guarantees. They also identify a regime where V-SHARE mitigates the rare-action bottleneck of asynchronous Q-learning and uncover a contraction-variance tradeoff, motivating decreasing residual-preconditioning schedules and a two-timescale analysis. This work fills a long-standing theoretical gap for advantage-based value-learning methods, which are widely used in deep reinforcement learning but lacked rigorous convergence analysis. The identified contraction-variance tradeoff and rare-action bottleneck mitigation could directly influence future algorithm design and analysis in both tabular and deep RL settings. The algorithm decomposes the action-value function into a state-dependent value component and action-specific advantages, and uses importance-weighted Bellman-residual correction to correct for distribution mismatch. The authors develop decreasing residual-preconditioning schedules that combine faster early contraction with lower asymptotic noise, and a two-timescale analysis that removes the single-timescale residual-weight threshold while preserving convergence guarantees; experiments on discrete MDPs and deep RL benchmarks corroborate the theory.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: In reinforcement learning, Q-learning estimates the value of each state-action pair independently, which can be slow when some actions are rarely taken. Advantage-based methods instead share information across actions by writing the action-value as a state value plus an action advantage, an idea popularized by actor-critic algorithms such as A2C. Asynchronous Q-learning updates one state-action pair per iteration and is known to suffer from a rare-action bottleneck, where infrequently visited actions converge very slowly. V-SHARE provides the first complete convergence theory for advantage-based value learning, addressing both asymptotic and finite-sample behavior.

## [X-Fly: Staged Training for Full-Chunk Aerial Vision-Language Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21450) ⭐️ 7.0/10

X-Fly introduces a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial vision-language navigation that combines Recovery DAgger with Flow-GRPO, achieving 74.18% success rate on OpenFly test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen, versus 16.45% and 18.43% for full-chunk behavior cloning. The approach also cuts per-waypoint inference from 195 ms to 42 ms by executing complete predicted action chunks before replanning. Full-chunk execution is attractive for aerial VLN because it amortizes the high cost of querying large vision-language models, but it introduces severe no-stop failures and off-distribution states that standard imitation learning cannot handle. X-Fly's staged recipe directly addresses these failure modes, offering a practical path toward deployable, low-latency UAV navigation agents. Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state, while Flow-GRPO jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same-task closed-loop outcomes with outcome-verified stopping supervision. The method uses eight controls per decision, and no-stop failures accounted for 47.78% of full-chunk behavior cloning outcomes on OpenFly test-seen.

**Background**: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) tasks require UAVs to follow natural-language instructions through 3D environments using visual observations, and modern agents often rely on large vision-language models whose inference is expensive. Action chunking—predicting and executing a whole sequence of waypoints before replanning—amortizes that cost but shifts the policy into states not covered by expert demonstrations. DAgger (Dataset Aggregation) is a classic imitation-learning technique that iteratively queries an expert on the learner's own visited states, while Flow-GRPO adapts online policy-gradient reinforcement learning to flow-matching generative models.

## [SpecAgent turns strong LLMs into reviewers of weak-model tool-call drafts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21463) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21463) introduces SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol in which a weak model drafts tool-call trajectories grounded in real read-only observations, and a strong model verifies the longest semantically valid prefix in a single prefill pass, repairing only the first rejected step. On τ²-Bench it comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on MCP-Atlas edge-cloud deployments it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens. This reframes the strong model's role in agentic systems from author of every step to reviewer of grounded drafts, which could substantially cut latency and memory cost for long tool-calling workflows. It matters for anyone deploying multi-step LLM agents, since it suggests most routine steps need not be generated by an expensive frontier model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls while drafting and stops at the first action that would modify the environment, so verification is grounded in real observations rather than the strong model's own imagined actions. Because verification uses parallel prefill instead of autoregressive decoding, the strong model only decodes short verdicts and occasional repairs, though the approach still depends on the strong model's judgment of semantic validity.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the dominant design has a single strong model generate every step even though many steps are routine. Existing efficiency approaches keep the strong model as the generator: routers and collaborative agents decide which model handles each query or step, while speculative methods check a small model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. Speculative execution, borrowed from microprocessors and speculative decoding, lets faster models tentatively pursue likely next actions while a slower model validates them. Prefill is the inference phase that processes an entire prompt in one parallel pass, as opposed to decode, which generates tokens one at a time.

## [New Benchmark Shows LLMs Struggle to Tell Stories Out of Order](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21468) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces a benchmark of 83 published works to test whether large language models can generate nonlinear narratives, where the telling order differs from the chronological event order. Testing 19 models, the authors found that all models default to telling events more chronologically than the source works, and that both an automated judge and 71 human readers preferred the models' default chronological stories over the nonlinear ones they wrote on request. This work exposes a concrete limitation in LLM storytelling: models can follow an instruction to reorder events but cannot yet tell a nonlinear story well, which matters for AI-assisted fiction, screenwriting, and interactive narrative tools. It also provides a reusable corpus and evaluation framework for measuring temporal and causal structure in generated narratives, an area standard benchmarks largely ignore. For each of the 83 works, the authors annotated events in both chronological and telling order, plus a story graph capturing causal dependencies, character knowledge, and the questions the telling raises and resolves. Readers found the requested nonlinear stories harder to follow in 81% of decisive judgments, and preferred stories written from the story graph over those constrained to the published telling order in 72% of decisive judgments—a difference the automated judge failed to detect.

## [Poison Valleys Traces Path-Dependent Failures in LLM Code Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21514) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces 'Poison Valleys,' a diagnostic method that traces how misconceptions placed in an LLM's hypothesis or implementation plan stages lead to path-dependent failures in code repair. Across 1,844 model requests on two synthetic Python cases (PersistQueue and Dijkstra), moving a misconception from the hypothesis stage to the plan stage increased failure rates by 32.2% and 28.9% respectively. This work provides a measured, causal link from an upstream misconception to a specific code mechanism and failure form, offering a new diagnostic lens for researchers building and evaluating code-repair agents. It could help developers understand why agents fail even when final tests only reveal that a patch is wrong, not which earlier commitment caused it. The study uses an Oracle and targeted diagnostic coordinates to evaluate generated code, and finds that different misconceptions produce distinct, model-dependent patterns of violated software obligations, though several can converge on the same behavior. The experiments are limited to two synthetic Python cases, so generalization to larger real-world codebases remains to be tested.

## [Muon's Optimality Questioned: Radial Fragility and Minimax Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21549) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the Random-Radius Isotropic Curvature Model (RR-ICM) and the Polar-Factor Admissibility Set, providing an exact characterization of when Muon's scaled-polar update is optimal under arbitrary radial laws. It proves that all nonscalar admissible responses arise from radial atoms aligned with curvature kinks, and that atomless radial laws exhibit zero-capacity rigidity, meaning exact optimality only occurs when the gradient is already a scaled column isometry. This work challenges the generality of curvature-based explanations for Muon, showing that the average-curvature justification is fragile under radial perturbations. It provides a new minimax variational characterization of Muon's polar direction, which could guide the design of more robust matrix optimizers and inform theoretical understanding of why Muon works in practice. The Minimax RR-ICM replaces directional averaging with worst-case optimization over probability laws on the sphere, and its admissibility geometry is a positive-semidefinite trace slab, in sharp contrast to the spherical-zonoid geometry of the RR-ICM. The scale of the global minimizer is determined by a one-dimensional convex problem, and every nonzero global minimizer lies on the polar ray of the gradient.

Researchers released DialFork, the first benchmark to measure procedural hallucination in conversational agents, built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting four hallucination types to yield 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains. They also propose dialog-flow-aware metrics FlowKL and FlowScore, with FlowScore significantly outperforming all baselines across seven encoders at the dialogue level. It shifts evaluation focus from content factuality to procedural fidelity, potentially affecting how developers monitor and guardrail agents in real-time. DialFork contains 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains, validated by 30 human annotators, and defines three evaluation tasks at different granularities: monitoring deployed agents, procedural retrieval, and real-time guardrails. The benchmark is released under the MIT license at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, and the results show that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity.

## [BiShield-TEE Exposes Flaw in TEE-Shielded LLM Weight Obfuscation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21565) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21565) identifies a vulnerability called the Solution Determinacy Property (SDP) in unilateral weight obfuscation used for TEE-shielded on-device LLM partitions, showing that existing methods GroupCover and ArrowCloak provide negligible protection. The authors propose BiShield-TEE, a bilateral obfuscation framework that jointly obfuscates input and output dimensions to create ambiguous solutions, confining attack accuracy to the full-shielding black-box baseline while improving inference efficiency on real hardware. This finding is significant for AI security and model IP protection, as it demonstrates that widely used TEE-based obfuscation techniques can be broken, potentially exposing proprietary LLMs deployed on edge devices to reverse engineering and theft. The proposed defense offers a more secure and efficient alternative, which could influence future designs of confidential on-device inference systems. The SDP vulnerability arises because the obfuscation secret is uniquely determined, exposing the true key structure; under the authors' attacks, GroupCover and ArrowCloak achieve attack accuracy over 2.4 times the full-shielding black-box baseline, recovering near-complete model functionality. BiShield-TEE mitigates this by inducing ambiguous solutions through joint input-output obfuscation, hiding the true key among many equally valid candidates, and experiments across diverse models and datasets show it confines attack accuracy to the baseline while being more efficient than prior methods.

## [AVALON Enables Zero-Shot Indoor Navigation via Human-Seeded Topological Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21586) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AVALON is a zero-shot indoor navigation framework that combines human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and evidence-gated human-robot memory co-updating, requiring no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. On a Unitree Go2 robot, AVALON with X-NavDP completed a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5 success) with no mapping, 40.9% faster than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP timed out in all 5 runs. This work addresses a practical gap in service robotics: robots often enter buildings whose layouts are familiar to humans but unseen by the robot, and AVALON shows that human-seeded memory plus lightweight robot validation can enable reliable navigation without expensive mapping or training. If validated more broadly, such human-robot co-updating could reduce deployment costs and improve robustness for indoor service robots in real-world settings. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment; visual depth point-goal navigation uses verified node arrivals for translational re-anchoring without a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human operators specify task constraints unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, while the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation, with task relevance gating whether human-reported changes undergo robot validation.

**Background**: Zero-shot indoor navigation aims to let robots navigate new buildings without prior training or mapping, a challenge because most learning-based methods overfit to training environments. Point-goal navigation tasks a robot with reaching a coordinate goal using only onboard sensors and no map. AVALON combines these ideas with human input to handle the human-familiar, robot-unseen setting.

## [LLMs Fail at Direct iOS Protobuf Reverse Engineering but Excel as Toolmakers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21597) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21597) evaluates two frontier models, Claude Opus 4.8 and Codex GPT Sol 5.6, on reconstructing protobuf schemas from Apple binaries used by iOS location services. The authors found that most AI-generated schemas contained substantial errors that were hard to detect because they were internally consistent, but they successfully used Claude to write a validated Python tool called Extractor that reliably recovers schemas from Apple binaries. This work has direct implications for privacy and forensic research, warning that LLM-generated schemas should not be trusted for analyzing what iPhones send to Apple, while offering a validated tool-building paradigm for AI-assisted reverse engineering. It also provides a concrete methodology for decoding iOS location services traffic, demonstrated on a jailbroken iPhone 8 running iOS 16.7.11. The Extractor tool was validated against binaries compiled from schemas with known answers, previously published schemas, and network measurements, and it was then used to decode and analyze location services network traffic from a jailbroken iPhone 8. The key caveat is that direct AI use is unsuitable for forensic and privacy analysis because erroneous schemas are internally consistent and therefore difficult to detect.

## [Router Drift Control Mitigates Off-Policy Degradation in MoE RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21682) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Router Drift Control (RDC), a method that uses routing disagreement between rollout and training routers as a signal of off-policy staleness and selectively rejects high-drift responses at the sequence level. In asynchronous training, RDC combined with Truncated Importance Sampling (TIS) improves average peak validation accuracy across AIME 2024 and AIME 2025 by 5.5 points over TIS and 4.5 points over Rollout Routing Replay (R3). Off-policy degradation is especially harmful in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models because rollout-training discrepancies can change routing decisions and cause router drift, so RDC offers a targeted fix for a key bottleneck in scaling RL post-training of MoE-based large models. The gains growing with policy staleness and remaining effective in asynchronous RL suggest practical value for distributed training pipelines. The analysis shows that Rollout Routing Replay (R3) introduces gradient bias by losing contributions from experts selected by the training router but not the rollout router, whereas RDC's sequence-level filtering avoids this bias while preserving native expert selection and its learning signals for retained responses. RDC is evaluated on AIME 2024 and AIME 2025, and its benefit grows as policy staleness increases.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning can become off-policy due to training-inference mismatch, mini-batch updates, and asynchronous training, meaning the data used for updates comes from a policy that differs from the one being optimized. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to only a small subset of expert networks, so when the rollout and training policies disagree, the routing decisions themselves can change, a phenomenon called router drift. Rollout Routing Replay (R3) was previously proposed to mitigate this by reusing expert selections from the rollout stage during training, but the new paper shows it introduces gradient bias.

## [Human Interventions as Labels to Localize and Steer LLM Agent Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21708) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21708) proposes treating human interventions on misbehaving LLM agents not as discarded training data but as measurement labels that point to the internal computation that failed. In a controlled agent environment focused on over-asking behavior, a direction learned from intervention labels flipped 72-100% of held-out over-asks across five eligible model families (Qwen2.5-3B, gemma-2-2b, OLMo-3-7B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, Phi-4), while random directions under the same procedure flipped at most one episode. This work suggests human oversight signals can be repurposed as a cheap, scalable source of causal supervision for mechanistic interpretability, potentially improving agent reliability and AI safety without relying on expensive manual circuit discovery. It also shows that probe-gated steering can remove most of the simulated oversight burden while legitimate clarifying questions survive, which matters for anyone deploying LLM agents in production. Over-asking showed two mechanistic signatures: in four families the model demonstrably knows the request is unambiguous (the belief is decodable, causally inert, and orthogonal to the decision) yet asks anyway, while in the fifth family rare over-asks track different world-representations. Consolidating the fix into weights yielded a map rather than a rule — a LoRA confined to the causal band passed every pre-fixed criterion on one model while behavior cloning on identical data broke retention, the reverse held on three families, and on the fifth the outcome crossed the boundary across seeds; a pre-written geometric rule failed on two out-of-family tests and the authors report the failure rather than fitting a replacement.

**Background**: Mechanistic interpretability is a subfield of explainable AI that reverse-engineers the internal algorithms and circuits of neural networks, often by analyzing the residual stream — the linear path through a transformer's depth that carries information across layers. Activation steering methods intervene on hidden states during the forward pass to change model behavior, and prior work such as EAST has applied this to LLM agents. This paper combines these ideas by using human interventions as labels to causally localize and steer a specific agent failure mode.

## [Language Embeddings in Recommenders Leak Item and User Identities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21713) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21713) shows that a simple cosine-similarity attack can recover item identities from language embeddings used in recommender systems, achieving high mean reciprocal rank across multiple language models and candidate-set settings on two real-world datasets. The authors further demonstrate that this item-level leakage propagates to user re-identification from sparse ratings, and that obfuscating item descriptions only yields a clear leakage-utility tradeoff. Recommender systems increasingly rely on language embeddings to represent item content, so this work exposes a privacy risk that platform operators and ML engineers may not have accounted for. It matters because the attack requires only auxiliary item text from external sources, meaning real-world deployments could be vulnerable without any direct access to the model's internal data. Leakage is strongest when the adversary's partial information overlaps with the victim representation, but it also persists through semantic alignment between independently sourced descriptions, and the mitigation of obfuscated descriptions does not eliminate the risk without degrading utility. The evaluation uses mean reciprocal rank as the privacy metric across two real-world datasets and multiple language models.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Recommender systems commonly convert users and items into low-dimensional continuous vectors called embeddings, which capture preferences and item characteristics for tasks such as collaborative filtering and content-based recommendation. Language embeddings are a recent variant that encode item text using language models, and cosine similarity is a standard measure of how close two vectors are in direction. Mean reciprocal rank (MRR) is a ranking metric that averages the reciprocal of the rank position of the first relevant result, and is often used to evaluate how well an attack or retrieval system places the correct answer near the top.

## [FIRM: Fisher-Informed Retention Merging for Federated LLM Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21720) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose FIRM (Fisher-Informed Retention Merging), a single-round framework for stable, retention-aware server-side aggregation in federated LLM unlearning. FIRM uses client-local Fisher statistics to build a Fisher-normalized base merge and adds a second-order retention projection with a unique minimum-distance solution, mitigating the magnitude explosion that degrades retained utility. Federated LLM unlearning is important for privacy-preserving removal of targeted knowledge when forget and retain data stay on private clients, but naive cross-client aggregation can blow up update magnitudes and hurt retained utility. FIRM offers a theoretically grounded, single-round aggregation fix that could make federated unlearning more practical for real deployments. FIRM's second-order retention projection admits a unique minimum-distance solution whose dual scales with the number of retain clients rather than model dimension, keeping it computationally tractable. Experiments on WMDP, TOFU, and MUSE-HP with Zephyr-7B and Llama-3-8B show utility gains at comparable forgetting on WMDP and MUSE-HP, but metric-dependent trade-offs on TOFU.

**Background**: Federated learning trains models across decentralized clients without sharing raw data, typically by aggregating locally trained updates on a server. LLM unlearning aims to remove specific knowledge from a model, and federated unlearning combines the two so that forget and retain data remain private on clients. Fisher information measures how sensitive a model's output is to parameter changes and is widely used in machine learning for regularization and continual learning.

## [Why Search-Augmented LLMs Read Snippets but Not Sources](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21731) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21731) investigates why search-augmented LLMs produce outdated answers even when relevant evidence is available, using temporal facts whose values changed after the models' training cutoffs. Testing one proprietary model with deployed web search and six open-weight configurations under controlled retrieval, the authors find models frequently answer from search snippets without opening the underlying source pages, which correlates with more outdated answers and unfaithful citations. The findings expose a reliability gap in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and search-augmented LLM systems: having evidence available does not mean the model actually uses it, which directly affects the trustworthiness of citations and the freshness of answers. This matters for anyone building or relying on search-grounded assistants for time-sensitive information such as news, prices, or policy changes. The study uses controlled experiments plus a layer-wise analysis showing a gap between evidence availability and effective use: even when retrieved evidence measurably influences the model's internal predictions, the model may still favor outdated information in its final answer. The evaluation covers one proprietary model under deployed web search and six open-weight model configurations under controlled retrieval, with snippet-only answering linked to higher rates of outdated answers and unfaithful citations.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique in which a large language model first retrieves documents from an external source and then uses them to answer a query, supplementing the knowledge baked into its training data. Because LLMs are trained on static snapshots of data up to a knowledge cutoff date, they have no built-in knowledge of later events unless browsing, search grounding, or prompt-provided context supplies it. Search-augmented LLMs extend this idea by querying the live web, but the new paper shows that retrieving a page and actually reading it are two different things.

It also runs simulations with LLM agents, finding that polycentric structures repeatedly emerge but remain fluid, and that different-capacity models (Sol vs. Luna) differ in how they exercise authority. The reduced-form model shows that while larger constituencies offer greater cost-sharing benefits, the marginal value to a center of retaining any single constituent declines as group size grows, so the threat of individual exit can discipline delegation only up to an endogenous accountable size. A new arXiv paper (2610.21750) formalizes 'intervention harm' in concept-based models and proves that the previously proposed sufficiency and localisation criteria are not sufficient to guarantee that concept interventions improve downstream performance. The authors introduce a complementary monotonic intervention objective that penalizes increases in task loss along partial intervention trajectories, and show that combining it with endpoint training substantially reduces harmful partial corrections. This work challenges a widely held assumption that benign leakage—where concept representations encode extra task-relevant information—is safe for human-in-the-loop oversight, which matters for deploying concept-based models in high-risk domains like healthcare and finance. It provides both a theoretical counterexample and a practical training objective for researchers building interpretable and intervenable AI systems. The paper distinguishes harm after all concepts are intervened on (endpoint harm) from harm under partial interventions, the more realistic use case, and finds that concept supervision incompleteness correlates with increased intervention harm. Optimizing the model when all concepts are intervened on—a previously proposed leakage mitigation objective—reduces endpoint harm but does not reliably prevent harmful partial corrections, motivating the new monotonic objective.

This paper shows that assumption fails under partial interventions, where users correct only some concepts.

## [Offline Risk-Sensitive RL Gets Provable Guarantees via Optimized Certainty Equivalents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21870) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces pessimistic value-iteration algorithms for offline risk-sensitive reinforcement learning using optimized certainty equivalents (OCE), covering both dynamic-OCE (recursive per-step) and static-OCE (single OCE on cumulative rewards) formulations. It establishes tight sublinear suboptimality upper bounds and matching minimax lower bounds in the tabular setting, and extends to large state spaces with pessimistic least-squares value iteration under linear function approximation with explicit dependence on feature dimension d. This is the first work to provide offline algorithms with both upper and lower suboptimality bounds for general OCE-based risk-sensitive RL, filling a gap where prior work only handled online settings or specific risk measures. It matters for safety-critical applications such as healthcare and finance where environment interaction is costly and risk aversion is essential, and it advances the theoretical foundations of safe and robust RL. The bounds explicitly capture how risk sensitivity, encoded by utility functions, affects learning difficulty, and the linear function approximation results depend on the feature dimension d. The work is purely theoretical with no empirical validation, so practical performance remains untested.

Optimized certainty equivalent (OCE) is a general class of convex risk measures that unifies mean, mean-variance, CVaR, and entropic risk through optimization over cash compensations, making it a natural framework for a unified analysis.

## [Theory Explains Why Sequence Models Learn In-Context Before Specialising](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21901) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.21901) develops a learning theory in a solvable topic model showing that in-context learning and specialised prediction emerge at distinct sample complexities: the in-context predictor appears early, while the specialised predictor only emerges once training tokens outnumber the parameters of the data-generating process. Trained transformers reproduce both scales and the crossover between them with no fitted parameters. This addresses a fundamental open question in deep learning theory: why models favour one generalisation strategy over another, which determines behaviour beyond the training distribution and thus controls potential capabilities and risks. It could inform how pretraining data quantity and quality shape model behaviour, affecting researchers designing and evaluating large sequence models. The theory is built on a solvable topic model where documents are drawn from a finite mixture of latent topics, mirroring the heterogeneity of modern pretraining data, and the dataset admits two distinct solutions: a specialised predictor that stores the finite topic mixture and an in-context predictor optimal for topics never seen during training. The predicted sample-complexity scales and the separating crossover match transformer training results remarkably well without any fitted parameters.

A new arXiv paper introduces the concept of strategic identifiability for inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) in strategic multi-agent environments, proving that learning from a fixed policy pair can fail to identify rewards regardless of the number of expert samples K. To address this, the authors propose an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games that combines maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, achieving finite-sample guarantees on Stackelberg sub-optimality that match a minimax rate of K^{-1/2} up to polylogarithmic factors. This work reveals a fundamental limitation of applying standard IRL to strategic settings, where a reward that explains observed behavior may not induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. The paper focuses on two-player repeated Stackelberg games, where the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. The finite-sample guarantees bound the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, and the approach is evaluated in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.

A pre-registered observational study of 465 agent-authored pull requests from 246 repositories found that higher baseline CodeHealth significantly reduces the token cost of agentic code review and fix across three LLMs, with each CodeHealth point associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. Agentic-Priors lets an LLM state a new user's trade-offs in interpretable terms, such as willingness to pay or value of time, which are then mapped to a prior over multinomial logit coefficients and refined by a Bayesian learner as choices are observed. The dataset covers five European languages and was constructed using translation for some tasks and regeneration pipelines where translation was insufficient. ## [TIPS: A Tiny Learned Controller for Inference-Time Scaling in Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22099) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced TIPS, an approximately 600K-parameter controller that learns both unmasking and remasking policies for masked diffusion language models while keeping the underlying model frozen. On GSM8K and MATH-500 with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, the full-canvas and two-block TIPS variants reach 58.46% and 57.97% micro-averaged accuracy at a budget of 32 decoder evaluations, exceeding the strongest baseline by 12.1 and 11.6 percentage points. This work shows that a lightweight learned decoding policy can substantially improve the accuracy-compute trade-off in diffusion language models without retraining the large backbone, suggesting a cheap and transferable path to better inference-time scaling. It could influence how future masked diffusion models such as LLaDA are decoded and how test-time compute is allocated for reasoning tasks. TIPS uses visibility-aware confidence features and a shallow transformer to decide which tokens should be visible, while a fixed schedule controls the expected visible fraction; it is trained via supervised warmup followed by reinforcement learning from terminal correctness rewards. Both variants are trained at a budget of 32 evaluations yet remain competitive at higher budgets without retraining, though the results are from a preprint with limited community discussion so far.

## [Causal Integrated Gradients Routes Attribution Along Causal Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22126) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Causal Integrated Gradients (CIG) and Causal Expected Gradients (CEG), which extend the integrated gradients attribution method by routing the integration path along a known causal graph among input features. The authors show CIG matches causal Shapley value accuracy on a synthetic benchmark at a fraction of the computational cost, and outperforms DeepSHAP and standard integrated gradients on simulated single-cell gene expression data and real interferon-β stimulation data. Existing gradient-based attribution methods that account for feature dependencies do not scale to high dimensions, and they tend to credit a feature's downstream effects rather than its true upstream cause. By embedding causal structure into the attribution path, CIG can recover upstream drivers that current methods miss, which matters for explainable AI and causal inference in domains like genomics where causal relationships such as transcription factor regulation are partially known. CIG decomposes each feature's attribution into a direct effect and effects mediated through its causal descendants, and it retains the computational efficiency and, under conditions on the causal graph, the axiomatic guarantees of standard integrated gradients. The method is evaluated in three settings of increasing realism: a synthetic benchmark with a known causal model, simulated single-cell gene expression data with a known gene regulatory network (Dyngen), and real interferon-β stimulation data where only an approximate causal graph is available.

## [EMO: Training-Free Test-Time Framework Alternating Context Optimization and Logits Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22160) ⭐️ 7.0/10

EMO introduces a training-free, closed-loop test-time computation framework that alternates between an E-step (revising a system context using textual gradients from an external judge) and an M-step (constructing a confidence-constrained logit correction by contrasting next-token distributions under revised and preceding contexts). Across eight models and six benchmarks under greedy decoding, EMO improves the zero-shot baseline in 39 of 40 aggregated settings, averaging +9.10 percentage points, and adds +1.53 points over context-only optimization (TextGrad) with the same judge. This work offers a theoretically grounded, training-free way to adapt frozen language models at inference time, which could reduce reliance on fine-tuning or parameter updates for domain or task adaptation. Its connection between context optimization and parameter optimization, plus the finding that test-time compute should be split between candidate generation and verification, may influence how future LLM adaptation and inference-budget allocation methods are designed. Theoretically, EMO connects parameter and context optimization through a shared target-KL objective and additive logit representations, deriving the steering vector from context-induced logit displacements; under context-improvement and faithful-steering assumptions, it proves a one-round decrease in target KL divergence for sufficiently small steering strength. At matched target-model generation budgets, accuracy advantages over best-of-N are strongest on Llama, while oracle coverage is higher in most comparisons despite fewer candidates, highlighting a coverage-selection gap.

**Background**: Test-time computation refers to spending extra compute during inference—rather than during training—to improve a model's outputs, and it has become a major focus for boosting LLM reasoning. Expectation-maximization (EM) is a classic iterative algorithm for maximum-likelihood estimation with latent variables, and EMO adapts this alternating E-step/M-step structure to context and distribution refinement.

## [Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22174) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Mosaic introduces Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a general setting allowing an arbitrary number of sessions within a single trajectory, and proposes a critic-free hierarchical optimization method that incorporates session-usage signals at the trajectory level and shapes session advantages by estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show Mosaic outperforms trajectory-level advantage broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Existing agentic RL methods assume single-session trajectories, but inference-time techniques like context compaction and subagent forking produce multi-session trajectories, creating a train-inference mismatch. Mosaic addresses this gap and could improve how LLM agents allocate and use sessions, benefiting researchers and practitioners building long-horizon agentic systems. The method is critic-free, avoiding a separate value network, and operates hierarchically: trajectory-level advantage estimation incorporates session-usage signals, while session-level advantages are shaped by estimated marginal contribution. Experiments were conducted on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B, and further analyses showed improvements in session utility and allocation, which the authors suggest is a promising target for future multi-session agentic RL research.

## [Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22244) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces LinguaGuardBench, built from the 1,220 labelled steps of TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj, in which only the user instruction is translated into German, French, Turkish, Swahili and Amharic while every tool call, observation and label stays byte-identical. Testing 19 guards, the authors find that most open, small and purpose-built guards change their safety verdicts under translation beyond their own noise floor, with the effect growing for rarer languages. This reveals a previously unrecognized multilingual security surface: a guard's safety verdict can depend on the language of the user request, meaning an attacker could bypass protections simply by phrasing a malicious request in a low-resource language. The finding has direct implications for anyone deploying agent guards in multilingual environments, and it shows that English-only guard training and evaluation benchmarks are insufficient. Among the nine guards below 13B parameters, the mean placebo-adjusted flip rate rises from +1.5 percentage points on French to +4.4 pp on Amharic; open guards of 12-30B parameters block more benign steps (up to +5.0 pp false positives), while every significant recall loss is in a guard below 10B (up to -7.4 pp). Frontier guards shift by at most about one point, with Gemini 3.8 Flash returning identical verdicts with and without the request, and English paraphrase moves every guard less than translation does.

## [Subspace Tuning (SST) Mitigates Catastrophic Forgetting in LLM Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22293) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Subspace Tuning (SST), an optimizer-agnostic method that restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace of weight matrices, eliminating changes along principal singular directions. Experiments show that protecting up to 99% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving target-task performance, with the effect strengthening as model and data size grow and nearly eliminating forgetting in the large-model regime. Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs, and SST advances the learning-forgetting Pareto frontier, making it a practical default for fine-tuning pre-trained language models. It composes well with SFT and self-distillation, potentially benefiting researchers and practitioners in LLM training and adaptation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. It also keeps the model close to its base distribution, inducing 2–4× less KL drift than baseline recipes.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Catastrophic forgetting refers to the phenomenon where a model loses previously acquired capabilities when learning new tasks. Recent work connects forgetting to how far and along which directions fine-tuning moves the weights, with on-policy methods avoiding updates to principal singular directions. Singular value decomposition (SVD) decomposes a matrix into singular values and vectors, and the principal singular directions correspond to the largest singular values that capture the most important information.

## [Linear Decodability Before Fine-Tuning Predicts Generalization After](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22300) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.22300) introduces a distinction between 'active' facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, and 'inert' facts, which can be recalled but do not support generalization. Across 11 language models and 70 relations, the linear readability of a relation in pretrained representations strongly predicts whether fine-tuning on a relabeled version of that relation generalizes to held-out subjects, with Pearson correlations of r = 0.87 to 0.92. This finding suggests that whether a model can generalize a newly fine-tuned relation depends less on whether it can recall the original facts and more on how readily their shared structure can be linearly read out from pretrained representations. It offers a practical diagnostic for predicting which facts will transfer, with implications for model editing, knowledge injection, and understanding of transfer learning in language models. The association persists when controlling separately and jointly for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model's accuracy on the original relation, and subject frequency in pretraining text, and it is robust to re-randomizing label assignments and fine-tuning seeds. When mapping a fine-tuned model's wrong label back to its original answer, the recovered answers are more often among the linear probe's top answers than among the pretrained model's own top answers.

Researchers propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation that separates scene dynamics from camera-induced variation for predictive 3D world modeling. A scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view geometry foundation model features into a view-decoupled scene state, which an autoregressive world model predicts and a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. By removing view dependence from world states, GeoState makes future state evolution easier to predict and enables decoding under either predicted or externally specified cameras. The method builds on frozen geometry foundation model features and an autoregressive world model that models camera motion separately.

It also proposes Text2potential, which converts vision-language critic diagnoses into staged potentials for action-chunk value learning, raising out-of-distribution success from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6% across four manipulation task families. Its gains on LIBERO-Pro, from 25% to 84% under position perturbations and from 1% to 76% under instruction perturbations, suggest the approach could substantially improve robustness of manipulation policies. Text2potential provides dense supervision for policy updates while preserving the task's optimal policy under standard potential-based shaping assumptions, and measured learning progress guides further generation and program refinement. CoDA exceeds the strongest closed-loop baseline by 9.5 percentage points using the same generation budget, though results are limited to four manipulation task families and simulation-based evaluation.

## [Self-Programmed Execution Lets LLM Agents Orchestrate Themselves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06898) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.06898v2) introduces self-programmed execution (SPE), an agent architecture in which the model completion itself serves as the orchestrator program, with the harness only evaluating it rather than imposing a fixed orchestration policy. The author also presents Spell, a Lisp dialect whose programs can edit and re-evaluate themselves without replaying side effects, and shows that frontier models not trained for SPE or Spell can learn it in-context and complete challenging agentic tasks. This work challenges the dominant design of LLM agents, where an external harness hard-codes the turn-to-turn control loop, by letting the model itself decide state transitions. If validated, it could shift agent architectures toward self-orchestration and open research into what strategies models might learn when explicitly trained for SPE. Because the program's source code doubles as the model's context window content, SPE requires a language with unusual features; Spell supports programmatic self-reference via a quine form, and its effectful expressions (such as model invocations) are structured so that re-evaluating an edited program does not replay side effects. The experiments use existing models not trained for SPE or Spell, and code is available at github.com/lukejoconnor/spell.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Most LLM agents today run inside a harness (or orchestrator) that maintains state, manages interaction history, selects tools, and decides when to prompt the model again. Self-programmed execution replaces this fixed policy with the model's own completion, which is executed as a program to load the next agent state. Spell is a Lisp dialect chosen because Lisp's homoiconic structure makes it natural for programs to treat their own source code as data and modify it.

## [Preping Builds Agent Memory Before Any Task Appears](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13880) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.13880v2) introduces Preping, a proposer-guided framework that lets an agent build procedural memory before it ever sees a target-environment task, using only self-generated synthetic practice. The framework centers on proposer memory, a structured control state where a Proposer generates synthetic tasks, a Solver executes them, and a Validator decides which trajectories enter memory and feeds feedback back to the Proposer. It targets the cold-start gap that every agent faces when dropped into a new environment with no task-specific experience, a problem that offline demonstration-based and online post-deployment memory construction both fail to solve. If the approach generalizes, it could make agents useful from their first interaction while cutting the cost of memory building, which the paper reports as 2.99x lower on AppWorld and 2.23x lower on BFCL v3 than online memory construction. Experiments on AppWorld, BFCL v3, and MCP-Universe show Preping beats a no-memory baseline and matches strong playbook-based methods built from offline or online experience. The authors stress that gains come not from synthetic volume but from proposer-side control over feasibility, redundancy, and coverage, combined with selective memory updates; the work is an arXiv preprint and appears as a NeurIPS 2026 poster.

## [Life-Harness Adapts Frozen LLM Agents at Runtime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22166) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released Life-Harness, a lifecycle-aware runtime harness that improves frozen LLM agents by evolving reusable interventions from training trajectories without changing model weights or evaluation environments. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct, it beats Meta-Harness and AHE by 28.7 and 7.5 percentage points in mean accuracy across seven shared environments while using 8.5% and 68.4% fewer optimization tokens. The work shifts agent adaptation from updating model parameters to engineering the runtime interface, which matters for deterministic, rule-governed domains where failures often stem from model-environment mismatches rather than model capability. The evolved harnesses also transfer to frontier models like GPT 5.5, Opus 4.8, and Gemini 3.1 Pro, yielding an average 3.5 percentage point accuracy gain. Life-Harness converts recurring interaction failures into reusable interventions across four areas: environment contracts, procedural skills, action realization, and trajectory regulation, and then remains fixed for evaluation on unseen tasks. Evaluation covered eight environments from AgentBench, τ-bench, τ²-bench, and AppWorld using 18 open-weight backbones, plus three frontier models on seven environments.

## [Harness-Bench: Benchmarking Agent Harness Effects Across Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27922) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Harness-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates how different agent harness configurations affect performance across multiple LLM backends under shared task environments, budgets, and evaluation protocols. The benchmark contains 106 sandboxed offline tasks and analyzes 5,194 execution trajectories, revealing substantial variation in completion, process quality, efficiency, and failure behavior across model-harness pairings. This work argues that agent capability should be reported at the model-harness configuration level rather than attributed to the base model alone, addressing a critical gap in how agent systems are evaluated. It could guide future agent infrastructure design and provide a reproducible foundation for diagnosing reliable, efficient, and auditable agent execution stacks. Harness-Bench preserves each harness's native execution behavior while recording final artifacts, execution traces, usage statistics, and validator outputs, enabling analysis beyond final completion. The analysis identifies recurring execution-alignment failures where plausible reasoning becomes decoupled from tool feedback, workspace state, evidence, or verifiable output contracts.

## [KACE: Knowledge-Adaptive Context Engineering for Math Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00532) ⭐️ 7.0/10

KACE introduces a knowledge-adaptive context engineering method that decides per problem both how much inference to spend and which learned knowledge to show, using a fixed tiered self-consistency schedule (2, 3, then 5 samples behind agreement gates). It reaches 77.3% on MATH-HARD versus 72.7% for Best-of-5 self-consistency with fewer solver calls, and also achieves 61.1% on AIME 2025 and 48.1% on OlymMATH-EN. This addresses a known failure mode in context engineering where a single learned prompt lets irrelevant lessons compete with relevant ones, and it shows that adaptive knowledge selection plus tiered inference can beat standard self-consistency while spending fewer solver calls. The approach could improve reliability and token efficiency in production LLM reasoning systems that rely on accumulated execution feedback. Offline, a teacher-guided learner distills failed training traces into short typed cards kept in a store partitioned by difficulty tier and domain, and each escalated tier reads only the cards of its (tier, domain) cell. A component analysis shows the store adds 4.0 points on MATH-HARD and 3.7 on OlymMATH-EN over the tiered schedule alone, and the (tier, domain) reading rule outperforms every alternative rule for choosing cards from the same store.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Context engineering is the practice of optimizing the context elements that accompany a user prompt — such as system instructions, retrieved knowledge, and task metadata — to improve reliability and token efficiency in LLM systems. Self-consistency is a prompting technique that samples multiple reasoning paths and aggregates their answers to improve accuracy. Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from a stronger teacher model to a learner, and here it is used to compress failed execution traces into reusable prompt cards.

## [SkillDAG exposes a self-evolving typed skill graph as an agent-callable interface](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03056) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SkillDAG introduces a self-evolving typed skill graph that LLM agents can query and update directly, rather than consuming it through a fixed retrieval pipeline. It uses a propose-then-commit protocol to register execution-backed edges, and reports +14.3 points of ALFWorld success over full-library prompting, vector retrieval, and Graph-of-Skills, with ranking holding flat across a 10x pool expansion. Skill selection is becoming a core bottleneck as LLM agents scale to large skill libraries, and treating skills as independent documents misses dependencies, conflicts, and duplicates. By making inter-skill structure queryable and revisable by the agent itself, SkillDAG points toward more robust agent architectures that can grow with their skill pools instead of degrading. The propose-then-commit protocol is agent-driven and bounded by three structural invariants—acyclicity, non-contradiction, and append-only reversibility—rather than a statistical confidence threshold, so a single execution observation can suffice to commit an edge. Search returns vector matches, typed-edge neighbors, and conflict signals, and a two-view cold-start constructor recovers cross-functional pairs that flat self-similarity misses.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents increasingly rely on large libraries of reusable skills, and the subset of skills placed into the prompt determines what the agent can accomplish. Conventional approaches either enumerate the library or use top-K embedding retrieval, both of which treat each skill as an independent document and assume relevance is a property of one skill at a time. Graph retrieval encodes relations between skills but typically spends them in a fixed pipeline, handing the agent an opaque bundle rather than letting it inspect and revise the structure.

## [EvoFlux uses inference-time evolution to repair tool workflows for small agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12674) ⭐️ 7.0/10

EvoFlux introduces an inference-time evolutionary search method that repairs executable tool plans by iteratively editing structured graphs of tool calls and dependencies based on live execution errors. On held-out MCP-Bench tasks spanning 28 live servers and 250 tools, it improves execution success from roughly 3% to 17–24% across four small planners (1.5B–4B parameters). This shows that execution-guided inference-time repair can reliably boost small, low-cost tool-using agents when supervised fine-tuning data is scarce, potentially making capable agents deployable on cheaper hardware. It also highlights a practical alternative to expensive ReAct-style prompting, which reached higher peaks only at 4–20x greater planner-token cost per solved task. EvoFlux performs targeted edits such as replacing tools, correcting parameters, inserting missing steps, and removing redundant ones, guided by real execution errors against live servers. Notably, SFT and SFT+DPO trained on the same 177 demonstrations and 624 preference pairs match or underperform the zero-shot baseline, suggesting that inference-time search can outperform limited supervised fine-tuning.

## [LLM-as-an-Investigator: Evidence-First Agentic Reasoning for Robust Interactive Problem Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13220) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces LLM-as-an-Investigator, an evidence-first methodology for interactive problem diagnosis, implemented through the Solution Investigator Agent (SIA). SIA orchestrates three complementary reasoning behaviours—a Diagnostic Reasoner, a Hypothesis Investigator, and a Counterfactual Investigator—through a shared investigation state, and is evaluated on a structured corpus built from 303 technical forum threads across mechanical, electrical, and hydraulic domains. LLM-based troubleshooting often suffers from premature commitment to an incorrect hypothesis when problem descriptions are incomplete and multiple causes can explain the same symptoms. By separating diagnostic quality from hypothesis coverage and oracle potential, and by making diagnoses traceable through cited dialogue evidence, this work could improve the reliability of AI-driven diagnostics in technical support and industrial fault diagnosis. Final selection in SIA uses cited dialogue evidence and a separate verification step, while explicit hypothesis and evidence records preserve unresolved alternatives. The evaluation compares SIA with direct, reasoning-based, interactive, and search-based baselines, including adaptations of ReAct and Tree of Thoughts, and uses ablations and paired stress tests to assess robustness to plausible but misleading user hypotheses.

The paper proposes Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM), a framework for population-level storage and retrieval of agent trajectories, where producer agents contribute trajectories to a shared repository and consumer agents retrieve them to improve task execution. A new arXiv survey (2606.21550v2) examines recent work that applies social choice theory to the problem of aggregating conflicting human judgments in AI alignment from human feedback. It shows how this perspective exposes failure modes in the feedback aggregation layer and reveals a broader design space for handling disagreement in explicit, principled ways. As language models are aligned using human preferences, disagreements among annotators are typically collapsed into a single objective, which can hide whose values are being encoded. The survey is a review rather than a new method, and it focuses on the aggregation layer where individual human judgments are combined into a training objective. It draws on social choice results such as voting rules and impossibility theorems to characterize failure modes and possible design choices for handling disagreement.

## [BEA Estimator Enables Latency-Aware Routing Across Heterogeneous LLM Pools](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18253) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces the Batch Evolution Aware (BEA) estimator, which predicts time-to-first-token (TTFT) for arriving queries by replaying the serving framework's token-batch formation from a snapshot of an instance's current workload. Built on BEA, the BEAR router jointly balances accuracy, cost, and latency, improving the utility of responses delivered within their targets by 63% on average over existing latency-aware routers and by 30.5% over the best baseline. Current LLM serving stacks typically decouple accuracy-cost routing from latency-aware load balancing, which can produce suboptimal decisions when a query is sent to a replica that is actually congested. By making fine-grained TTFT prediction fast enough for the critical routing path, this work points toward serving systems that can simultaneously optimize response quality, monetary cost, and user-perceived latency. BEA predicts TTFT within roughly 5% error and each prediction takes about 0.1 ms, accounting for prefill and decode compute and memory requirements as well as contention among queries served in the same batch. The paper also provides an analytical framework for a model instance under a limited processor-sharing scheme that calculates expected TTFT in closed form and captures qualitative latency trends as load increases.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Time-to-first-token (TTFT) measures how long a user waits from submitting a prompt until the model generates its first output token, making it a key latency metric for interactive LLM applications. LLM query routers usually pick a model based on accuracy and cost, while separate load balancers such as join-the-shortest-queue or round-robin spread requests across replicas using coarse signals like queue length or historical average latency. Because these two layers are decoupled, a router may not know that a chosen replica is currently slow, which is the inefficiency this paper targets.

## [ContinualSkillBench Tests Whether LLM Agents Truly Evolve Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03874) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.03874v3) introduces ContinualSkillBench, a dynamic benchmark for in-context continual skill learning spanning five domains with 100 difficulty-ordered tasks each. Experiments show sequential execution generally improves performance, but retaining context and feedback without any explicit skill library yields nearly the same mean performance as maintaining one across two models and three domains. The result challenges the assumption that explicit skill libraries are the key mechanism behind agent improvement, suggesting much of the observed gain may come simply from accumulated context and feedback. This has direct implications for how agent frameworks are designed and where engineering effort should be invested. Explicit skills still provide selective benefits for tasks requiring reusable procedures or precise outputs, and the weaker model (GPT-4o) accumulates more skills but reuses them less often, indicating difficulty consolidating task-specific experience into reusable procedures.

## [LLMs Show Newer-Law Bias in Temporal Legal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14610) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.14610v2) formalizes Temporal Applicable-Law Determination (TALD) and introduces TALD-Bench, a benchmark of 51,956 Chinese civil judgments spanning the enactment of China's Civil Code. Evaluating nine advanced LLMs, the authors find a strong bias toward newer law (over 70% accuracy on new-law cases versus below 25% on old-law cases) and a disconnect between statutory knowledge and its application. This work matters because legal reasoning requires identifying which version of a statute applies based on when the legally relevant events occurred, not when the case is adjudicated, and LLMs are increasingly deployed in legal-tech pipelines. The findings suggest that improving legal knowledge or general reasoning alone may not fix temporal errors, pointing to a need for better capability deployment rather than more knowledge. The benchmark spans the enactment of the Chinese Civil Code and includes 51,956 civil judgments; temporal-law hints substantially improve TALD accuracy but also increase uncertainty during statutory-version reasoning. Stronger general reasoning performance does not consistently translate into better TALD accuracy, indicating a bottleneck in how models deploy existing capabilities.

The framework organizes six composable capabilities — Act, Evaluate, Investigate, Correct, Learn, and Observe — across a constitution layer, a runtime inference pipeline, and a learning loop, and ships an open-source reference implementation for invoice processing. The technical contributions include a hybrid deterministic-LLM correction engine with 21 condition operators and three tiers of actions, a three-layer investigation architecture for ground-truth-free compliance validation, and a programmatic safety loop that verifies rule correctness before human approval. ## [MegaMem: Dual-View Retrieval for Ultra-Large Context Windows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22137) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MegaMem, a source-resolved dual-view retrieval system, was released as an arXiv preprint (2608.22137v2) with code on GitHub. It separates semantic search from generation evidence, resolving every distilled hit to an immutable source ID before reciprocal-rank fusion, deduplication, and cross-encoder reranking, and on EnterpriseRAG-Bench (500k+ documents, ~650M tokens) it lifts Overall from 68.22 to 82.26 and reaches 86.50 Correctness. The work targets a real bottleneck for long-context LLM applications and agent memory: keeping hundreds of millions of tokens searchable while passing only a bounded, attributable evidence set to the generator. By decoupling searchable memory scale from answer-context size, it offers a practical path toward accurate retrieval over memories ranging from hundreds of millions to one billion tokens, which matters for enterprise search, codebase assistants, and long-running agents. The pipeline uses original and transformed queries against both distilled records and detailed evidence, applies reciprocal-rank fusion, deduplication, and cross-encoder reranking, and only the top-ranked detailed evidence within a fixed budget is loaded for generation; post-answer attribution then identifies which loaded sources support the answer. Notably, this is an arXiv preprint without peer-review validation, and no community discussion was provided.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) augments an LLM by fetching external documents at query time, but classic RAG pipelines struggle when the underlying memory grows to hundreds of millions of tokens. Reciprocal rank fusion is a rank-aggregation algorithm from 2009 that merges multiple ranked lists into one ranking, while cross-encoder reranking rescores candidate passages with a more precise model that jointly encodes query and document. MegaMem combines these ideas with a source-resolved design so that searchable memory can scale far beyond the context window actually fed to the generator.
