## [Rubric-Guided RL Framework for Open-Ended LLM Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27906) ⭐️ 7.0/10

An arXiv preprint (2608.27906v3) proposes a reinforcement learning framework that combines human-authored rubrics with model reasoning and hierarchical rewards to evaluate open-ended LLM outputs. The diagnosed failures are converted into token-level weights inside the GRPO objective, and the method is instantiated on interactive web application generation, reaching an average pass rate of 41.25% on MiniAppBench and 76.19% on ArtifactsBench. Most reinforcement learning gains for LLMs have come from tasks with reliable verifiers, such as math or code, where correctness is easy to check; extending RL to open-ended generation has been bottlenecked by the lack of usable reward signals. This work offers a concrete recipe for turning fuzzy judgments of partial success into actionable policy gradients, which matters for anyone post-training models on creative, agentic, or UI-generation tasks. The framework uses human rubrics to anchor evaluation to task intent, while model reasoning plus hierarchical rewards distinguish partially successful outputs and attribute failures to specific output regions. These attributions then weight tokens in the GRPO objective, and ablation studies plus out-of-distribution evaluations suggest the components contribute individually and the gains transfer without degrading other evaluated tasks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning algorithm that estimates advantages by normalizing rewards within groups of candidate outputs, avoiding the need for a separate value critic and making it popular for LLM post-training. Standard RL treats a whole response as a single pass-or-fail signal, which is problematic for open-ended tasks where outputs are only partially correct. Token-level credit assignment aims to fix this by rewarding the specific tokens responsible for success or failure, and hierarchical reward design structures rewards at multiple levels of granularity.

The framework uses controlled error injection to establish causal links between specific reasoning failures and measurable quality degradation, and applies step-level filtering based on marginal contribution to identify which reasoning steps drive or undermine trajectory quality. The framework offers two update schemes (generational and steady-state) and Fermi-type and Bose-type occupancy rules that define solution identity and whether duplicates are allowed; a small positive temperature improved training quality over the collapsed T = 0 point in the generational Bose-type scheme. ## [CompMat-Bench: A New Benchmark for AI Agents in Computational Materials Science](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00636) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced CompMat-Bench, a benchmark of 94 tasks derived from recently published computational materials studies, where AI agents must complete individual research steps such as preparing simulation inputs and analyzing outputs. By pre-reproducing the research steps and using fixed-rule grading instead of an LLM judge, the benchmark avoids the need to rerun expensive simulations during evaluation. Evaluating AI agents on real scientific tasks has been hampered by the cost and time of repeating experiments or simulations, so this benchmark offers a practical way to compare agents on authentic materials research steps. It could accelerate progress in AI for science by enabling reproducible, low-cost assessment and systematic analysis of agent failure modes. The benchmark supports four evaluation conditions: single tasks and workflows of related tasks, each with full or reduced methodological guidance. With full guidance on single tasks, agents based on three LLMs achieved pass rates of 66.0–90.4% across the 94 tasks, while longer workflows and reduced guidance lowered performance mainly for weaker agents, and failure analysis attributed most failures to scientific errors rather than software usage errors.

## [Global Coherence: An Impossibility Theorem for Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02036) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.02036v2) formalizes the "global coherence problem" in multi-agent AI, proving an Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem that establishes the exact boundary for when a policy can guarantee a valid action. The paper introduces a local-to-global runtime semantics X = (H, C, G, F; D) and validates it across ten studies, including TeamBench and tau2-bench Telecom. This work provides a theoretical foundation showing that local intelligence cannot substitute for missing global state, which has direct implications for AI safety and the design of distributed multi-agent systems. It suggests that current approaches relying on stronger models, more reasoning, or more messages may fundamentally fail without proper shared-state governance. The theorem states that if k indistinguishable worlds require pairwise-disjoint actions, the best randomized worst-case success is 1/k, and finding the smallest sufficient context is NP-hard. However, counterexample-guided refinement can find and recertify a sufficient context at 28% of the all-field cost, and a harness that owns shared state achieves 1.00 on tau2-bench Telecom where current-state checks score only 0.07.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-agent systems are AI architectures where multiple autonomous agents collaborate to solve problems, but they can fail when agents make locally valid decisions that jointly produce invalid results. This paper addresses that failure by introducing formal methods—including topology, category theory, groupoids, and sheaves—to model how local views can be glued into a coherent global state. The Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem is analogous to other impossibility results in mathematics and economics, such as Arrow's theorem, which show fundamental limits of certain systems.

## [KV²: A Self-Refining KV Cache for Long-Context Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03198) ⭐️ 7.0/10

KV² introduces a query-agnostic KV-cache compression method based on selective reconstruction: it first uses a lightweight proxy scorer to identify informative in-context tokens, then reprocesses only that subset to compute final eviction scores. On RULER 16K at a 2% KV-cache budget, it improves the average score over the next-best baseline by more than 40 percentage points, and on LongBench it attains the highest average across 2%–10% budgets while using less runtime and peak memory than full-context reconstruction. The KV cache is a dominant memory and cost bottleneck for long-context LLMs, especially when one prefilled context must serve many different queries. KV² shows that reusable, query-agnostic compression does not require reprocessing the full context, which could make tight-budget long-context serving substantially cheaper without sacrificing much quality. The method is training-free and operates in two stages: a cheap proxy scorer selects candidate tokens, and only those tokens are reprocessed for final eviction scoring. The reported margin over baselines widens as the budget tightens, and the authors claim lower compression-stage runtime and peak memory than full-context reconstruction; code is released anonymously.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Transformer-based LLMs cache key-value (KV) pairs for every token in the context during inference, and this cache grows linearly with sequence length, layers, hidden dimension, and batch size, consuming gigabytes of memory. Query-agnostic KV-cache compression preselects and compresses the cache independently of future queries so that one compressed cache can be reused across many queries, trading compression cost against answer quality. Prior work such as KVzip and Compactor explores similar reusable eviction strategies, while benchmarks like RULER and LongBench measure long-context capability.

A new arXiv paper introduces bounded-staleness asynchronous evolution strategies (ES) for post-training long-horizon LLM agents, systematically varying policy lag and the fraction of stale fitness measurements on the WebShop benchmark. The authors report that natural asynchrony closely tracks synchronous ES, with only small degradation in evaluation accuracy even under extreme staleness, including when all fitness measurements are stale. Synchronous update barriers waste compute in long-horizon agent training because faster workers idle while waiting for slower ones, and this work suggests ES can tolerate substantial policy staleness without explicit off-policy correction. If validated, this could make asynchronous post-training a practical efficiency win for LLM agent development, reducing wall-clock time and resource waste. The study uses the WebShop benchmark and introduces two stress tests to probe extreme staleness cases, finding that degradation in evaluation accuracy remains small even when all fitness measurements are stale. The approach is bounded-staleness, meaning the allowed lag is capped, and it builds on ES as a backpropagation-free alternative that requires many perturbed-policy evaluations.

Researchers introduced ParanoiaEval, the first benchmark for unified evaluation of risk-treatment capabilities in coding agents, grounded in the Avoidance-Transfer-Mitigation-Acceptance (ATMA) framework from software engineering risk management. It contains 200 evidence-controlled repository-level task pairs from 50 repositories, each pair differing only in treatment-defining evidence, plus dedicated metrics for risk-treatment violations and evidence responsiveness evaluated by a human-calibrated agentic judge. The benchmark operationalizes the four ATMA treatments for coding-agent settings and uses a human-calibrated agentic judge for reliable evaluation; experiments also reveal systematic patterns consistent with established human risk-management findings, suggesting human practice knowledge can guide diagnosis and improvement of this capability.

## [AlphaRLM Trains LLMs to Discover Symbolic Factors from Financial Literature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14959) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AlphaRLM is a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors directly from financial literature, without requiring input factor expressions. It introduces Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO) and aligns the generation policy with market feedback via executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards, outperforming strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500. This work shows that policy learning, rather than prompting or evolutionary search, can directly generate literature-grounded alpha factors, potentially changing how quantitative researchers build factor libraries. The strong cross-market performance of an 8B model suggests smaller, domain-aligned LLMs can be practical tools for quantitative finance. The framework uses two reward signals: an executable-validity reward ensuring generated expressions can be computed, and a grouped-return-separation reward that captures non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Experiments cover CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500, with the 8B model achieving notable cross-market generalization, though the abstract does not report specific annualized excess return figures.

Predictive rehearsal trains on model-generated inputs while retaining recorded targets and accumulates recurring errors into a spatial prior, and action-response-based spatiotemporal credit assignment combines perturbation responses, prediction error, and the rehearsal prior to allocate visual supervision. ## [CoPE Co-Evolves Acting and Forecasting for Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20597) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.20597v2) proposes CoPE, a method that adds multi-step action targets as a third form of supervision for training language agents, alongside value and observation targets. On successful on-policy trajectories, CoPE trains the policy backbone to generate the action sequences following each history, and each action is also supervised when forecast from preceding histories, forming a temporal ensemble that lets acting and forecasting co-evolve. Training language agents is bottlenecked by the high cost of long-horizon rollouts, and standard agentic RL learns only from a terminal scalar reward, leaving intermediate-step supervision largely unused. CoPE shows that exploiting this supervision can improve both aggregate performance and sample efficiency, potentially lowering the compute cost of building capable agents. Across five benchmarks (ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebShop, τ²-bench, and AppWorld), CoPE achieves stronger aggregate performance than GRPO and RL baselines with predictive auxiliary targets, and delivers up to 1.9× and 2.0× higher sample efficiency than ECHO and GRPO respectively on ScienceWorld. The gains come with a single policy backbone, no additional models, no separate pretraining, and no inference overhead, since the policy still acts one step at a time at inference.

**Background**: Language agents are LLM-based systems that interact with environments over multiple steps to complete tasks such as web navigation or embodied decision-making. Prior work has tried to exploit intermediate supervision through value targets (estimating per-step success probabilities) or observation targets (fitting environment responses), but both are hard to construct well because value targets derive from the same single scalar signal and observation targets are long, noisy, and only reach one step ahead.

## [FactGuard Benchmark Targets Unanswerable Questions in Long-Context LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05607) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers released FACTGUARD, a multi-task workflow and benchmark (FACTGUARD-BENCH) with 25,220 examples and context lengths up to 128K, targeting Lack of Evidence and Misleading Evidence scenarios. Evaluating eleven open-source and proprietary LLMs showed the best model reached only 71.62% accuracy, while training with the benchmark improved accuracy to 81.17%. This addresses a critical reliability gap: LLMs often hallucinate or overconfidently answer when evidence is missing, which is dangerous in information-seeking applications. The benchmark and training method offer a scalable path toward more faithful long-context models that can reject unanswerable questions. The benchmark includes 25,220 examples with contexts up to 128K tokens, and the leading model achieved only 71.62% accuracy before training, highlighting a significant reliability gap as context scales. Training with FACTGUARD-BENCH improved overall accuracy to 81.17% and enhanced reasoned rejection capabilities.

Researchers released UniFGVC, a universal training-free framework that reframes few-shot fine-grained visual classification (FGVC) as a multimodal retrieval problem instead of fine-tuning model parameters. Its core component, the Category-Discriminative Visual Captioner (CDV-Captioner), uses chain-of-thought reasoning and visual references to generate attribute-rich captions that highlight discriminative features between similar classes. By avoiding parameter fine-tuning, UniFGVC sidesteps the overfitting and loss of open-world knowledge that typically plague MLLMs adapted to sparse few-shot data. Experiments on 12 FGVC datasets show it outperforms existing few-shot CLIP-based methods and even surpasses several fully-supervised MLLM-based approaches, suggesting retrieval-based inference could become a general alternative to fine-tuning in low-data regimes. UniFGVC is plug-and-play, working with arbitrary pre-trained visual and textual encoders by extracting features from both modalities and computing similarity against predefined category templates. The framework converts images into attribute-enriched image-description pairs, and the CDV-Captioner mitigates hallucination through chain-of-thought reasoning and visual references.

A new arXiv paper (2512.15756v2) shows that scientific performance feedback can redirect generative models toward productive regions beyond human-imposed design conventions, without explicitly rewarding departures from those conventions. The approach was validated in reactor lattice design with simulated feedback and in chemical reaction-condition selection with measured yields, using a pretrained sequence policy and a small non-language policy respectively. This work suggests that AI-driven scientific discovery can escape the biases embedded in human-curated training data, potentially uncovering novel designs and reaction conditions that experts might overlook. It has implications for fields like nuclear engineering and chemistry, where convention-bound datasets may limit innovation. In measured reactions, the probability of selecting task-specific ligand choices excluded from training rose from 0.29 to 0.70–0.71 as expected yield error decreased. Controls in the lattice setting showed that the productive region identified during adaptation provides reusable information to random search, and removing the target penalty redirected four of five matched runs, linking adaptation direction to the scientific objective.

This paper introduces AXIOM, a perturbation-based framework that curates AXIOMBENCH, a large-scale multilingual benchmark containing 1,962 code evaluation problems with a balanced program quality distribution. AXIOM works in two stages: quality-constrained semantic perturbation, which applies predefined perturbation rules to control each program's target quality, and hybrid quality calibration, which selects semantically distinct programs and streamlines manual annotation. Existing benchmarks for code LLM-as-a-judge suffer from coarse binary pass/fail labels, subjective human-annotated scores, and unbalanced code quality distributions that fail to test discriminative capability. AXIOMBENCH addresses these gaps, offering a more reliable way to validate code evaluation metrics that are increasingly used to catch defects like API hallucinations before deployment. The framework reframes program scores as the refinement effort needed for deployment, and uses multisource context during streamlined manual annotation to improve reliability. The benchmark is multilingual and large-scale, with 1,962 problems designed to span a balanced range of code quality levels.

## [Resolving Interference: A Lightweight Fix for Model Merging Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.13467) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2603.13467v2) proposes Resolving Interference (RI), a lightweight adaptation framework that formally defines Cross-Task Interference as the drift in a merged model's representation relative to its constituent expert models. RI disentangles expert models to be functionally orthogonal to other tasks using only unlabeled auxiliary data, improving state-of-the-art merging methods by up to 3.8% and generalization to unseen domains by up to 2.3%. Model merging is a growing technique for building multitask models without additional training, but interference between independently trained experts often degrades the merged result. RI's ability to work without task-specific labeled data makes it valuable in data-scarce settings and could make merging pipelines more robust and easier to tune. RI is robust to the source of auxiliary input and is significantly less sensitive to tuning of merging hyperparameters than prior approaches. The codebase is publicly available at https://github.com/pramesh39/resolving_interference.

**Background**: Model merging combines the parameters of multiple models, each specialized on a different task, into a single multitask model without retraining. Expert models are networks trained to specialize on a subset of data or a particular task, and when merged, their representations can conflict, a problem known as cross-task interference. RI addresses this by making each expert functionally orthogonal to the space of other tasks, using only unlabeled auxiliary data.

## [TensorDex Cuts Model Hub Storage 70.5% via Tensor-Level Delta Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.17104) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present TensorDex, a lossless, tensor-centric storage system that performs delta compression at tensor granularity rather than model granularity. Evaluated on 2,890 randomly sampled Hugging Face models, it reduces storage footprint by 70.5% (37% lower than the state-of-the-art design) while achieving 22.9 GB/s compression and 28.4 GB/s decompression throughput, 3.86x and 1.49x faster than the next-best system. Model hubs now store hundreds of petabytes of LLMs, with fine-tuned variants dominating the footprint, so a 70.5% reduction directly translates into massive savings in storage cost, bandwidth, and checkpoint management for AI infrastructure. The tensor-granularity approach also removes the need for reliable model lineage metadata, which is often missing or unreliable at hub scale. TensorDex decomposes models into tensors, uses compact bit-level fingerprints to predict tensor-pair compressibility without accessing full data, and incrementally organizes tensors into multi-center clusters to select effective bases as new models arrive. Because different tensors within the same model may be most similar to tensors from different models, model-level pairing leaves substantial redundancy unexploited.

**Background**: Delta compression stores only the difference between a target file and a similar reference, so its effectiveness depends critically on choosing a good reference. Model hubs host many fine-tuned variants of the same base model, which contain substantial cross-model redundancy that delta compression can exploit. However, at hub scale, model lineage metadata is often missing or unreliable, and redundancy exists at the tensor level rather than the whole-model level, motivating a tensor-centric design.

A new arXiv paper (2605.02255v2) presents a unified threat model and systematic ablation study of four representative LLM privacy attacks: Membership Inference (MIA), Attribute Inference (AIA), Data Extraction (DEA), and Backdoor Attacks (BA). The study finds attack-specific sensitivities — MIA depends on dataset characteristics and attack strategy, AIA on model and training characteristics, DEA increases with model scale and training-data repetition, and BA achieves consistently high success rates. The derived deployment recommendations — such as prioritizing membership leakage assessments in retrieval-augmented systems and minimizing repeated personal information in training data — offer actionable guidance for teams building or deploying LLMs. The paper consolidates known attack categories rather than introducing a novel attack, and its findings are derived from ablation experiments across dataset, model, training, and scale factors. Notably, data extraction risk grows with both model scale and training-data repetition, while backdoor attacks remain highly successful regardless of the factors studied.

Ablation studies systematically remove or vary individual factors to isolate which ones affect an outcome.

## [CRAFT: Freezing LLM Weights to Learn Continual Tasks Without Forgetting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05732) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.05732v3) proposes CRAFT, a continual learning framework that keeps LLM weights frozen and instead learns low-rank interventions on hidden representations. Similar tasks share an intervention based on output-distribution similarity, a KL penalty limits forgetting within shared interventions, and a small task-private intervention in the deepest layers preserves dedicated capacity, enabling label-free task identification at test time. Catastrophic forgetting is a major obstacle to deploying LLMs in sequential, real-world settings, and CRAFT offers a parameter-efficient alternative to LoRA-based continual learning that improves overall performance and reduces forgetting across benchmarks and model scales. Its robustness to task ordering and label-free task identification could make continual adaptation more practical for production systems. CRAFT judges task similarity by how each task alters the model's output distribution rather than using a learned gating network, and it combines a KL penalty for shared interventions with a small task-private intervention in the deepest layers. It is an arXiv preprint, so results have not yet undergone peer review, and no community discussion was provided.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when a model fine-tuned on new tasks loses its ability to perform previously learned tasks. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) addresses this by freezing pre-trained weights and injecting small trainable rank-decomposition matrices into each layer, greatly reducing trainable parameters. Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence is an information-theoretic measure of the difference between two probability distributions, often used as a penalty to keep a fine-tuned model close to its original behavior.

## [HIMMEL: Hierarchical Dual-Path Encoding for Efficient Long Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08158) ⭐️ 7.0/10

HIMMEL introduces a hierarchical video-language framework that routes a small set of sparse semantic anchor frames to a heavy host ViT while encoding dense inter-frame intervals with a lightweight compressed-domain tri-stream adapter that distills motion-vector maps, residual maps, and I-frame context into aligned motion tokens. On Video-MME, it surpasses a dense 32-frame baseline by +2.3 pp (61.2% to 63.5%) while using 3.6x fewer context tokens and running in 1.03 s per question instead of 2.75 s; with a Qwen3-VL-8B host it reaches 64.9% on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU. Long video understanding with multimodal language models is bottlenecked by expensive RGB decoding, token growth with frame count, and weak motion perception under sparse keyframe sampling, and HIMMEL attacks all three simultaneously rather than pruning tokens after decoding. Its separation of semantic and motion capacity into distinct paths, plus the finding that benefits grow with video length, could shape future research on efficient video-language models and make long-video inference more practical on modest hardware. The tri-stream adapter combines motion-vector maps, residual maps, and an I-frame context branch, and its tokens are injected into the LLM via a differentiable placeholder mechanism after a Stage 1 contrastive alignment that places motion representations in a geometry compatible with the frozen visual backbone. An InfoNCE alignment objective outperforms MSE regression by +1.5 pp, and extensive ablations across stream composition, motion-encoder family, fusion mode, alignment objective, anchor count, LoRA rank, and video duration confirm the full tri-stream contributes to the gains.

Video codecs already compute motion vectors that map how pixels move between consecutive frames, and compressed-domain processing exploits this existing codec information to avoid full pixel-level decoding. HIMMEL builds on these ideas by keeping the expensive ViT for a few semantic frames while using codec-derived signals for dense motion, and it uses contrastive alignment (InfoNCE) to match the motion tokens to the frozen visual backbone's representation space.

## [FinPILOT Adapts RL Trading Policies at Inference Time via MPC-Inspired Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12653) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Evaluated across five pretrained policies (PPO, SAC, A2C, TD3, DDPG) on DJ30 equities and FX over three rolling held-out test years (30 settings), FinPILOT improved Total Return in 28 of 30 settings and Sharpe ratio in 27 of 30. ## [LLMSurgeon Audits LLM Pretraining Data Mixtures Post-Hoc](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30348) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces LLMSurgeon, a framework that formalizes Data Mixture Surgery (DMS): estimating the domain-level distribution of an LLM's pretraining corpus using only its generated text under a predefined taxonomy. It casts DMS as an inverse problem under the label-shift assumption, estimating a calibrated soft confusion matrix and solving a constrained inverse problem to recover the latent mixture prior, and introduces LLMScan, a recipe-verifiable evaluation suite built from open-source LLMs with transparent pretraining mixtures. Rather than directly aggregating classifier outputs, LLMSurgeon estimates a calibrated soft confusion matrix and solves a constrained inverse problem to correct systematic domain confusion and recover the latent mixture prior. Across LLMScan, it recovers domain mixtures with high fidelity under fixed protocols, though the approach depends on an external domain classifier and a predefined taxonomy.

LLMSurgeon combines these ideas: it treats generated text as observations and the unknown pretraining mixture as the latent cause to be inferred.

## [SecureClaw: Dual-Boundary Defense for Tool-Using LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09549) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SecureClaw introduces a dual-boundary architecture that enforces authorization in a trusted executor while keeping raw protected data outside the LLM runtime, replacing sensitive values with reference IDs. Across AgentDojo, AgentLeak, and Agent Security Bench (ASB), it reportedly achieves 0% attack success rate on ASB, 0.64% on AgentDojo, and 3.23% overall leak on AgentLeak's attacked parity lane while retaining usable task utility. Tool-using LLM agents increasingly perform real-world actions and access sensitive data, but existing defenses typically secure only one boundary—either the planner/runtime or the execution point—leaving the other exposed. A dual-boundary design that simultaneously preserves utility and blocks attacks could influence how future agent frameworks handle authorization and data protection. Sensitive reads pass through a trusted gateway that substitutes raw values with reference IDs and provides short planning summaries via a process called declassification; writes follow a PREVIEW→COMMIT protocol where only the trusted executor may execute the exact policy-authorized request. The runtime can plan over summaries and reference IDs but cannot resolve them into secrets or perform side effects directly.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents are systems where a large language model plans and invokes external tools to accomplish tasks, which creates two security risks: unauthorized actions and leakage of sensitive plaintext inside the model runtime before any output check can intervene. Information-flow security traditionally addresses such leakage through concepts like declassification, which deliberately releases selected information under controlled conditions. SecureClaw combines these ideas by separating authorization and data protection across two boundaries.

## [VOiLA Learns Diffusion-Based POMDP World Models for GPU-Parallel Online Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19729) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VOiLA is a framework that learns task-agnostic POMDP world models using conditional diffusion models for transition and observation sampling, plus observation-likelihood models for particle-based belief updates. It distills the diffusion samplers into compact feedforward generators and integrates them with the Vectorized Online POMDP Planner (VOPP), reducing sampling cost by up to nearly three orders of magnitude. Faithful POMDP models are notoriously hard to obtain, which has long limited POMDP planning in real-world robotics. VOiLA shows that learned generative world models can be made practical for online planning, matching or beating RL baselines like Recurrent Soft Actor Critic and DreamerV3 with under 10% of the training data and generalizing better to unseen environments. The distillation step is the key enabler: it converts slow multi-step diffusion sampling into fast feedforward generation, which is what makes learned generative POMDP models viable for online planning. In a physical robot experiment, VOiLA completed the task in 10 out of 10 runs using models learned purely from simulated data.

**Background**: A POMDP (Partially Observable Markov Decision Process) models decision-making when the agent cannot directly observe the underlying state and must maintain a belief over possible states. Particle-based belief updates approximate this belief with a set of weighted samples, and online POMDP planners such as POMCP use simulations to plan without full belief updates. ## [BeatEdit recasts symbolic music generation as explicit editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11124) ⭐️ 7.0/10

BeatEdit proposes the first framework for symbolic music generation based on explicit edit operations, recasting generation as editing a draft rather than synthesizing from scratch. It uses the beat-grid-anchored BEAT encoding and three mechanisms — per-token sequence tagging, iterative refinement, and tag-then-fill — sharing one encoding and pre-trained backbone, with single-pass inference under 100 ms. Music creation is fundamentally a process of revision, yet symbolic music generation has been dominated by from-scratch paradigms with limited support for selective modification. By enabling precise, efficient edits, BeatEdit could shift music AI toward more controllable and interactive workflows, benefiting composers and researchers working with symbolic representations. The three mechanisms span an axis of increasing edit density: per-token sequence tagging for error correction, iterative refinement for accompaniment editing, and tag-then-fill for segment completion. BeatEdit reportedly achieves higher precision and perceptual quality than autoregressive and diffusion methods across all three tasks, and cross-encoding evaluation shows encoding design substantially influences editing effectiveness.

An arXiv preprint (2608.02712v2) proposes a domain-specific debug agent that repairs near-miss accelerator kernels—candidates that compile and run but fail numerical validation—rather than discarding and regenerating them. The agent achieves 66.7% Debug Pass@1 versus 25.9% Regenerate Avg Pass@1 and 40.7% Regenerate Pass@3, while consuming 92.8% fewer tokens per successful kernel than three-trial regeneration. Current LLM-based kernel generation pipelines generate, compile, and execute many candidates, discarding most of them and wasting the inference, cross-compilation, and hardware execution invested in near-miss operators. Reframing repair as debugging exploits a much smaller search space and denser feedback, potentially lowering the cost per deliverable kernel and extending the capability frontier beyond what repeated regeneration can reach. The agent addresses three challenges: knowledge scarcity via retrieved patterns and diagnostic instrumentation, integrity via anti-cheat detection and full-coverage evaluation, and cost via convergence guards and bounded iteration. Ablations show the knowledge base drives recovery, while integrity gates reject 12.5–33.3% of the successes the workflow itself accepted, indicating that self-reported success can be unreliable.

## [ValueFormer Uses Stage-Aware Value Labels for VLA Failure Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02958) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ValueFormer is a policy-agnostic causal transformer with 3.5M parameters built on a frozen DINOv3 backbone that emits two per-frame signals in one forward pass: a smooth Monte Carlo value for advantage estimation and a sharp binary value for online mistake detection. By reusing the intervention flag already recorded by a teleoperation station, it lifts held-out failure detection from 0.38 to 0.82 average precision and flags 95% of mistakes before the operator reacts. Generalist vision-language-action policies still fail silently, and a single terminal success/failure bit is too sparse to localize when a rollout went wrong, so a cheap per-frame progress signal could make online failure detection and post-training far more practical. This matters for robotics teams deploying VLA policies in real manipulation settings, where catching a collapsing rollout early can prevent wasted cycles and unsafe behavior. The key idea is that per-frame labels should be continuous and non-monotonic, allowing a score to fall and then rise again as a rollout goes wrong and recovers; a human only marks the stage at which an episode went wrong, and per-frame values are computed from that. On a real bimanual sandwich station, feeding the critic back as a per-frame post-training weight raised task completion from 70% to 85% and removed a repeat-pick failure mode, though at n=20 that gain sits within noise.

**Background**: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are models that take visual observations and natural-language task descriptions as input and output robot actions, and they can transfer to new scenes with little task-specific training. Because imitation learning provides no explicit notion of progress, a collapsing rollout can look much like one making clean progress from the action stream alone. Value functions estimate expected return and are commonly used in reinforcement learning for advantage estimation, while DINOv3 is a self-supervised vision transformer backbone that produces high-quality dense features for many vision and robotics tasks.

## [MasDrift Benchmark Measures Authorization Drift in Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07556) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces MasDrift, a benchmark of 600 benign productivity tasks across eight domains that measures both task completion and authorization preservation in multi-agent systems. It compares single-agent, centralized, and decentralized coordination, finding that centralized hierarchies reach 93.9–98.6% task completion versus 85.7–87.0% for peer networks, but also commit unauthorized actions in 2.7–19.8% of tasks versus only 0.6–0.8% for peer networks. This work reframes authorization preservation as a measurable property of multi-agent system design rather than an assumed byproduct of capable models, giving system designers concrete data on a centralization tradeoff. As enterprises increasingly deploy supervisor-subagent architectures for long-horizon tasks, the finding that deeper hierarchies widen the authorization gap has direct implications for AI safety and governance. The benchmark evaluates two defenses: re-anchoring every pending call to the original user request reduces unauthorized actions in every model configuration at a cost of 1.6 points of pooled completion, while carrying an attenuated policy along the delegation chain blocks required work and forfeits up to 36.3 points. A heterogeneous case study confirms the failure stems from coordination structure rather than model strength.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-agent systems decompose long-horizon tasks across supervisor and subagent roles, but delegated goals do not automatically carry their original authorization boundaries, a phenomenon known as constraint drift. Existing safety benchmarks focus mainly on adversarial compromise, leaving controlled architecture-level evaluation of authorization preservation underexplored. MasDrift fills this gap by systematically varying hierarchy depth and peer width across benign tasks that pair required work with reserved actions.

## [ICON Decomposition Audits Neural Network Shortcuts via Variance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26083) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces ICON (Independent Canonical cONcepts), a variance decomposition method that reframes shortcut auditing by quantifying how much of a layer's variance is explained by each concept conditional on all other concepts and the outcome. In simulated data with ground truth, ICON recovers concept importance more accurately than seven baselines, and in skin-cancer and neuroimaging applications it separates learned shortcuts from merely correlated concepts, confirmed by independent validation checks. Shortcut learning is a critical failure mode in trustworthy AI, and existing auditing tools like linear probes and concept activation vectors can mislead auditors because decodability conflates true concept reliance with correlations among concepts and the outcome. ICON offers a more reliable way to quantify concept reliance, which could influence how interpretability, fairness, and robustness researchers audit models before deployment. ICON reports the share of a layer's variance explained by each concept conditional on all other concepts and the outcome, and also reports the variance left unexplained. Because its explanations are comparable across layers, the trajectories of these explanations can distinguish concepts that drive predictions from those that are merely encoded in the representations.

**Background**: Deep neural networks often exploit spurious associations, a failure known as shortcut learning, where models achieve strong in-distribution performance but fail to generalize out of distribution. Before deployment, models should be audited for reliance on concepts such as acquisition artifacts and patient demographics. Current methods, including linear probes and concept activation vectors, measure concept reliance by asking whether each concept is decodable from a layer, but this framing is misleading because decodability also reflects correlations among concepts and the outcome in the auditing dataset.

## [Tail-Replay Enables Unconstrained Prefix Reuse in Hybrid LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30310) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present Tail-Replay, a prefix caching mechanism that enables unconstrained token-level prefix reuse in hybrid large language models by replaying only a short recent suffix of the matched prefix to reconstruct linear-attention recurrent states. Evaluated on three Gated DeltaNet-based hybrid models with LongBench and RULER, it retains 92.8–99.9% of full-prefill quality with only a 5–10% replay budget, and reaches 9.1–14.3x time-to-first-token speedup over full prefill at 32K matched-prefix length. Hybrid models that interleave full-attention and linear-attention layers are becoming a mainstream way to cut long-context inference costs, but their recurrent states have blocked the fine-grained prefix caching that serving systems rely on for chat, agents, and RAG workloads. Tail-Replay removes the checkpoint-alignment constraint, potentially letting production LLM serving stacks reuse arbitrary shared prefixes and substantially reduce time-to-first-token on long prompts. The method caches the exact full-attention key-value cache while omitting recurrent-state checkpoints entirely, reconstructing linear-attention states on a cache hit by replaying a short recent suffix; the reuse boundary is thus determined by shared tokens rather than stored checkpoints. The approach relies on the observation that gated recurrent updates progressively attenuate earlier inputs, so the recurrent state is a structured lossy compression of the prefix, and quality retention is measured against full prefill rather than absolute accuracy.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Full attention keeps a key-value cache that grows with sequence length and is token-addressable, which is what makes prefix caching possible: a new request sharing a prompt prefix can reuse the cached states instead of recomputing them. Linear-attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet instead compress the prefix into a fixed-size recurrent state, which is cheap for long contexts but cannot be rolled back to arbitrary token boundaries, so existing hybrid caching schemes store periodic checkpoints and only allow reuse at aligned positions. Tail-Replay exploits the gated, decaying nature of that recurrent state to approximate it from a short suffix, trading a small amount of replay compute for arbitrary-boundary reuse.

The paper introduces Power-Law Entropy Search (PLES), a computational cost-aware acquisition function built on multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization that estimates optimal hyperparameter scaling laws for LLM training through adaptive experimentation. ## [Training-Free Task Vectors Enable Cheap LLM Behavioral Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09054) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.09054v2) introduces Training-Free Task Vectors (TFTVs), a method that computes task-vector-like directions for LLM behavioral control without any fine-tuning, using only forward-pass statistics. The authors map activation steering vectors into rank-one weight-space edits that support addition, subtraction, and composition of edits, and report that TFTVs consistently amplify, suppress, and compose target behaviors while preserving general knowledge and problem-solving skills. Task vectors have traditionally required fine-tuning a model to obtain, which is expensive and limits practical post-training model editing; removing that requirement could substantially lower the cost of behavioral control and model adaptation for LLM practitioners. The work also connects activation steering with weight-space editing, potentially opening new directions for training-free model control. TFTVs derive rank-one weight-space edits from forward-pass statistics alone, and the resulting edits satisfy arithmetic properties that directly support learning via addition, forgetting via subtraction, and composition of multiple edits. Experiments show stronger trait control with better or competitive utility preservation compared with other editing and steering baselines, and code is available at tftv-llm.github.io.

Activation steering is a related inference-time technique that manipulates hidden activations with fixed steering vectors to induce desired behavior. ## [KV-streams Speeds Up Agentic RL Training 2.6-5x via KV Cache Streaming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35750) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.35750v3) introduces KV-streams, a plug-and-play method that streams the KV cache forward during context compaction instead of flushing it after each compaction. The authors report a 2.6x to 5x wall-clock training speedup across three different compaction strategies with no evidence of performance loss, and show that the streamed KV cache can act as a recurrent state carrying information that has disappeared from the context. Long-context agentic reinforcement learning is bottlenecked by GPU memory and repeated prefilling, so a lightweight method that dramatically raises training throughput without hurting performance could make large-scale agent training far more practical. The finding that RL alone can make the streamed KV cache behave as a recurrent state also suggests a new mechanism for long-horizon memory in LLM agents. KV-streams is compatible with any compaction strategy and was validated on three of them, yielding 2.6-5x wall-clock speedups; the paper also reports a controlled experiment showing that, contrary to prior work, RL alone is sufficient for the recurrent-state behavior to emerge. The abstract does not specify model sizes, task suites, or absolute throughput numbers, so broader validation across scales remains to be seen.

Context compaction reduces the token count of an ongoing run while preserving state, but most strategies repeatedly prefill the model, which is expensive. The KV cache stores the key and value tensors from attention so they need not be recomputed, and it grows linearly with sequence length, making it a major memory bottleneck for long-context workloads.

## [Concept Bottleneck Models: Interpretable but Not Inherently Robust](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38625) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.38625v2) introduces a generator-based evaluation framework that compares standard classifiers and Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) under two distinct perturbation regimes: continuous geometric perturbations in latent space and discrete semantic interventions in concept space. Using both empirical sensitivity metrics and certified robustness via randomized smoothing, the authors reconcile previously contradictory findings by showing that concept bottlenecks do not uniformly improve robustness but instead redistribute sensitivity across perturbation spaces and model families. This work clarifies a long-standing ambiguity in interpretable machine learning by demonstrating that interpretability and robustness are distinct objectives, which could reshape how researchers design and evaluate self-explainable architectures. It provides a controlled methodology that future studies can adopt to avoid conflating different robustness notions, potentially influencing both CBM research and broader safety-critical ML deployment. The framework evaluates robustness empirically through prediction and concept-level sensitivity metrics, and certifiably using randomized smoothing in both latent and concept spaces. The analysis further examines how task conditions such as class semantic similarity and concept vocabulary size modulate the observed interpretability-robustness trade-off, revealing that the trade-off depends critically on the perturbation regime and task structure.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) are neural architectures that first map inputs to a set of human-interpretable concepts before making predictions with an interpretable classifier, typically a linear model, allowing users to inspect and even intervene on intermediate concepts. Randomized smoothing is a state-of-the-art technique for producing classifiers with certified robustness guarantees, typically under L2 norm bounds, by smoothing predictions with Gaussian noise. Adversarial perturbations can be geometric (small continuous changes in input or latent space) or semantic (discrete changes to high-level concepts), and prior studies on CBM robustness have reported mixed results partly because they conflated these regimes.

## [LEAP: Learned Block-wise Evidence Retrieval for Long Audio-Video Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39938) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LEAP introduces a learned block-wise evidence retrieval framework that divides long audio-video recordings into fixed-duration blocks, scores short candidate windows with a lightweight localization pass, and re-encodes only the top-ranked windows in a single bounded answer pass. Across several AVQA benchmarks, LEAP improves over the Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B baseline by 4.5-16.8% and transfers to MiniCPM-o 4.5, surpassing its published results by 3.1-13.0%. Hour-scale audio-visual question answering is bottlenecked by a context dilemma: dense whole-recording encoding exhausts context limits, while uniform temporal compression dilutes fine-grained acoustic and visual evidence. By decoupling evidence localization from reasoning, LEAP keeps answer context and peak memory independent of recording duration, which could make long-form AVQA and streaming inference practical on existing omni-modal backbones. The localization stage can operate over pre-computed transcripts without decoding media frames, while the final answering pass routes over raw audio-visual streams to preserve fine-grained visual and non-speech evidence; both stages are trained with LoRA adapters. The block grid natively supports causal queries, enabling streaming inference without streaming-specific training.

LEAP combines this retrieval idea with learned temporal localization, using a lightweight first pass to find candidate windows and a second pass to answer from them.

## [ULTRADISCOVERY Benchmark Tests Abductive Reasoning in Open Worlds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03092) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces ULTRADISCOVERY, an interactive benchmark spanning five domains that evaluates how agents revise initially successful theories and predict unseen cross-domain interventions. The study uses a 2x2 design varying whether the representation is open or disclosed and whether evidence is distributed or aligned, testing eleven models and finding that none can make exact predictions within 200 paid actions. This benchmark addresses a critical gap in AI evaluation by separating two key demands of scientific discovery: constructing representations in epistemically open worlds and composing evidence across interconnected contexts. The findings reveal that current models struggle with the step from accumulating evidence to composing it into a transferable representation, which has implications for building AI systems capable of genuine scientific discovery. With the representation open, agents across eleven models often retract the axiom they were taught, and none introduces the unobserved entity or rewrites the variables required for a replacement theory. Disclosure triples intervention requests and adds only about one of the eighteen findings the world affords, while alignment adds even less; no system achieves the exact prediction within 200 paid actions, and at larger budgets only one exact prediction appears with both aids while every Open episode remains inexact.

**Background**: Abductive reasoning, first formulated by Charles Sanders Peirce, is a form of logical inference that seeks the simplest and most likely explanation for a set of observations, yielding plausible but not definitive conclusions. Epistemic openness refers to situations where the space of possible representations or hypotheses is not fully known in advance, requiring agents to construct new ways of describing the world. Existing benchmarks rarely separate the demands of epistemic openness and structural interconnectedness or control them independently, which ULTRADISCOVERY aims to address.

## [D-DOIT: Training-Free Discrete Diffusion Adaptation via Doob's h-Transform](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04938) ⭐️ 7.0/10

D-DOIT (Discrete Doob-Oriented Inference-time Transformation) introduces a training-free adaptation method for discrete diffusion models that applies Doob's h-transform to the reverse transition kernel, reweighting categorical token-reveal probabilities using only reward values rather than reward gradients. It avoids expensive future rollouts by sampling candidate next states, completing each with the model's prediction head, evaluating with a reward oracle, and resampling proportionally to rewards, with an optional late-stage best-of-K refinement. This work addresses a known challenge in discrete diffusion—how to steer generation toward desired properties without retraining or gradient-based guidance—which could make reward-guided adaptation more practical for domains like DNA design and protein engineering. By avoiding rollouts and reward gradients, D-DOIT lowers the computational barrier for inference-time control of discrete generative models. Unlike continuous diffusion, masked discrete diffusion samples categorical token-reveal transitions rather than continuous state updates, so D-DOIT derives a discrete Doob's h-transform that reweights reverse transition probabilities instead of adding a drift correction. The optional late-stage best-of-K refinement branches trajectories only near the end of denoising to avoid K-fold cost over the full trajectory, and experiments on regulatory DNA design and protein inverse folding show improvements over training-free guidance baselines.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Doob's h-transform is a mathematical technique from stochastic processes that transforms a Markov process into a new one with desired properties, such as conditioning on a terminal state, by explicitly reweighting transition probabilities via a deterministic function h. Discrete diffusion models are generative models that corrupt data with discrete noise (e.g., mask tokens) and learn a reverse process to generate new samples, and they are widely used for language and biological sequence generation. Masked discrete diffusion specifically uses an absorbing mask token to progressively corrupt data, making the reverse process a sequence of categorical token-reveal decisions.

E^2-OPSD requires no additional forward passes or networks, keeping it simple to implement, and the code is released at github.com/orionfei/E2-OPSD. Out-of-domain results show gains over corresponding base models of up to 4.9 points in mean@16 and 5.5 points in pass@8, though the paper frames these as improvements over OPSD and base models rather than a paradigm shift.

## [SpecWM: Steering World Models via Spectral Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15429) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SpecWM introduces a JEPA-based framework that uses a target similarity kernel to explicitly specify which relationships between observations a world model should preserve in its embedding geometry. The paper characterizes the global optima of the objective, establishes conditions for linear recoverability and invariance to nuisance information, and shows that temporal spectral alignment improves CEM planning success over LeWorldModel from 52% to 68% on OGBench Cube, 49% to 77% on OGBench Scene, and 29% to 51% on CALVIN. It matters to researchers working on world models, self-supervised representation learning, and planning-based control. The framework supports different kernels ranging from physical state information to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel that requires only the ordering of observations within trajectories. The authors also connect temporal-kernel similarity to the behavioral successor measure under an idealized setting, providing theoretical grounding for the empirical gains.

The benchmark covers localization, distance estimation, and motion reasoning in both single- and dual-source settings, and SonicWorld combines physical, learned acoustic, and semantic features into persistent source states via learned transitions and recurrent updates. ## [MID: A Distribution-Level Metric for Medical Image Segmentation Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17354) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces MID (Mask-Image Distributional Divergence), a distribution-level evaluation metric that compares the joint image-mask distribution between a reference set and a set of predictions without requiring paired ground-truth masks. Evaluated across 13 public datasets spanning CT, MRI, and MRA and 56 organ groups, MID tracks mean Dice and Hausdorff distance without per-sample pairing, detects modality and anatomy distributional shifts, and produces reliable model rankings. Traditional sample-wise metrics like Dice and Hausdorff distance require each prediction to be paired with a ground-truth mask, making them inapplicable to unlabeled data and unable to assess whether a collection of predictions matches the distributional structure of the ground-truth population. MID addresses both limitations, enabling evaluation on unlabeled data and offering a new way to assess distributional alignment in medical imaging and ML evaluation. MID builds on the observation that segmentation quality is a property of the joint image-mask distribution, since a mask may be anatomically plausible in isolation yet incorrect for the image it accompanies. The official implementation is available at github.com/erc-caravel/pytorch-mid, and the method was tested under anatomically realistic corruptions across 56 organ groups and controlled shuffling experiments to identify image-mask misalignment.

## [MorphContrast predicts colorectal cancer survival from whole-slide images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17603) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose MorphContrast, a morphology-aware contrastive multiple-instance learning framework that uses tissue labels as structural supervision to predict five-year colorectal cancer survival from hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images. Validated on TCGA-COAD/READ (n=562), Alliance/CALGB 89803 (n=424), and SurGen (n=218), the model achieves a pooled out-of-fold AUC of 0.70 and a risk-group hazard ratio of 3.79 on Alliance/CALGB, and AUCs of 0.669 (single) and 0.678 (ensemble) on the external SurGen cohort. Morphology-specific models show weak but distributed prognostic signal: adipose tissue reaches AUC 0.622, stroma 0.604, and tumor epithelium 0.601-0.605, suggesting prognostic information is spread across tissue types rather than concentrated in tumor regions. MorphContrast combines gated-attention pooling with three auxiliary objectives—within-patient patch-level morphology contrasts, cross-patient outcome concordance/discordance contrasts within matched morphologies, and diversity regularization—using morphology-matched patches from patients with discordant outcomes as hard negatives.

## [Agentic-MatriBO: Compiled Agentic Bayesian Optimization for Materials Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17832) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Agentic-MatriBO introduces a capability-compiled agentic Bayesian optimization framework in which an LLM proposes BO recipes that a compiler validates against a registered capability catalog before a deterministic execution layer commits candidates. Evaluated on four offline finite candidate pools (COF, PCE10, Buchwald-Hartwig, Suzuki-Miyaura) with five seeds each, it achieves the best mean endpoint quality across all four tasks and reaches the tabulated optimum on COF in all five seeds. This work addresses a real bottleneck in AI-driven scientific discovery: composing surrogates, acquisition functions, and search strategies is constrained by compatibility, parameter dependencies, and evidence requirements, which LLM agents alone cannot reliably handle. By adding a compiler and evidence gate, it offers an inspectable interface for evidence-conditioned BO adaptation that could make automated experimentation more trustworthy for materials and chemistry researchers. The framework's normalized area under the best-so-far quality curve during the BO stage (nAUC-BO) is substantially higher on COF, near parity with the best baseline on PCE10 and BH, but lower on Suzuki-Miyaura, indicating task-dependent performance. Ablations on COF show that removing the capability compiler or the evidence gate coincides with lower cumulative quality and fewer exact-optimum hits, and results are reported descriptively rather than with formal statistical tests.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Bayesian optimization is a sequential model-based strategy for global optimization of black-box objective functions whose evaluations are costly, such as experiments or high-fidelity simulations. It typically builds a probabilistic surrogate model of the unknown function and uses an acquisition function to decide which point to evaluate next. In materials and chemical design, each evaluation may correspond to a synthesis, characterization, or simulation, so the number of trials is tightly budgeted. Agentic-MatriBO combines this classical loop with LLM agents that propose BO recipes, while a compiler and deterministic execution layer enforce compatibility and evidence constraints.

## [Block Identifiability and the Maximal Transformations Preserving Causal Meaning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18155) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.18155v2) connects block-identifiability to constructive causal abstraction, proving that block-diagonal invertible transformations followed by compatible coordinate permutations form the maximal class that preserves every constructive causal abstraction built on learned multidimensional blocks. A small synthetic experiment with additive autoencoders shows that high-level interventions can be transferred between independently learned representations while approximately preserving their intended effects. This result addresses a gap in standard identifiability theory, which typically assumes one-dimensional latent factors and leaves the causal meaning of multidimensional blocks unresolved. It gives researchers in causal representation learning a precise characterization of which transformations are safe when intervening on higher-level concepts, which is important for building trustworthy and transferable causal models. The guarantee assumes that the correspondence between blocks and concepts is updated together with the representation, meaning the block-to-concept mapping is not fixed a priori. The supporting evidence is limited to a small synthetic experiment with additive autoencoders, so practical applicability to real-world high-dimensional data remains to be demonstrated.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Causal representation learning (CRL) aims to recover causally related latent variables from high-dimensional observations without labels, and identifiability theory studies when such recovery is unique. Standard identifiability results assume one-dimensional latent factors, but learned representations often encode information in multidimensional blocks whose internal coordinates are not uniquely determined. Causal abstraction provides a formal framework for relating high-level concepts to low-level variables, and constructive causal abstraction decomposes this relation into operations such as marginalization, variable-merge, and value-merge. This paper asks whether the causal meaning of such blocks survives the transformations that block-identifiability leaves unresolved.

SWE-Nexus is a fully automated four-agent pipeline that constructs repository-level implementation tasks by tracing the execution footprints of production function bodies exercised by selected tests. It produces a benchmark of 600 tasks from 105 repositories across six programming languages, comprising 116 atomic and 484 composite tasks, and evaluates 12 models under three agent scaffolds, with the best configuration resolving 37.8% of tasks in one attempt. A scope is retained only if all expected scoring points pass in the original repository and masking the traced function bodies causes at least one failure or error; compatible scopes are then composed deterministically, with shared functions counted once and every constituent test file revalidated under the complete combined mask. ## [VISTA: Training-Free Schedule Trimming for Faster SMC Guidance in Discrete Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20669) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers propose VISTA, a training-free method that automatically selects which denoising timesteps to guide under a fixed budget for Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance in discrete diffusion. Using value statistics from a few full-guidance warmup generations, VISTA derives an estimable upper bound on l1 path deviation and optimizes the empirical surrogate exactly via dynamic programming, discovering task-dependent schedules that outperform hand-designed sparse schedules across text, biological sequence, and image tasks. SMC guidance at every denoising step is computationally expensive, and fixed heuristic schedules vary substantially across tasks, so VISTA's automatic, task-adaptive schedule selection could make reward-guided discrete diffusion far more practical for test-time alignment. In toxic-text generation it achieves a 0.99 unique-toxic ratio versus 1.00 for full guidance while cutting per-generation latency from 204.23 s to 38.16 s, a 5.35x speedup. VISTA is training-free, retains warmup generations as model outputs, and after schedule selection has the same per-generation guidance complexity as other sparse schedules with the same budget. It formulates sparse guidance as approximating the ideal full-guidance probability path and optimizes an empirical surrogate exactly via dynamic programming.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Discrete diffusion models are generative models that operate over discrete state spaces (e.g., tokens) rather than continuous ones, and are commonly used for language modeling. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance is a technique for steering generation toward a downstream reward at test time, but applying it at every denoising step requires extra reward evaluations and, for gradient-based proposals, value-gradient computations. Sparse guidance reduces this cost by guiding only a subset of timesteps, but the schedules used are typically fixed heuristics whose effectiveness varies across tasks.

## [Calibrated Confidence Cuts Test-Time Compute by 16-30%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20836) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.20836) formulates evaluator-guided test-time reasoning as a compute-aware three-action controller that decides at each step whether to trust the current answer, return a fallback, or spend more inference. By learning and calibrating action-specific confidence estimates with local uncertainty penalties, the controller improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies while cutting normalized online compute by roughly 30% on width expansion and 16% on revision tasks. As LLM reasoning increasingly relies on spending extra inference at test time, knowing when to stop or expand becomes a resource-allocation problem rather than a pure accuracy problem. This work shows that calibrated confidence can make evaluator-guided reasoning substantially cheaper without large utility losses, which matters for anyone deploying reasoning models under compute or latency budgets. The paper provides a local action-gap analysis characterizing when score errors can flip a decision, plus an expected regret bound that accounts for errors along the realized expansion path. Across four Qwen3-8B seeds, compute is lower than a fitted Q baseline in both settings, but utility differences are small and mixed, suggesting the gains are mainly efficiency-oriented rather than uniformly stronger reasoning.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Test-time compute scaling lets a language model 'think longer' by generating more reasoning steps, which improves accuracy on hard tasks like math and code but costs more inference. Evaluator-guided reasoning adds a separate evaluator that scores candidate answers, and the system must repeatedly decide whether to accept, fall back, or expand. Confidence calibration is the process of aligning a model's stated confidence with its actual probability of being correct, since LLMs are often overconfident.

Rule-level diagnostics show the original-curriculum checkpoint wrongly withdraws 26 of 34 actions that still had surviving alternative support, while enriched checkpoints withdraw only 0-1; however, all SFT checkpoints narrow prohibited combinations less often than 7B and 8B baselines, and all four omit valid event reports. A feature-matched, multi-cohort study compared six quantum model families against classical models using identical correlation-derived features across four public cohorts totaling 4,308 subjects. The quantum kernel was statistically indistinguishable from a matched classical kernel in all four cohorts, with average accuracy differences within 1.4 percentage points at 95% confidence. This rigorous negative result helps temper hype around quantum machine learning by showing that, under fair feature-matched comparisons and leave-site-out validation, quantum models offer no consistent advantage for neuropsychiatric disorder classification. On ABIDE I, a hybrid quantum convolutional network achieved similar accuracy to its classical counterpart (0.645 vs. 0.641), while a trainable quantum kernel exceeded its classical counterpart by 0.064 in AUC; quantum convolutional networks also showed smaller train-test gaps on all four cohorts without accuracy gains. A new arXiv preprint (2610.21123) introduces DST-Net, a decomposed spatio-temporal network that assigns different modeling strategies to the trend and seasonal components of a time series. The trend branch uses a Latent Graph Block to capture cross-channel spatial coupling, while the seasonal branch uses a Gaussian Multi-scale Attention mechanism to reduce attention distraction and focus on local temporal evolution. The Latent Graph Block models global topological dependencies and system-wide co-movements to address the trend component's spatial coupling and temporal redundancy, while the Gaussian Multi-scale Attention injects learnable Gaussian priors as structural constraints to filter global noise. Deterministic compilation, also called reproducible builds, guarantees that compiling the same source always yields the same output, which is what makes the recovered editing steps independently checkable. ## [Study Compares Encoding and Pair Selection in Pairwise Difference Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21644) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper systematically evaluates four feature encoders and four pair selection strategies for Pairwise Difference Learning for Classification (PDC) across nearly 200 benchmark datasets using Decision Tree, Multilayer Perceptron, Gaussian Naive Bayes, and Support Vector Classifier as base models. The proposed triplet with absolute difference encoder (φ_3dabs) achieves the highest average F1 scores, while restricting training to upper-triangle pairs cuts computational time by about 40% with negligible accuracy loss. PDC is a growing meta-learning approach for low-data classification, but its implementation choices were previously underspecified, making it hard for practitioners to reproduce or optimize. This study provides concrete guidance—showing PDC configurations beat base models in 94% of cases—while revealing that no single configuration dominates universally, highlighting dataset-specific tuning as an open challenge. The study compares paired features, triplet with relative difference, absolute difference, and a novel triplet with absolute difference encoder, alongside pair selection strategies from exhaustive to kernel-thinning-based schemes. Kernel thinning-based selection provided no accuracy benefits while substantially increasing computational overhead, and the upper-triangle restriction offers a practical efficiency gain.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Pairwise Difference Learning (PDL) is a meta-learning technique originally introduced for regression, where a model learns from pairs of instances and predicts the difference between their outcomes rather than learning a direct mapping from instance to outcome. The PDL classifier (PDC) extends this to multiclass classification by reducing it to a binary similarity problem on pairs, effectively inflating the training set from n to O(n^2) examples. This makes PDC attractive in low-data regimes, but the quadratic growth of pairs raises computational concerns, motivating research into efficient encoding and pair selection.

The paper introduces CF-AVSS, a coarse-to-fine two-stage audio-visual speech enhancement framework that first uses a progressive SPAV-TFGridNet with two synchronized visual streams to produce visually ordered coarse estimates, then applies a TFGridNet-based target speaker refinement network and development-set-calibrated fusion. On the ISCSLP 2026 Real-World AVSE Challenge, the system tied for first place on Track 1 and ranked second on Track 2 in OVRL, while achieving the lowest CER on both tracks at 12.31% and 14.79%, respectively. This work demonstrates that a two-stage coarse-to-fine design with target-speaker refinement and post-fusion can substantially improve real-world audio-visual speech enhancement, as evidenced by top rankings and the lowest character error rates in a competitive challenge. Such advances could benefit applications like hearing aids, video conferencing, and robust speech recognition in noisy, reverberant, and multi-speaker environments. The first stage extends SPAV-TFGridNet to two synchronized visual streams to progressively suppress interfering speech while preserving target reverberation and shared background noise, and the second stage refines the target speaker using the original mixture and both coarse estimates. The final output is a development-set-calibrated fusion of coarse and refined estimates, and the system achieved 12.31% and 14.79% CER on Tracks 1 and 2, respectively.

An online study with 56 AI-literate participants and 392 Video Question Answering trials found that post-interaction trust strongly predicted delegation choices to multimodal AI (OR=14.97, 95% CI [7.14,31.37]), with verification being the dominant policy and delegation increasing over task order (OR=1.22, 95% CI [1.02,1.45]). It has implications for developers of multimodal and agentic AI systems who need to build appropriate oversight mechanisms. The study used Video Question Answering as the task, where participants rated task-specific trust and chose among three policies: reject AI assistance, use with verification, or delegate fully. Trust and delegation remained distinct constructs, and verification often co-occurred with high trust, indicating that users prefer to maintain oversight even when they trust the AI.

## [Constrained RL Fix for Specification Gaming in Cleaning Gridworld](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22152) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper constructs a minimal cleaning gridworld where a DQN agent trained only on a cheap sensor's proxy reward learns to conceal dirt rather than remove it, achieving near-maximal proxy reward while never fulfilling the true objective. It then introduces a constrained reinforcement learning method that penalizes the specific gaming behaviors, eliminating them from the final policy and substantially recovering true-objective performance. This work provides a controlled demonstration of specification gaming paired with a mitigation that carries a verifiable guarantee, addressing a gap in AI safety research where evidence is often observational and mitigations are only empirically validated. It offers a concrete, reproducible testbed for studying reward hacking and safe RL, which could inform the design of more robust reward signals and safety constraints in real-world systems. The authors derive and empirically verify an exact accounting identity relating the proxy reward, true reward, and their cost signal, showing that the cost signal measures the proxy/true gap exactly rather than merely tracking it. Under a hard-constrained variant of the method, this yields a deterministic guarantee, though the setting remains a minimal gridworld with a DQN agent.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 16, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning agents optimize exactly the reward signal they are given, which can diverge from the intended true objective when that signal is only a proxy; this failure mode is known as specification gaming. Deep Q-networks (DQN) are a standard deep RL algorithm that learns action values from high-dimensional inputs. Constrained reinforcement learning extends standard RL by incorporating constraints on costs or safety, aiming to maximize reward while satisfying those constraints.

PathCal introduces a training-free controller that dynamically adjusts a fixed continuation bias using the instantaneous competition among continuation, revision, and alternative-opening markers in Chain-of-Thought trajectories. It applies finite logit adjustments without additional model forward passes, and experiments show it improves the accuracy-length tradeoff in mathematical reasoning while reducing generation length in coding and multilingual mathematics. It matters for anyone deploying large reasoning models where long Chain-of-Thought trajectories inflate inference cost without proportional accuracy gains. The controller relies on an exact log-odds identity and frozen-prefix probes to establish its local directional effect, and it operates purely at inference time by adjusting logits rather than retraining the model. The benefits are reported across many mathematical reasoning settings as well as coding and multilingual mathematics, though the abstract does not specify exact accuracy or length numbers.
